News.title: Wildfire spotted from space as helicopter brought in to tackle blaze
News.content:
Satellite images have captured plumes of smoke and the damage caused by a wildfire in north Wales.

Data gathered by BBC Verify suggests an estimated 951 hectares (2,350 acres) of the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd have been devastated by a wildfire that broke out earlier this month.

Nasa's satellite-based fire monitoring system has also detected heat signatures from four areas of Wales where wildfires have recently occurred.

It is also showing heat sources at Blaenavon in Torfaen, Presteigne in Powys, and Pentre Halkyn in Flintshire.

News.title: King's Tardis entrance as Commonwealth Games begin
News.content:
One of the louder cheers came for the Falklands Islands â in the news recently following Argentina's victory over England in the football World Cup semi-finals â and another followed when the Samoa team emerged and performed a haka in front of the dignitaries in the Royal Box.

But nothing compared to the noise which greeted the arrival of the Scotland team, who entered the arena last in their white shirts and kilts and lifted many in the capacity crowd from their seats.

A large Loch Ness Monster representation then emerged, before, backed by bagpipers and drummers, a rousing rendition of Flower of Scotland followed.

The next section of the evening featured theatrical performances â a show billed as "a love letter to Glasgow and the Commonwealth".

It began with a performance by Scottish folk and country singer Nathan Evans and a dance under a replica of Glasgow Central Station's iconic clock.

The saying "Meet me under the clock" is famous in these parts.

Singer Callum Beattie's rendition of Baccara's Yes Sir, I Can Boogie â the 1970s disco tune recently adopted as Scotland's unofficial anthem - had the Scottish athletes dancing in their seats.

Held indoors in front of about 10,000 people, this was a more intimate ceremony than the last time Glasgow hosted the Commonwealth Games, when a 40,000-strong crowd witnessed the opening of the Games in 2014 at Celtic Park.

There was a point, after the Australian state of Victoria withdrew as hosts in 2023, when some thought these Games would not happen. Glasgow stepped in at short notice to ensure otherwise.

There are eight fewer sports involved compared to 2014, given the short build-up, and venues from 12 years ago have been repurposed.

But Commonwealth Sport president Donald Rukare, wearing a tartan kilt in the colours of his home country Uganda, said this edition has been made possible by the "extraordinary legacy of 2014 and by a city that once again welcomes us with warm hearts and open arms".

News.title: Burnham pauses plan to release some prisoners early from September
News.content:
Andy Burnham has announced he is pausing a scheme which would have seen thousands of prisoners in England and Wales eligible to be released early.

It came after criticism of the scheme from survivors and victims' families, including the widow of PC Andrew Harper who described the possibility of his killers' early release as "deplorable".

The Sentencing Act, which was due to come into effect in September, would have seen some offenders let out at varying stages in a bid to ease prison overcrowding.

The new Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the pause aimed to "give victims and survivors certainty" and the government wanted to make sure it got "the implementation of this policy right".

He added a review would also look at the information given to survivors and victims' families as part of the early release process.

Burnham earlier said: "No prisoners will be let out under this policy until we have conducted an urgent review and done everything we can to minimise risk to the public."

He added: "Where changes are needed, we will not hesitate to make them."

Under the act, some offenders would have been let out after serving a third of their sentence, rather than half.

The rest of their sentence would be spent in the community, where they would be monitored and could be returned to prison if they offended again.

More serious offenders would have been released after serving half of their sentence, rather than two-thirds.

The policy was brought in to ease overcrowding in the prison system but has been criticised by opposition parties, as well as victims and their families.

The scheme would have seen around 700 prisoners released in early September, the BBC understands.

The decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added to the scheme.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie, called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

His mother, meanwhile, said her son had not been given "proper justice" and "every victim will be feeling the same" about the early prison release scheme.

Thousands of letters had been sent to victims in recent weeks, warning them that the early release scheme was coming in September.

Norris, who voted in support of the Sentencing Act under Starmer's government, later said the decision to pause was made after "listening to victims" and he hoped to provide them "certainty as soon as we can".

He said: "The prime minister and I have heard from victims and survivors and from people across the country about their concerns about the implementation of some very important elements of the Sentencing Act."

One element the government needed to get right was the information provided to victims before prisoners were released, Norris added.

Norris refused to be drawn on why he did not raise concerns when the Sentencing Act was first introduced but said Burnham was "quite right" to review the scheme.

Jade Belgrove, a survivor of sexual assault who has been campaigning against the early release scheme, said it was "such a relief that we've been heard".

She told BBC News that when she received a letter informing her that her attacker might be released early "it was horrific".

Belgrove said it even led her to question whether reporting the assault in the first place was worth it.

News.title: UK complacent about war threat, warns BAE boss
News.content:
The UK has been too complacent about the risk of foreign attack, the boss of Europe's biggest defence contractor BAE Systems has warned.

Dr Charles Woodburn told the BBC in an exclusive interview that the level of threat was the highest he'd seen in his lifetime.

He welcomed the recent boost to defence spending but said much more would be needed to hit the government's commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.

He also warned we were not far from the use of autonomous lethal weapons by countries that may not follow the UK's policy of maintaining human control.

In a rare interview, Woodburn told the BBC the reality of modern warfare had "changed quite profoundly" and that UK defence spending had to change with it.

He said Russia and Ukraine had become "incredibly adept" at using autonomy in the form of drones and counter drones.

"It's something that we now have to really understand and make sure that we're able to provide the capabilities that can counter that and deter aggression," he said.

Viktoria Terekhova shipped virtually her entire summer collection of children's clothes last week to the giant warehouse of online retailer Wildberries at Elektrostal, east of Moscow.

Within a couple of days, it was destroyed in a Ukrainian drone strike.

Fashion designer Terekhova says she lost 12,000 ⁠items, amounting to about 45% of her company's total inventory, and another 4,000 items in attacks on Wildberries hubs in southern Russia.

Eight Wildberries warehouses accounting for more than 10% of the company's storage capacity have been attacked since July 18 in a wave of strikes against Russia's leading online retail company.

They appear to be part of a wider Ukrainian campaign to make ordinary Russians feel the impact of a war ⁠which has raged on Ukrainian territory for more than four years.

open image in gallery Oleg Kondratyev, co-founder of the clothing brand Airbase, which suffered significant losses after warehouses of Russian online retailer Wildberries were damaged in Ukrainian attacks in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, ( Reuters )

Ukrainian ⁠President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said this week Kyiv was "bringing the war back home to Russia", which continues to pound Ukrainian cities. Moscow accuses Ukraine of terrorism and attempts to destabilise Russia.

The consequences are severe for thousands of ⁠Russian small businesses that use Wildberries as their main online marketplace. Terekhova says her company, Fareal Kids, makes up to 70% ​of its ⁠sales through the site.

"Simply losing inventory worth ‌10 million roubles ($128,000) has much larger economic consequences because we cannot meet our existing obligations and plans. We have no way of settling them," she told Reuters.

"On top of that, the summer collection was produced using borrowed funds. It was ‌supposed to cover the remaining payments we still owed, as well as help ‌finance the next collection."

open image in gallery Smoke billows from the burning Wildberries warehouses following a Ukrainian drone attack, according to local authorities, in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, in Saint Petersburg, Russia July 24, 2026. ( Reuters )

Oleg Kondratyev, co-founder of the clothing brand Airbase that manufactures mostly women's tracksuits, said he had lost about 5 million roubles of stock in the warehouse attacks, several of which caused massive fires.

That has placed him in a dire financial position, he said.

"For ⁠today, we cannot pay our loans because sales through Wildberries have stopped. Tax payments are not due yet, but they will be soon, and most likely we will not be able to pay those either," Kondratyev told Reuters in the city of Kazan, where he is based.

"I am hoping for payment deferrals from either the government or the banks. If that does not happen, I could potentially become the next bankrupt business owner."

Kondratyev said he would "take legal action all the way to the highest court" to recover his losses from Wildberries.

However, the company states in its terms of business that it is exempt ‌from liability in "force majeure" circumstances. It specifically lists drone strikes as one such scenario.

Reuters has requested comment ​from the company on how it will handle demands for compensation or what other help it may offer ‌to sellers.

open image in gallery Remains of the Wildberries warehouse that burned down after a recent Ukrainian drone attack in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, in the city of Elektrostal in the Moscow region, Russia July 23, 2026 ( Reuters )

Terekhova, the children's clothes maker, said the ⁠warehouse attacks were part of a long chain of blows to her business, including a January increase in ⁠VAT and a hike in Wildberries' commission at the start of July.

She plans to keep going by developing her website, storing goods in her own warehouses ‌and shifting towards a model of delivering ​direct to customers instead of through intermediaries.

"This has been an ‌expensive lesson, like going through an incredibly costly training programme," ​she said.

"In the future it should help us because now we know from firsthand experience what we will never do again." (

The UK Government is being urged to give the controversial Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gas projects the green light as part of what could be a “powerful reset” for the sector from Andy Burnham’s new government.

David Whitehouse, the chief executive of industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) insisted there is an “overwhelming” case for both to go ahead – despite the objections of environmentalists.

He spoke out on the issue as reports claimed that the UK Government could approve them as early as August.

Such a move could be part of what Mr Whitehouse described as a “powerful reset for the sector that shows that the Burnham Government is supporting British industry”.

open image in gallery Industry body Offshore Energies UK wants to see Andy Burnham’s government back domestic oil and gas production – saying this will cut the UK’s reliance on imported fuels. (Doug Peters/PA)

The OEUK chief executive told the Press Association: “What would be really significant, and what we look for now, is for this UK Government to say while we use oil and gas we back our own production, that is what we want to hear.

“That would be significant, and what would flow from that I believe is positive decisions about Jackdaw and Rosebank.”

Speaking about those two projects – both of which lie in Scottish waters – Mr Whitehouse declared: “The case to support them is overwhelming, both from an environmental perspective, but also the wider social impacts of the fact that they will support jobs and value in the economy.”

Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank are due to run until August 10 and August 17 respectively, with the Offshore Petroleum Regulator for Environment and Decommissioning (Opred) due to make a recommendation to the UK Government after that.

If the decision is in their favour, work could commence “very quickly”, Mr Whitehouse added

He told how “considerable amounts of money and considerable activity” had already been put into both fields, adding that “the Jackdaw platform itself is installed, the wells are drilled”.

open image in gallery Environmental campaigners have urged new Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to oppose the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments. (Yui Mok/PA)

While climate campaigners continue to object to the planned developments, the OEUK chief executive said both these, and a “significant number of additional projects” which could come afterwards could “help the UK meet more of its own production” needs for oil and gas, without having to rely on imported fuels.

Adding that a decision on Jackdaw could be made towards the end of August or possibly in September, Mr Whitehouse said: “Jackdaw will produce a significant amount of the gas the UK will need over the winter period.

“In my view it would be right to approve it. But we need it online ahead of winter.”

open image in gallery New Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh was in Aberdeen on Thursday to meet industry leaders. (Stefan Rousseau/PA)

While the UK Labour Government has so far been opposed to new oil and gas developments – in line with its 2024 manifesto pledge – Mr Whitehouse said the new Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh had told him she would take a “pragmatic approach”.

He met with Ms Fahnbulleh on Thursday, as she went to Aberdeen in what was her first visit since taking over from Ed Miliband.

Mr Whitehouse pointed out that Mr Burnham also “speaks a lot about the importance of place, and the importance of industry, reindustrialisation”.

He said: “That narrative lends itself, I think, that the UK should be supporting its own industries.”

The OEUK chief executive accepted it is “fundamentally right we build out renewable energy, it is right that we tackle climate change”, but adding that the UK will “use oil and gas for decades to come” he said it was “right that the Government should be supporting our own production over imports”.

He stated: “When we produce oil and gas in the North Sea we will produce it cleaner than imports, and we put real value back into the economy. We pay significant taxes which the Chancellor can use to support people’s bills.

“For all those reasons it is right we should be backing UK industries.”

However he warned the “consequences would be truly significant” if consent for both Jackdaw and Rosebank is refused.

“It would send a signal that the UK is choosing not to support its own industries,” Mr Whitehouse stated.

“It would send a signal that jobs of people up and down the country are not important, it would send a signal that the value in our economy, the taxes that those projects would pay are not important.

“And it will send a signal that actually the UK doesn’t want to control its own emissions. So I think that would be significant.

“Certainly there would be a huge impact on what we see as a £50 billion pipeline of projects that would follow.”

Jurgen Klopp insists he will quit his job as Germany manager if his family come under attack from the German media during his tenure.

Klopp, 59, has taken on his first coaching role since leaving Liverpool, citing fatigue, two years ago. The head coach has signed a contract through to the 2030 World Cup to lead his country, after their World Cup last-32 exit to Paraguay last month.

Klopp has taken on something of a low-profile since his trophy-laden nine-year stint at Anfield, occupying a role as Red Bull’s Head of Global Soccer since January 2025. He was also a pundit for German television at the World Cup.

Talks took place with the DFB after Germany’s exit and Julian Nagelsmann’s resignation, and while excited after the link-up was confirmed on Friday, Klopp had a firm warning for the media at his first press conference.

"The day you don't want me anymore, I'm gone - without any severance pay,” he said at his unveiling.

“If you say tomorrow that he's s***, I'm gone. Not just one person, it would have to be more than that. If the DFB says he's s***, I'm gone.

“If you behave badly and don't leave my family in peace, I'm gone. Criticise me if something doesn’t work. I’m happy to work on it. It’s all about the job.

“Jurgen Klopp doesn’t have a career after the national team. Ideally, this is the highlight of my career."

Klopp, who won every club trophy possible at Liverpool after his successful stint at Borussia Dortmund, created headlines during his punditry stint at the World Cup by suggesting that Deniz Undav should have started ahead of Jamal Musiala and then saying that “Julian Nagelsmann is still picking the team – for now.”

open image in gallery Klopp has signed a contract until the 2030 World Cup ( Getty )

Klopp was called out over the “for now” comment by former German players and apologised, saying he felt like “punching himself in the face”.

Following these incidents and ahead of Nagelsmann’s resignation, the 59-year-old played coy about the prospect of replacing him by saying: “I understand that when the national coach position is discussed, my name is mentioned in some form but it's not the moment to really talk about it.”

Klopp’s national team ambitions were well known during the World Cup and his contract with Red Bull included a special exit clause designed specifically so that he could take on the Germany job should it become available.

“The national team brings us Germans together like almost nothing else can. That's what makes this task so special for me,” Klopp said at his unveiling in Frankfurt on Friday morning.

Meanwhile, Klopp’s long-time managerial rival Pep Guardiola has turned down the chance to coach Italy after his departure from Manchester City.

Angela Rayner has indicated she does not expect Labour to meet its major manifesto pledge to build 1.5 million homes before the next election.

Andy Burnham’s newly appointed housing minister denied she was abandoning the commitment, but compared achieving it to her chances of “running the London Marathon”.

The promise to construct 1.5 million homes over the five-year parliamentary term was a key part of Labour’s 2024 election manifesto.

But asked if the target was still realistic, Ms Rayner told BBC Breakfast on Friday: “I’m not dropping it – I’m just saying it’s a really difficult challenge.

“I am going to keep the target, but it’s like me saying I’m going to run the London Marathon in under five hours. That would be a real challenge for me, but I would do it.”

She added: “This isn’t an excuse, but houses don’t go up in five minutes. I wish they did – it takes time.”

Ms Rayner was reappointed housing minister – the job she was to resign from after a row over whether she dodged stamp duty – when Andy Burnham became prime minister on Monday.

Ms Rayner said the housebuilding commitment was “very challenging” when it was made two years ago – and was even “more challenging” now as a result of increased construction costs and other factors which had had “a real negative impact”.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham’s newly appointed housing minister denied she was abandoning the commitment, but compared achieving it to her chances of ‘running the London Marathon’ ( AFP/Getty )

However, Ms Rayner was defiant after it was pointed out to her that in its first two years the government had built fewer than 300,000 homes – well short of the number needed to meet the 1.5 million target over five years.

She said: “I’m a straight-talking person, 1.5 million homes is a difficult target… but I’m going to keep it, I’m not going to be defeated.

”People have underestimated me all my life. If you tell me I cannot do something I will fight like hell to get it done.”

England saw 208,600 new homes built in 2024/25, a 6 per cent fall on the previous year and the lowest annual total since 2015/16, highlighting the scale of the challenge facing Labour’s pledge to deliver 1.5 million homes during this parliament.

Since Labour entered government in July 2024, around 392,400 net additional homes have been delivered, leaving ministers running at roughly two-thirds of the rate required to hit their goal by 2029.

The housebuilding industry has warned that without stronger consumer confidence, lower mortgage costs and healthier balance sheets across the construction sector, delivering the scale of housebuilding needed to meet Labour’s targets will remain an uphill battle.

open image in gallery England saw 208,600 new homes built in 2024/25, a 6 per cent fall on the previous year and the lowest annual total since 2015/16 ( PA )

Torrin Wilkins, director of Centre think tank, said the government should abolish stamp duty and impose binding housebuilding targets on councils to boost growth in the sector.

“The 1.5 million target comes up again and again. It’s almost turning the tens of thousands immigration target in the Cameron era in that we never seem to be able to meet it and yet it's constantly brought up,” he said, adding it was “unlikely” the government will meet its target if it does not change direction.

Mr Wilkins said the government should replace stamp duty with a proportional property tax to “unlock” housing sales and give developers incentive to build.

“Developers will look at who can afford homes in this local area and stamp duty is a real block,” he said.

open image in gallery Since Labour entered government in July 2024, around 392,400 net additional homes have been delivered, leaving ministers running at roughly two-thirds of the rate required to hit their goal by 2029 ( Reuters )

“If Andy Burnham's aim is breathing space, then abolishing stamp duty is probably the number one on that list because it allows people to upsize and downsize more easily and create that extra space.”

He also recommended councils and local authorities are handed binding targets with consequences for not meeting them.

“I think it would be a good step forward as well, just to really push that this isn't an optional housing target. This is a national situation and a national emergency that needs to be taken seriously.”

Senior research and policy analyst at the Resolution Foundation, Hannah Aldridge, said both soaring construction costs and a lower ability for many to buy houses have contributed to the challenges of housebuilding.

“A few things that have happened in the last few years is essentially construction costs have gone up,” she said.

“Then at the same time, we've also seen interest rates being slightly higher than what we were used to in the 2010s. So actually the amount that people are able to borrow to buy a house, it’s becoming harder for people to get the mortgages to buy a house that costs that much.”

A tapeworm has been found to reshape ageing and behaviour in worker ants, making the infected live nearly 10 times longer and to adopt queen-like features, a discovery that reveals how parasites may affect longevity.

The worm, Anomotaenia brevis, develops fully in woodpeckers, but ants serve as intermediate hosts.

Previous studies have shown that the queens of the ant species Temnothorax nylanderi live for up to 20 years, while workers usually live only one to two years.

However, once infected, ants of the species live several times longer than their uninfected nestmates, bridging the gap in lifespans with their queens, researchers found.

open image in gallery A worker ant of the species Temnothorx nylanderi infected with the tapeworm Anomotaenia brevis, recognizable by its yellowish coloration, alongside an uninfected worker ( Susanne Foitzik )

The infected ants become less active, and their metabolism becomes partly more similar to that of queens, according to the study.

“Queens and workers of social insects share the same genetic basis, but differ greatly in lifestyle and lifespan,” explained Susanne Foitzik, an author of the study published in the journal BMC Genomics.

By living a less active, longer life, the ants seem to promote further transmission of the tapeworm, scientists say.

In the study, researchers examined three groups of ants from the Lenneberg Forest near Mainz, including queens, workers infected with the tapeworm, and uninfected workers.

They dissected and closely assessed the ants’ brain and abdomen tissue to gain insights into their metabolism and immune system.

Scientists also analysed the genome data of both the tapeworm and the ants.

“Our genetic analyses show that the infection does not simply make the ants sick, but alters their physiology in a highly targeted way,” said Susanne Foitzik, an author of the study from Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz.

Researchers found that the infected workers had a profile of gene activity that was “partially queen-like” and get “royal treatment” from their uninfected peers.

Genes linked to metabolism in the ants’ guts, including those behind the immune system, stress resistance, and ageing, were active in the infected workers.

open image in gallery Anomotaenia brevis tapeworm in its larval stage ( Susanne Foitzik )

In comparison, gene activity in the brains of the infected workers was much less similar to queens.

“The effect of the infection is therefore tissue-specific,” explained Giulia Blasi, another author of the study.

“These tissue-specific responses suggest that infection primarily engages conserved ageing and metabolic networks and stabilises infected worker physiology in a manner that partially resembles the queen phenotype without recapitulating queen-like neuronal profiles,” researchers wrote.

Scientists found that the tapeworm influences the ant by intervening in the host’s gene activity patterns.

They suspect it does so mainly to evade the host’s immune system, but in the process it alters their metabolism, immunity, ageing, and behaviour.

Some of the UK’s biggest high street banks are set to have grown their profits over the first half of the year, but experts said there could be warnings over the risk of more bad loans as the Iran war pushes up the cost of living.

Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group and NatWest will report their half-year on Tuesday, Thursday and Friday respectively.

It follows an uncertain few months for households and businesses with mortgage rates spiking following the start of the US-Israel’s war with Iran and higher oil prices pushing up fuel and energy bills.

But most experts are expecting the lending giants to have grown their profits over the first half of the year.

Barclays is forecast to report a pre-tax profit of about £5.9 billion for the first six months of the year, up from a £5.2 billion profit the year before.

And Lloyds is expected to have generated £4.1 billion, up from £3.5 billion in the same period in 2025.

Steve Payne, KPMG’s UK head of banking, told the Press Association that banks are likely to continue benefiting from interest rates staying higher for longer, in response to concerns about inflation.

Average fixed mortgage rates shot up in April due to the financial uncertainty prompted by the conflict in the Middle East and have been ticking higher again in recent weeks.

Mr Payne said the impact of the conflict means “we will probably see at least some marginal, maybe slightly bigger than marginal, increases in the bad loan provisions that they put in place for people defaulting”.

“We’ve seen the impact of the war in terms of things like higher fuel and food costs and generally pushing the cost of living higher,” he said.

“And inevitably at some point that has to have an impact on credit quality.

“There is a lag… the longer it goes on for, the more likely we are to see that credit quality deteriorate.”

He said banks were likely to take a “realistic approach” by increasing their provisions.

Richard Hunter, head of markets for Interactive Investor, said: “Amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, concerns have grown for higher inflation and crimped consumer spending, which has left the banking sector under some pressure at various points throughout the year.

“As such, levels of customer defaults and impairment charges for possible bad debts will be central for sentiment.

“In a similar vein, interest rates are now expected to remain higher for longer which, all things being equal, should be positive for the sector.

“However, it also raises questions around mortgage availability and affordability, such that reported loan demand will be under the spotlight.”

A seaplane carrying 11 people crashed and erupted into a fiery blaze off the coast of Washington state, leaving one victim fighting life.

The Kenmore Air plane was forced to attempt an emergency landing in Shallow Bay just off Sucia Island, around 80 nautical miles from Seattle. Coast Guard Sector Puget Sound immediately deployed its search and rescue assets upon receiving reports of the crash at around 5.25 p.m. Thursday, the agency said.

​Footage of the crash showed the de Havilland DHC-3 Otter aircraft soaring just above the water, before appearing to make contact with its surface. Then, the video cuts to rescuers helping passengers from the crashed aircraft to the nearby shore.

Later in the video, the jet becomes engulfed in flames with plumes of black smoke stretching out from the crash site into the air. ​

open image in gallery The Coast Guard says that all 11 people onboard, which included 10 passengers and 1 pilot, were accounted for ( USCGNorthwest )

The Coast Guard has confirmed that the plane caught fire after the landing took place and remains against the rocks on Sucia Island. ​

The aircraft was carrying 10 passengers and one pilot at the time of the emergency landing, all of whom have been accounted for. Several injured passengers were taken to hospitals in Friday Harbor, Skagit County and Bellingham for medical treatment, the agency says. ​

The San Juan County Sheriff’s Office confirmed to KING 5 on Thursday that one person remains in critical condition and that the passengers’ injuries range from “head injuries to broken bones and lacerations.”​

San Juan County Sheriff Eric Peter told ABC News that a civilian vessel that saw the crash helped to get people out of the water. The aircraft was already ablaze when the sheriff’s office arrived.

open image in gallery The passengers and pilot were rushed from Shallow Bay to nearby hospitals (file photo) ( Public domain )

A spokesperson for Kenmore Air confirmed to KING 5 that the aircraft had taken off at 4.30 p.m. from Lake Union in Seattle and went down at around 5.15 p.m. The plane was heading for Roche Harbor. ​

The spokesperson also provided more detail on where the passengers were sent to hospital, with 6 being sent to PeaceHealth St Joseph Medical Center in Bellingham.

Four passengers were transported to PeaceHealth Peace Island Medical Center in Friday Harbor, with the pilot being taken to Skagit Valley Hospital.​

In a statement, Kenmore Air CEO David Gudgel thanked the Coast Guard, local emergency responders and those assisting the response to the crash.​

open image in gallery One person is fighting for life after the crash ( USCGNorthwest )

“We are grateful that everyone aboard has been accounted for, and our immediate focus is ensuring our passengers and pilot receive the care and support they need,” Gudgel said, noting that the company is fully cooperating with investigators. ​

The company has also confirmed that all of its scheduled flights on July 24 have been canceled, in order to support the passengers, pilot, family and employees affected by the emergency landing. ​

The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration are investigating the cause of the crash and the fire, the Coast Guard says. ​

News.title: Africa improves health defences, but it remains vulnerable to pandemics
News.content:
Africa is significantly better prepared for a pandemic than it was five years ago, a major review of the continent’s health security has found.

The review, which tracked dozens of health metrics across the continent, found that local and international investments in Africa’s health sector since the pandemic have “paid off.”

Published by the Brown University Pandemic Centre and the Nuclear Threat Initiative, a US non-profit, the report is the third of its kind and provides an update on two previous reviews from 2019 and 2021.

Investment in health by African governments grew rapidly during the pandemic. Post-pandemic, the average spend now sits at around 7.4 per cent of GDP, roughly $135 billion per year across the continent.

That figure still falls significantly below those of high-income countries, where the average spend on health sits at around 11.2 per cent of GDP.

The new African Health Security Index report found that almost every African country – 53 out of 54, excluding only the Republic of the Congo – has improved its ability to prevent, detect, and respond to disease outbreaks since 2021, the last time the index was updated.

Overall, the continent scores 41.2 out of 100 on its health security – up from 32.9 five years ago.

The score is built from hundreds of specific indicators covering things like how far people live from a hospital, how well infectious patients can be isolated, the size and training level of the health workforce, laboratory capacity, and the availability of vaccines and other critical medicines during an outbreak.

News.title: Ebola death toll passes 1,000 as outbreak shows no signs of slowing
News.content:
More than 1,000 people have now died in the outbreak of Ebola in the Congo, as medics struggle to curb the fastest-growing epidemic of the virus.

Dozens of deaths are being recorded each day and modelling has forecast that, in a worst case scenario, it could become the worst Ebola outbreak in history.

The outbreak, centred on the north east of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), passed the four-figure death milestone little more than two months after it was first declared.

By contrast, the worst outbreak of the haemorrhagic fever on record, which struck West Africa from 2014 to 2016, took eight months from the first case to reach 1,000 deaths. It went on to kill 11,000 people.

The latest figures from the DRC’s national public health institute show 2,536 confirmed Ebola cases and 1,033 deaths, with at least 738 patients in isolation or hospitalised.

News.title: Inflation fall a ‘false dawn’, Burnham warned
News.content:
Falling inflation is a “false dawn” for Andy Burnham, economists warned after the pace of price rises slowed in June.

The consumer prices index (CPI) fell from 2.8pc in May to 2.6pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), beating economists’ expectations of a drop to 2.7pc to mark the lowest rate in 15 months.

Lower petrol and diesel prices drove the slowdown amid a short-lived peace deal between the US and Iran, while price pressures from chocolate, oils and fats, dairy and meat also weakened.

However, economists warned a rise in household energy bills in July may already have pushed inflation back up above 3pc.

Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants, said: “June’s slowdown is a false dawn as it may have already been reversed this month with higher energy bills, following Ofgem’s energy price cap rise, likely to have lifted inflation above 3pc.”

July’s 13pc increase in the energy price cap has pushed typical annual bills to around £1,862, while renewed fighting between the US and Iran has reignited concerns over oil and gas supplies.

Mr Thiru said elevated inflation would create a fresh headache for John Healey, the newly appointed Chancellor, by squeezing household budgets, raising government borrowing costs and limiting his room for tax cuts or spending increases.

Charlotte O’Leary, at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “June’s peace deal and the subsequent reduction in oil and gas prices helped cool consumer price inflation. This will be a welcome figure to start the new Prime Minister’s premiership, but the honeymoon period will be short-lived.”

The Bank of England will also be watching closely as it weighs further interest rate cuts, though economists warned renewed instability in the Middle East and higher energy bills could keep inflation close to 3pc for the rest of the year.

Mr Healey said: “Falling inflation is news families want to hear, but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need.”

News.title: Russia destroys Ukraine HIV warehouse
News.content:
A Russian missile strike has destroyed $2.6m (£1.9m) worth of HIV prevention supplies in Ukraine, according to an international aid group.

The Alliance for Public Health said the attack on Sunday night near Kyiv hit a warehouse holding 62 million prevention items earmarked for Ukraine’s harm reduction programmes next year. It includes syringes, needles, alcohol wipes, and condoms intended to support more than 300,000 people.

“This is not just another strike. It is an attack on 300,000 Ukrainians who depend on HIV prevention services and on their fundamental right to health,” said Andriy Klepikov, executive director of the Alliance for Public Health.

Efforts to prevent the spread of HIV rely heavily on harm reduction programmes that supply sterile syringes and needles to people who inject drugs, alongside condoms and other supplies that help curb sexual transmission.

Mr Klepikov said the destruction of the warehouse would not immediately disrupt services, because his organisation had moved its supplies for the rest of the year out of central storage and into regional distribution centres several weeks ago as part of contingency planning.

“Russia failed,” he said, adding that the Alliance had notified international partners and appealed for urgent support to rebuild next year’s inventory.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

Sports.title: Per Mertesacker lands major new job six months on from quitting as Arsenal’s academy chief
Sports.content:
PER MERTESACKER has landed a job with the German FA after leaving Arsenal.

The former defender was the Gunners’ academy manager but left the role at the end of last season.



Mertesacker had held the position for eight years, taking it in 2018 after finishing a playing career that included over 200 games for Arsenal.

The 41-year-old left the club as he was eager for a new challenge and he has now secured a job with the German FA.



Mertesacker will become their managing director of sport from January 1 next year, succeeding Andreas Rettig.

The former centre-back, who won the World Cup with Germany as a player in 2014, will be responsible for the national teams and their academy.



His arrival coincides with that of Jurgen Klopp, who was announced as the country’s new head coach on Friday.

The German FA are aware of the need for change after failing to reach the last 16 in any of the past three World Cups.

Mertesacker said: “I am very much looking forward to this new task and the responsibility that comes with it.

“My connection to the DFB never broke off, even after the end of my national team career.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“That’s why it’s something special for me to return in this role. German football has enormous potential.

“With humility, the will to work hard, and the necessary patience, we want to foster the talents and personalities who make the difference.

“Together, we want to create an environment in which players can take on responsibility, grow through challenges, and develop their full potential – from the grassroots level all the way to the national teams.

“It is an honour for me to be able to help shape and further develop the DFB on this path.”

Sports.title: Chelsea exclude TWO new summer signings from pre-season squad to Australia and Asia in worrying start for Xabi Alonso
Sports.content:
CHELSEA have left TWO new summer signings behind as they travel to their pre-season training camp.

The Blues confirmed 27 players had travelled to Sydney for the club’s pre-season tour of Australia and Asia.



That squad list included summer signing Marco Palestra, the 21-year-old defender signed from Atalanta for £43million.

The likes of Morgan Rogers, who just completed a £117m transfer to Stamford Bridge from Aston Villa, are on holiday following a deep run at the World Cup with England, with the same going for club captain Reece James.



However, two summer signings were not named on Alonso’s list; Emmanuel Emegha and Geovany Quenda.

Both players saw deals with their respective former clubs, Strasbourg and Sporting Lisbon, agreed prior to the summer, but they have only officially linked up with the team this summer.



Dutch forward Emegha, 23, is understood to have suffered a hamsting injury in a behind-closed-doors friendly win over League One side Bromley at Cobham.

The issue for Quenda, an exciting 19-year-old right-sided wide player, currently remains unclear.

Despite the blow to Alonso’s pre-season plans, both players could yet link up with the squad on tour at a later date.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK



While not naming names, Chelsea said in a statement: “Several other first-team players are expected to join the Blues squad during the tour.”

Chelsea secured a 3-0 win over Bromley in that behind-closed-doors friendly, with Joao Pedro, Jamie Gittens, and Emegha all on the scoresheet.

Sports.title: Rodri’s back surgery outcome to have major knock-on effect over Man Utd and Real Madrid transfers
Sports.content:
RODRI’S planned back surgery could have a bearing on whether he leaves Manchester City this summer.

The 30-year-old is scheduled to go under the knife on Monday and is expected to miss the start of the Premier League season, which gets underway on August 21.



The transfer windows in England and Spain both close at 11pm on September 1.

Real Madrid are prepared to move for Rodri if they can sell Aurelien Tchouameni amid a fresh enquiry from Manchester United.



Spain international Rodri has entered the final year of his City contract and a return to his homeland on a free next year is also possible.

Madrid have signed several players in recent years after their contracts at previous clubs had expired.

David Alaba, Antonio Rudiger, Kylian Mbappe, Ibrahima Konate and Bernardo Silva were all free agents.

Madrid paid Liverpool a fee of £8.4million a month before Trent Alexander-Arnold’s deal ended so he could play in last year’s Club World Cup, which began in June.

Madrid endured a trophyless 2025-26 season and have already bolstered their squad with the arrivals of Konate, Bernardo, Marc Cucurella and Denzel Dumfries under new manager Jose Mourinho.

Rodri was named the best player at the World Cup after helping Spain to a second triumph in the tournament.



City signed Rodri from Atletico Madrid in 2019 and the Spain international won the Ballon d’Or in 2024.

Rodri has helped City to four successive Premier League titles, the Champions League, three League Cups, two FA Cups and the Club World Cup. He started in Spain’s European Championship and World Cup final wins.

Speculation surrounding Rodri’s future has intensified this week now that the World Cup is over and the only Madrid player in the Spain squad was Cucurella, who signed from Chelsea last month.

Sources in Madrid say United have shown “strong” interest in Tchouameni after they established he is available.

Madrid value Tchouameni at around €80million (£68.37m), which is cheaper than Bournemouth’s asking price for Alex Scott, who United have monitored.



Tchouameni has entered the final two years of his contract and is a specialist defensive midfielder, a priority position for United.

United have bolstered their midfield with the arrivals of Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa but neither is an outright No.6.

Club sources insist they have a “long list” of options and do not have a set target.



Despite reports claiming that Tchouameni had signed a new deal at the Bernabeu, Madrid have not confirmed a renewal as they are keen on bringing in Rodri.

Sports.title: Chelsea ‘receive £25million offer from club legend for World Cup star with ace keen on transfer’
Sports.content:
COMO have made another bid for Chelsea defender Trevoh Chalobah – and the player is keen to move, according to reports.

Chalobah, 27, has been a big target for Blues legend Cesc Fabregas all summer.



But Chelsea are holding out for their academy graduate and want at least £30million.

Fabrizio Romano says that their latest offer is worth around £22million with £3million more possible in add-ons.



That falls short of Chelsea’s valuation for Chalobah, who made his World Cup debut last week.

Chalobah came on as a late sub under Thomas Tuchel in England‘s crazy 6-4 third- placeplay-offf win over France.

He was a late call-up to the squad as a replacement for former Cobham team-mate Tino Livramento.

Chalobah has two years left on a long-term contract signed in 2022.

Chelsea hold an option to extend that for another 12 months but are also happy to cash in on him now.

They have agreed a deal to sign Crystal Palace centre-back Maxence Lacroix.

Sports.title: Chelsea still £10million short of Rayo Vallecano asking price for Pep Chavarria with LaLiga club standing firm
Sports.content:
CHELSEA are £10million short of Rayo Vallecano’s valuation of defender Pep Chavarria.

The Blues have been in talks over a deal for the full-back all summer, with the Spanish club standing firm over their asking price.



Chavarria, 28, has a £42.4m release clause, though they would still sell the defender for around £30m.

Despite that, Chelsea are prepared to offer up to £21m – well short of Rayo’s asking price. Chavarria is keen on a move to Stamford Bridge.



The Blues are in need of added competition and cover at left-back after the £47.5m sale of Marc Cucurella to Real Madrid.

There is confidence Dutch defender Jorrel Hato can step up and deliver, but support will be needed.

The former Real Zaragoza full-back would add much needed experience to the Blues squad, something new boss Xabi Alonso has identified as necessary this summer.

Chelsea, who have had a £15m bid for Chavarria rejected, attempted to sign Granit Xhaka, who played under Alonso at Bayer Leverkusen, from Sunderland for £8m to add leadership but saw that offer snubbed.

Talks over a deal for £60m-rated Crystal Palace defender Maxence Lacroix are accelerating, with Premier League experience identified as an important factor in the signing of a new defender.

Alonso also wants to add further in midfield, having seen a £64m bid for Bournemouth’s Alex Scott rejected.

It is currently unclear if the Blues will return with a second offer after Bournemouth made it clear they do not want to sell the England Under-21 midfielder.

However, Alonso has said he wants to keep the Argentine at the club and no one has yet suggested they are ready to meet Chelsea’s £120m asking price.

Chelsea have already secured four done deals for new boss Alonso as they look to improve on their difficult 2025-26 campaign.



Morgan Rogers was their big money deal after arriving from Aston Villa for a British record of £117m earlier this week.

They also brought in defender Marco Palestra from Atalanta for around £43m and teenage winger Geovany Quenda from Sporting Lisbon.

Sports.title: Ian Wright launches Arsenal’s stunning retro away kit as fans say ‘take my money already’
Sports.content:
ARSENAL fans have told the club to take their money after they drafted in Ian Wright for the Gunners’ latest kit launch.

The North London side revealed their new away kit for the 2026/27 season, made by Adidas.



It is a throwback shirt to the iconic Bruised Banana of the early 1990s, including the 1990/91 season when Arsenal beat Liverpool to the league title on the final day.

And the club brought ex-England star Wright into the fold to show off the new-look blue and yellow kit that follows their latest title win last season.



The release campaign also saw modern stars from both the men’s and women’s teams – with Declan Rice, Riccardo Calafiori and Chloe Kelly wearing the colours, as well as Islington-born rapper Little Simz.

Featuring a distinct navy base, the kit has reworked the original engineered geometric pattern with a contemporary execution that is complete with red and yellow accents.



A club statement also revealed it incorporates adidas’ latest CLIMACOOL+ technology to maintain a lightweight feeling.

Fans will have to fork out a fair bit, however, with the cheapest adult kit coming in at around £85, while a champions edition will set you back £113 or an authentic player kit version £148.

But fans on social media seem more than willing to pay for it, with one excited supporter saying: “Take my money already. Adidas just never misses with our away kits!”

A second said: “This is an elite kit.”

Sports.title: Pep Guardiola ‘REJECTS’ lucrative return to management with ex-Man City boss focusing on different priorities
Sports.content:
PEP GUARDIOLA has reportedly turned down the chance to lead the Italy national team.

While the iconic manager considered the role, he has decided to dedicate some time to his family for now.



Fabrizio Romano reported the news, saying that the Spanish manager has ‘said no’ to the Italian football federation.

Guardiola wants to prioritise time with his family to recharge before a return to football, according to Romano.



It was revealed earlier in the week that the three-time Champions League winning manager was in the running for the vacant Italy job.

The Italian federation were even willing to scrap their usual wage structure, in order to lure Guardiola.



But it seems that we won’t see the Spaniard in charge of the Azzurri ahead of Euro 2028.

He left the Etihad this summer after 10 years in Manchester.

Guardiola delivered six Premier League titles and a first ever Champions League for Man City, in a period of serial dominance.

Rumours have also circulated linking him to the England job, despite Thomas Tuchel being expected to continue for Euro 2028 on home soil.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Guardiola verbally agreed to the England job in 2024 before changing his mind.

Meanwhile, the Italians, who have failed to qualify for the last three World Cups, also reportedly had their eyes on legendary gaffer Carlo Ancelotti.

However, reports suggest that ‘Don Carlo’ plans to stay in his current role at Brazil.

Romano reported that the ex-Real Madrid manager has “no intention” to become Italy’s next coach.

So Ancelotti, who was part of Arrigo Sacchi’s Italy coaching staff from 1992-95, evidently has no intention of making a return to his country’s national team.



Brazil legend Romario recently called for Ancelotti to be sacked, labelling his nation’s last-16 exit to Norway an “embarrassment”.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp issues spiky ultimatum after taking Germany job - 'I will be gone'
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp issues spiky ultimatum after taking Germany job - 'I will be gone'

Jurgen Klopp has become Germany manager on a four-year contract and the former Liverpool boss did not hold back in his first press conference while addressing the media

View 2 Images Jurgen Klopp speaking at his first press conference as Germany manager (Image: Markus Ulmer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

Jurgen Klopp has threatened to walk away from his role as Germany manager on the first day in the job. The former Liverpool boss was announced as Julian Nagelsmann's successor on a four-year deal on Friday - and immediately went on the offensive.

‌



The 59-year-old has left his role as Red Bull's global head of soccer to try and turn around the team which was knocked out of the World Cup in the last 32 by Paraguay. Klopp will work alongside his former Liverpool assistants Pep Lijnders and Peter Krawietz.

‌



He left Liverpool in 2024, having grown tired of the intense job and has enjoyed stepping away from the spotlight. And it seems that while the national team job is a dream one, Klopp is not looking forward to the increased scrutiny.

‌



Klopp succeeding Nagelsmann has been an open secret for some time and that appears to have frustrated him - and prompted an ultimatum for the press. "Now is the time where I'm really in the middle of the media focus," he said at a press conference in Frankfurt.

Jurgen Klopp officially named as Germany boss as worst-kept secret in football confirmed READ MORE :

Argentina president goes on rant as calls for country to be banned from World Cup grow READ MORE :

"I was surprised, not negatively or positively surprised, at how fast news spread. And it's sometimes hard for people to just think 'let's turn a blind eye to things' and not to divulge any information. Sometimes that is the right thing to do, not to publish things that happened.

‌



“I know full well this is job number one for me. It is my mission to make the national squad better and to hope the pool for me to choose from is bigger.

“But it is not something I will do against you, but I’m doing it for you. It is an honour. I will be remunerated very graciously and if tomorrow it's 'Jurgen Klopp is s***', then I will be gone.

View 2 Images Jurgen Klopp gave the media an ultimatum (Image: Markus Ulmer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

‌



“But if the DFB (German FA) says ‘Come on let us not continue the job’ then that’s it. And if you (the media) behave badly and don’t let my family live in peace. I’ll be gone and I'll just turn away.

“I know there are other countries where the national team head coaches are treated even worse. But I love this job, but I’m always ready to call just call it quits if need be.

“Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any ‘career’ after the national team, this is the absolute pinnacle of my footballing career as a coach. I will give everything I’ve got."

Klopp won the Premier League, Champions League, FA Cup and two League Cups during a hugely successful nine-year spell at Liverpool. He departed two years ago due to burn-out but is now recharged for the Germany job.

Sports.title: Jude Bellingham's parting shot to Argentina referee in unseen World Cup footage
Sports.content:
Jude Bellingham's parting shot to Argentina referee in unseen World Cup footage

Jude Bellingham has been spotted clashing with the referee from England's defeat to Argentina in the World Cup semi-final in new footage

View Image Jude Bellingham was emotional following England's defeat to Argentina (Image: Justin Setterfield, Getty Images)

Fresh ref cam footage has surfaced showing Jude Bellingham lambasting the official's 'shocking decisions' following England's defeat to Argentina.

‌



The Three Lions' World Cup dreams were ended as La Albiceleste came from behind to earn a place in the final. There was no shortage of frustration on display from England as Argentina racked up fouls throughout the game.

‌



Moroccan-USA referee Ismail Elfath came in for considerable scrutiny before kick-off after being labelled Lionel Messi's favourite official.

‌



Argentina racked up 12 fouls in the opening half against England but received just one yellow card. Bellingham was dragged down on four separate occasions as he attempted to launch counterattacks.

The Stourbridge-born midfielder's frustration with Argentina's aggressive tactics was plain to see as they sought to halt him by any means necessary. Bellingham told the referee exactly what he thought after the full-time whistle.

Argentina FA intervene as World Cup final conspiracy theories emerge after Spain win READ MORE :

The Real Madrid star was visibly furious at how the match was handled. In the ref-cam footage, Bellingham can be seen shaking Elfath's hand before remarking, "Some shocking ones but all the best."

‌



During the game, Bellingham was also spotted in animated conversation with Argentina captain Messi. However, he played down their interaction following the match,

"The chat with Messi? Actually, we were arguing about a foul. It wasn't anything serious. I'm sure everyone will make a big deal out of it, but it was nothing," Bellingham said.

"I thought there was a foul earlier, and he said, ‘What about the one I was fouled on?’

‌

Arsenal are still keen on signing Julian Alvarez from Atletico Madrid and are reportedly willing to offer up one of their key stars

Viktor Gyokeres could be offered up to Atletico Madrid by Arsenal as a vehicle to sign Julian Alvarez. ‌



However, Alvarez has been a transfer target for the reigning Premier League champions all summer. Arsenal had the rug pulled from under them in their pursuit for Morgan Rogers, who was signed for £117m by Chelsea, while the Gunners were negotiating with Aston Villa.

‌



With the England international out of the picture, Alvarez appears to be back at the top of Arteta's transfer list. It's been claimed Arsenal are so interested in the Argentina international, they may offer up Gyokeres as part of any transfer deal.

‌

As per the Times, Arsenal are keen to present the Swedish player to Diego Simeone's team as part of a player-plus-cash deal for the Argentinian World Cup victor. Last summer, Gyokeres made the switch to the Gunners from Sporting and experienced a varied debut season.

He contributed 21 goals and three assists in 55 outings across all competitions, a commendable performance, but not one that sparked the same enthusiasm as the 54 goals and 13 assists he netted during his final campaign with Sporting.

Bruno Guimaraes of Newcastle United also sits atop their priorities, especially with Declan Rice battling his neural hamstring problem at the World Cup.

Pep Guardiola's telling reasons for rejecting Italy job as England learn stance

Italy were looking to appoint Pep Guardiola as their new manager following their disastrous failure to qualify for the World Cup this summer

View 2 Images Pep Guardiola has turned down the Italy job (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

Pep Guardiola has reportedly rejected the Italy job after telling bosses "I don't feel it". It is also claimed that he still needs a break and is not sure about international management - dealing a blow to England's prospects of appointing him.

‌



The Catalan left Manchester City this summer after a decade in charge. The 55-year-old had another year left to run on his contract with City, but decided to call time after a decade in the role.

‌



He won six Premier League titles, the Champions League, three FA Cups and five Carabao Cups. While he missed out on the league title for the second successive year, he bowed out with the FA Cup and Carabao Cup.

‌



And the Italian national team were hoping to persuade Guardiola for a swift return to management this summer. The Azzurri failed to qualify for a third successive World Cup after losing to Bosnia & Herzegovina in the playoffs.

But Italian publication La Gazzetta dello Sport claim that he has turned them down, having said: “Thank you, I’m honoured, but at this moment, I don’t feel it.”

The report claims that Guardiola's decision was not easy and he had given it considerable thought. However, it is said that reason prevailed over emotion.

Guardiola is also reportedly keen for a break after intense spells at Bayern Munich and City since his sabbatical 13 years ago. The ex-Barcelona boss is also said to have doubts over whether international football would suit him.

View 2 Images Pep Guardiola has been out of work since leaving Man City at the end of last season (Image: Nick Potts/PA Wire)

‌



Italian football president Giovanni Malago also hinted at a financial disparity in talks with Guardiola earlier this week . In an interview with the Italian media, he said: "There are certain financial aspects to be considered, and it's an understatement to say we'd have to grit our teeth for this.

The English FA could be watching the situation closely, with a long-term interest in Guardiola. Current Three Lions manager Thomas Tuchel is still in post, and despite calls for his dismissal following the World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, the FA is expected to stand by him.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan fans' bid for 'fitting tribute' to England legend in Scunthorpe where career began
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan fans' bid for 'fitting tribute' to England legend in Scunthorpe where career began

Keegan, known to fans as King Kev, enjoyed a glittering career, which saw him win 63 England caps, including 31 as captain and win an array of trophies, including two Ballon d’Ors

View 4 Images Keegan sadly died on Monday aged 75 just months after revealing he had been diagnosed with cancer (Image: Colin Lane/Liverpool Echo)

Football fans are fundraising for a statue to honour Kevin Keegan in the place he began his career after his death from cancer.

‌



The proposed likeness would be placed in Scunthorpe, North Lincs, where the two-time Ballon-D'Or winner began his career, making more than 100 appearances, before moving to Liverpool for £33,000 in 1971. David Beverley, vice chairman of supporters group The Iron Trust, who are leading the fundraiser, said the statue would be a "fitting tribute" to King Kev, who went on to become a legend of the game.

‌



He said: "You've got to remember his career started here. He'd been rejected by Coventry City and Doncaster Rovers before Ron Ashman, who again was a legend at the club, saw Kevin, got him signed and then sold him to Liverpool in 1971."

‌



View 4 Images Kevin Keegan back in Scunthorpe for a fundraising game in May 1982 (Image: Scunthorpe Evening Telegraph)

Kevin Keegan shared three things people will remember him for in heartbreaking final interview READ MORE :

Kevin Keegan planned one last St James' Park visit before cancer death to see fans he loved READ MORE :

Keegan, who died on Monday aged 75, also went on to play for Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle during an illustrious playing career, which also included 63 England caps, including 31 as captain. He won three league Division One titles, the European Cup, two Uefa Cups and the FA Cup with Liverpool.

He later joined Hamburg, where he won the Bundesliga and back-to-back Ballons d’Ors in 1978 and 1979 – becoming one of only four English players to win the award, and the only one to do it twice. He also went on to manage England, as well as Newcastle, Fulham, and Manchester City, but despite his incredible success, Keegan still remained a supporter of Scunthorpe and repeatedly returned there to help raise funds.

‌



His last visit came in December last year when he attended the club's National League match against Tamworth, even giving a speech in the dressing room before the match, visiting the boardroom and meeting fans around the ground, including in the club's Iron Bar.

View 4 Images Keegan reunited with fellow Scunthorpe legends Ron Ashman (left) and Jack Brownsword during one of his returns to the club some years ago (Image: Scunthorpe Telegraph)

Current players and staff held a minute's applause and laid flowers in tribute to the former Iron player there earlier this week. And a book of condolence has now been set up at the Attis Arena, where an old quote from Keegan saying: "People think that the club that made me was Liverpool, but the club that really made me was Scunthorpe United", is on permanent display.

‌



Steven Plumtree, 55, was among those who visited to sign the book of condolence, which is surrounded by pictures of Keegan during his time playing at the club, as well as a candle. Mr Plumtree recalled watching Keegan play for the club and described his death as a "big loss to Scunthorpe". He said: "I thought I'd just come down and say goodbye to him in the best way."

Jamie Benson, 28, who also signed the book, said Keegan had "Scunthorpe in his heart". He said: "He still came to visit people. He was just down to earth and genuine and I think that's why so many people fell in love with him."

The fundraiser says: "The Iron Trust is fundraising for a Kevin Keegan memorial statue at the birthplace of his glittering career, in Scunthorpe, North Lincolnshire. We are raising funds to commemorate the great, late, Kevin Keegan, following the sad news of his passing on the 20th July, aged 75, with a people's memorial and statue to be located in Scunthorpe, the home of the Iron, the club at which Kevin began his football career."

It adds: "The Iron Trust invites fans of Scunthorpe United, Liverpool, Hamburg SV, Southampton and Newcastle, as well as football fans around the world to donate towards a lasting memorial at the birthplace of King Kev's extraordinary football career."

Sports.title: Argentina forced to make change as FIFA ruling emerges after World Cup final
Sports.content:
Argentina forced to make change as FIFA ruling emerges after World Cup final

Argentina's disgraced team will be forced to make a change following their World Cup final loss

View 3 Images Argentina must make an alteration following the World Cup (Image: Getty)

Argentina are set to be given another brutal reminder of their devastating World Cup final defeat. The thuggish and negative tactics employed by Lionel Scaloni's side proved in vain as Spain clinched a deserved victory thanks to Ferran Torres's extra-time strike.

‌



Argentina had been aiming to lift the trophy for the fourth time in their history after Lionel Messi inspired the team to glory at Qatar 2022. Since becoming world champions, their strip had featured a gold crest displaying an outline of the trophy alongside the words "FIFA World Champions 2022".

‌



However, that prized addition to their iconic colour scheme must now be removed, as they are no longer world champions. Spain will now don the coveted emblem at the next World Cup, which they will co-host with Portugal and Morocco, with special one-off opening matches taking place in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay to mark the 100th anniversary of the World Cup.

‌



Argentina can at least continue to display a badge commemorating their Copa America victory in 2024, a title they will defend in 2028.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Argentina failed to relinquish the World Cup trophy or the gold badge with any grace. Leandro Paredes, along with team-mate Nahuel Molina and Argentina coach Roberto Ayala, were involved in the brawl seconds after the final whistle at the MetLife Stadium.

‌



Argentina president goes on rant as calls for country to be banned from World Cup grow READ MORE :

Argentina FA intervene as World Cup final conspiracy theories emerge after Spain win READ MORE :

Contrary to the belief at the time, Paredes was not shown a red card following the incident. But FIFA has announced that its disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to investigate possible breaches of the FIFA disciplinary code.

The South Americans attracted further condemnation for their combative style, with Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez sent off for two yellow cards.

View 3 Images Argentina must give up the gold badge in the centre of their shirt (Image: Getty Images)

‌



A FIFA statement read: "Following an assessment of the relevant match reports for the FIFA World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, and in line with article 36 of the FIFA disciplinary code (FDC), the FIFA disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the FDC with regard to the post-match incidents."

Retrospective punishments, such as fines and/or suspensions, are possible for the country's federation or individuals. However, Spain midfielder Gavi, who was grabbed by Paredes during the post-match melee, insists he doesn't not want the Boca Juniors star to be hit with a ban.

View 3 Images Leandro Paredes drags Gavi to the floor (Image: Marvin Ibo Guengoer - GES Sportfoto, Getty Images)

‌



Gavi told El Partidazo de COPE: "I don't think [Paredes] should be suspended. I understand it's not a good image for children, but I think there's also that side to football, which is a bit more physical, more aggressive.

"The most logical thing would have been to send him off during the match, and that's it. In the end, I think it's all football, and it has to be that way."
