Sports.title: Three Man Utd coaches have all given their opinion on JJ Gabriel
Sports.content:
Three Man Utd coaches have all given their opinion on JJ Gabriel

JJ Gabriel is in the Manchester United squad to face Rosenborg in Trondheim on Friday and could make his senior debut

View 2 Images JJ Gabriel has been made to wait for his senior Manchester United debut (Image: Ash Donelon, Manchester United via Getty Images)

Manchester United wonderkid JJ Gabriel could make his first team debut for the club in Friday's pre-season friendly against Rosenborg. The 15-year-old has joined the likes of Harry Maguire and Bryan Mbeumo in a squad packed with senior talent in Norway.

‌



Gabriel is unsurprisingly the youngest member of the squad but fans expect him to more than hold his own. This is, in part, due to the glowing praise he has received from multiple coaches at Old Trafford.

‌



Manager Michael Carrick has given the teenager a chance to train with the senior squad in the past. Were it not for Premier League rules, Gabriel might have emulated the likes of Max Dowman and Ethan Nwaneri in playing top-flight football before his 16th birthday.

‌



Former caretaker boss Darren Fletcher has similarly had big things to say about a player who bagged 23 goals in the Under-18 Premier League last season. Carrick and Fletcher aren't the only ones, either.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Man Utd identify World Cup star as new target after pulling out of Alex Scott transfer READ MORE :

Man Utd may have to scrap strict Arsenal transfer rule after latest Marcus Rashford blow READ MORE :

Head of academy Stephen Torpey joined United in 2025 and was clearly excited. "We have some special talents right now in our groups, and JJ is one of those, for sure," Torpey said.

‌



In March, Carrick admitted Gabriel wasn't allowed to play Premier League football but that didn't stop his glowing account of the youngster. "JJ is a big talent, it's pretty obvious to know that and he's had a really good season for the Under-18s," said the manager, who has since been installed on a permanent basis.

"We obviously think an awful lot of him, but patience is important in managing everything that comes with that and working with him in development as we do with all the different younger players and picking the right moment to step up," Carrick continued. "What he's done when he's trained, he's done well as you'd expect and it's good to have the younger players come up with us."

View 2 Images Gabriel has had chances to train with United's senior squad (Image: Ash Donelon, Manchester United via Getty Images)

‌



Fletcher, who has worked with Gabriel at Under-18s level, has perhaps unsurprisingly been blown away by the talent. He suggested the player would have been ready for first-team football last season had such a thing been permitted, also indicating in May that a pre-season opportunity was unlikely to faze him.

"JJ's an amazing talent and has an enthusiasm for football that he brings to the pitch every day: to learn, to want to play and be on the ball," the Scot told The Athletic. "He's been a pleasure to work with. He's a fantastic kid."

He also suggested United planned to be careful when it comes to the teenager's first-team exposure, adding: "Once you get thrown in there, you're judged very, very quickly, rightly or wrongly. It's important that we do right by his development.

‌



"JJ's more than capable to go in, as are a lot of our young players. They all get experiences with the first team. It goes under the radar how many of our young players get tastes of the first team."

Gabriel is not the only teenager in the squad set to face Rosenborg, though he is the youngest of the bunch. Several others have already had a taste of senior football, including 18-year-old striker Chido Obi and Fletcher's 19-year-old twin sons Jack and Tyler.

Sports.title: Could Adeyemi's Barcelona move see Flick unlock winger's true potential?
Sports.content:
Perhaps Karim Adeyemi's move to Barcelona should not come as a surprise even if usurping Lamine Yamal as the team's star left-footed right-winger is impossible. After all, it was Hansi Flick, Barca’s head coach, who gave Adeyemi his debut for Germany.

The hope is that his old coach can spark something new in a player whose vast potential has been obvious for years but is yet to truly explode. This is an opportunity for Adeyemi to become the player that Flick and many others have long suspected he could be.

He was still a teenager with Red Bull Salzburg when Flick first picked him. But Adeyemi is only 24 now. If it feels like he has been around far longer it is because he had almost 100 games for Salzburg even before making the move to Borussia Dortmund in 2022.

Image: Karim Adeyemi during his official presentation as FC Barcelona's new player

He was playing for Salzburg's feeder team Liefering even before that, debuting at the age of 16. Speaking to Adeyemi about this during his time at Dortmund, he saw it as the ideal schooling. "For me, it was the best move that I could do," he told Sky Sports.

He explained: "The most important thing for a young guy is to play. They have a second team who play against adults. I played in the second league as a 16-year-old, a lot of games. I adapted to men's football and this is what is important for a young player."

Image: Karim Adeyemi had his moments during four years at Borussia Dortmund

There have been plenty of highlights since then. As one of those fortunate enough to be inside the Westfalenstadion when he raced clear to score a Champions League winner against Chelsea in 2023, it is fair to say that Adeyemi's pace leaves an impression.

He was clocked at a Bundesliga-high 36.65 kilometres per hour in that debut season. His reply when speaking to him about whether he was the fastest around was emphatic. "Yes, I am very confident with that." Is anyone close? "Close, maybe. But not faster."

The speed stats have tailed off slightly, although Adeyemi has still ranked among the fastest dozen Bundesliga players in each of the past two seasons. The bigger problem was that he was not quite able to evolve beyond that role of impact player at Dortmund.

Image: Karim Adeyemi's heat map and shot map in his Bundesliga career with Borussia Dortmund

There were moments. Adeyemi came on as a substitute to score a wonderful goal against Atalanta in the Champions League. He scored home and away against Stuttgart - both off the bench. The latter turned out to be his final goal in a Dortmund shirt.

But there has been criticism too. That was particularly the case in December when Adeyemi was substituted on the hour against Borussia Monchengladbach and reacted badly. Former Germany international Markus Babbel publicly questioned his mentality.

Within Dortmund, there are those who defend him. He is a popular figure with staff past and present. Speaking to Alex Clapham, their former set-piece coach, he saw Adeyemi as a particular favourite. "He is an incredible guy. What a character," he told Sky Sports.

"As a coach, he probably taught me more than anybody because I had to work with him in a different way. It probably took me until Christmas of the first season to understand that." Adeyemi responded better to one-on-ones. "It is the little chats sometimes."

Image: It was Hansi Flick who gave Karim Adeyemi his Germany debut in 2021

Flick will understand that better than anyone. And this is why the move to Barcelona could unlock more from the player. This is a coach who has believed in his talent from a young age and always championed him. It is great for Adeyemi. But what about Barca?

It might seem incongruous given the scale of the club, but the expectation levels might be a little lower. At Dortmund, there was some frustration that Adeyemi did not grow into the role of the team's star player. That is clearly not the assignment at Camp Nou.

Barcelona do not need someone to lead the attack. This is a team that scored 95 goals in LaLiga last season, 18 more than Real Madrid. What they need is someone who can impact off the bench, cover across a range of different positions, make a contribution.

Image: Karim Adeyemi's minutes by position for Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga

"I can play in almost any position in the offensive line," Adeyemi told Sky Sports back in that 2023 interview. Since then, he has operated on both flanks and occasionally in the centre. Marcus Rashford did a similar job last season. There will certainly be minutes for him.

In fact, his role could be really important for Barcelona. Consider the template set by Paris Saint-Germain. The former Barca player Ousmane Dembele started only 11 games in Ligue 1 last season. He actually started as many games in the Champions League.

Perhaps it is easier to load the emphasis on European commitments in France than Spain but compare that to Lamine Yamal, who played 26 games from the start in La Liga last season. That was more than any midfielder or attacker in the Barcelona squad.

The chance to rest the star man, after a World Cup in which he went all the way with Spain while Adeyemi was omitted from Germany's campaign, is one that Flick will need to take when and where he can. He will want to be able to do so with minimal disruption.

Flick loves having pace in wide areas. Barcelona still play a possession game under him. Indeed, they averaged 69 per cent possession in La Liga last season, the highest in Europe's five major leagues - even ahead of Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain.

But Flick needs his team to have that speed to go with it. It is this that helps Barcelona break teams down, providing the counter-attacking threat as well as the domination of the ball. Adeyemi suits that style of play. He is someone who can make things happen.

Asking him how he saw his game, he said: "I think [my job is] to get on the nerves of the defenders all the time with one-against-one or runs behind the defenders. Being there where the defender cannot see me. Getting assists, getting goals. This, I think, is my game."

Adeyemi is at a crossroads in his career now. Raphinha was already 25 when he moved to Barcelona from Leeds and changed perspectives about his potential ceiling. Adeyemi is younger. With the right coach, at the right club, the sky is still the limit for him.

Sports.title: Guardiola rejects chance to become Italy head coach
Sports.content:
Pep Guardiola has turned down the chance to take the Italy head coach job, according to Sky in Italy.

Guardiola gave his response to the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) on Thursday night, with Sky in Italy reporting his decision was down to to personal reasons that go beyond football.

The FIGC had met with Guardiola to try and convince him to succeed Gennaro Gattuso as national team head coach and were willing to make an exceptional adjustment to their budget to hire him.

FIGC officials Paolo Maldini and his advisor Leonardo met with Guardiola over three days, explaining their project for the national team moving forward.

In their discussions with the former Manchester City manager in Barcelona, ​​Maldini and Leonardo presented an idea that went beyond simply offering him a coaching role.

In the FIGC's vision, Guardiola would have been the central figure in an 'Azzurro project' aiming to rebuild Italian football on solid foundations. Italy did not even qualify for the expanded World Cup this summer.

It would have been a complete overhaul that would have involved not only the senior national team but all other national teams. The Catalonian is understood to have listened attentively to Maldini and Leonardo's offer.

Alternative candidates for the role are thought to be Roberto Mancini and Andrea Pirlo.

The FIGC brought in Maldini and Leonardo as part of a huge shake-up in Italian football following their failure to qualify for a third consecutive World Cup.

Image: Pep Guardiola won 20 trophies across his Manchester City tenure

Their task was to find a successor to Gattuso, who left his role after missing out on qualification for this summer's tournament in North America.

Guardiola is a free agent for the first time in a decade after ending his 10-year association with Manchester City. He won 20 trophies during his time at the club and finished with a win ratio of 70.8 per cent.

Italy have failed to qualify for the last three major tournaments since winning the European Championships in 2021 under Mancini.

What Guardiola said on his future after City departure

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at the best moments from Pep Guardiola's press conference after the Spaniard confirmed he would leave Man City

Speaking to Sky Sports a year before leaving the Etihad, Guardiola revealed he would be taking a break from football when the time came for his tenure at City to end.

Following the official announcement of his departure, Guardiola doubled down on this suggestion by saying that a desire to spend more time with his family was the catalyst for his decision.

"No plans for [coaching] for a while. Otherwise I would be here. I need to step back. I will not [coach] for a while," he said during his final Manchester City press conference.

"I feel I will not have the energy every day, with expectations to fight for the title. I know myself, I have that energy, but I feel like I will not have it [in the future]."

Speaking exclusively with Sky Sports, he added: "There are things that I have not done that I want to do. I still have my father alive. I want to spend more time with him. My kids... And a lot of things as a human being I can do. I'm fortunate I can decide, that's why I took this decision."

What about England?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jack Gaughan looks at what the future may hold for Pep Guardiola following his Manchester City departure and suggests that a future role within the England national team shouldn't be ruled out

It was widely reported in 2024 that Guardiola had reached a verbal agreement with the FA to replace Gareth Southgate as the new England boss. However, he had a change of heart and opted to stay in Manchester, as Thomas Tuchel was eventually appointed, guiding England to their best World Cup finish on foreign soil.

Tuchel is contracted until the end of Euro 2028 and has vowed to see out his new deal, which was extended in February.

What is known is that Guardiola would be interested in the challenge of moving into international management. In an interview with chef Dani Garcia in 2024, he said: "What I'm not going to do is leave Manchester City and go to another country to do the same thing as I am now.

"I wouldn't have the energy to do so. I'm still here doing what I am today. But the thought of starting somewhere else, with all the process of the training and so on... no, no, no! Maybe a national team, but that's different."

Is international management the meeting in the middle for Guardiola?

Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

Pep Guardiola is the biggest commodity in football management. That's the case now, and that was the case when he took a break after managing Barcelona. That was followed by a move to Bayern Munich, but, as Guardiola is quick to say, he is older, lacks the energy and has too much love for Manchester City to jump into a similar job.

He has expressed an interest in spending more time with his family and resting. But we know what football obsessives are like. It doesn't take long for them to get the itch back, and Guardiola is certainly a football obsessive.

A role in international management could be enough to scratch both itches. On one hand, Guardiola wouldn't be on the training pitch day in, day out, allowing him to have the time with loved ones he desires.

However, every couple of months he could work with a group of players and teach them the Guardiola way across a Euros or World Cup cycle. Not to mention that he would be entering uncharted territory.

Having already achieved everything in club football, the switch to the international game may be incredibly appealing as it is, let alone with the improved work-life balance it offers.

Sports.title: Doyle: Masquerade Ball can clinch historic King George win
Sports.content:
Sky Sports Racing ambassador Hollie Doyle reveals her thoughts on the King George at Ascot on Saturday and runs the rule over the best of the other weekend action at Ascot and York.

Momentous success on cards for Japan

Japan has held a special place in my heart since riding in Tokyo for three winters, so I'll be rooting for their superstar MASQUERADE BALL in the King George VI and Queen Elizabeth Stakes (3.35) at Ascot on Saturday.

Takahisa Tezuka's colt has unfinished business with the mighty Calandagan after losing out right on the line in the Japan Cup back in November. Since then, he has finished a gallant second to Hong Kong's Romantic Warrior in the QEII Cup while the French ace has added the Sheema Classic and the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud to his amazing CV.

Whatever happens, it's going to be a thriller with Aidan O'Brien's Irish Derby winner Benvenuto Cellini getting a lot of weight from the pair but I have a feeling that everything is in place for Masquerade Ball to give the Japanese one of their most momentous successes ever. A year younger than Calandagan and still capable of better, he can take revenge as long as the uphill finish doesn't catch him out.

Moonrise can build on Royal Ascot form

MOONRISE can enhance her reputation in the big two-year-old fillies' race at Ascot, the Group 3 Princess Margaret Japan Cup Stakes (1.45).

Andrew Balding's daughter of Churchill took a step up in grade in her stride when finishing a close third in the Windsor Castle Stakes at the Royal Meeting and the combination of a good attitude and track form can make her hard to beat.

Richard Hannon's Dark Issue was fourth in the Group 3 Albany Stakes at this track last month - form that has since been franked by the runner-up, Sun Goddess, taking a Group 2 in Ireland for Aidan O'Brien - but Oisin Murphy's filly offers better value.

Moore booking looks significant in Valiant

There is no denying that Owen Burrows' filly Touleen was unlucky in the Coronation Stakes last time when she split two Guineas winners, despite enduring such a difficult passage.

She'll be a worthy favourite for the Group 3 Longines Valiant Stakes (2.20) under William Buick, but I prefer to side with Jane Chapple-Hyam's KON TIKI with Ryan Moore another significant booking.

Open to improvement, she is more than capable of winning at this level and shouldn't find this quite as demanding at the Group 2 Duke Of Cambridge when she chased home Blue Bolt for the second time this year.

Unbeaten Zain to take ultra-tough International

My husband Tom (Marquand) holds a favourite's chance in the Moet And Chandon International Handicap (2.55) at Ascot on the unbeaten EXTREMELY ZAIN, who has the potential to ply his trade in Pattern races later in the year.

Image: Extremely Zain returns to action on Saturday

He didn't enjoy the best of runs in a hot handicap at York last time but still found a way through to post an impressive success under Cieren Fallon and has the scope to defy an 8lb rise from what looks a decent draw.

This is ultra-tough though so keep an eye on Jack Channon's Mezcala, the Buckingham Palace winner for Tom who also has more to offer despite reappearing off a stiffer mark of 98.

Champion the one to beat in York feature

I am disappointed to see the Sky Bet York Stakes (2.35) at York attract only five runners, but it is a quality field, headed by the magnificent globetrotter ROYAL CHAMPION.

Karl Burke's eight-year-old has been given a well-deserved break since winning the valuable Neom Turf Cup in Saudi Arabia and finishing fourth behind Romantic Warrior and Masquerade Ball in Hong Kong.

Tough, resilient, and capable of finding his best form fresh, Royal Champion has less to prove than Dante winner Item, who may have had ground excuses in the Epsom Derby but now needs to take a big step forward to win this Group 2.

Ryan sprinter out to build on strong Chester run

The Sky Bet Dash Handicap (2.00) at York has a wide-open feel so I'm opting for value in Kevin Ryan's locally trained WE NEVER STOP, who looks set to go off a big price in the 6f feature.

Having his second start following wind surgery, he can build on an encouraging close second at Chester last month for a trainer who excels on The Knavesmire.

I expected Addison Grey to win after chasing home the subsequent Wokingham Winner Double Rush at Newmarket, but Clive Cox's grey hasn't capitalised in two runs since. Still, an unchanged mark of 94 should see him firmly in the mix once again.

Stepping up my rehab after positive news

Since getting the go-ahead last week to begin weight bearing on my broken left leg, I have been upping my rehabilitation routine at Oaksey House in Lambourn.

I'm working out there five days a week under the supervision of an excellent team, putting in some strong sessions in the gym, on the bike and in the hydro pool with the aim of achieving more movement.

It's a long road back from the injury I sustained in a fall at Bath in May, but it feels good to finally be more active.

Sports.title: Chelsea agree deal with Palace for Lacroix
Sports.content:
Chelsea have agreed a deal with Crystal Palace to sign Maxence Lacroix.

The 26-year-old defender has given permission to finalise the transfer for a fee in the region of £51m.

Sky Sports News understands Chelsea have given Palace the chance to discuss signing one of their defenders available for transfer during talks.

There has been interest from other clubs in Axel Disasi, Trevoh Chalobah and Benoit Badiashile.

Palace and Chelsea have a good relationship and they have done deals for players such as Chalobah and Ben Chilwell in the past.

The Eagles have been concentrating on Augsburg centre-back Chrislain Matsima. However, Sky Sports News understands they are now prepared to walk away from the deal, having become frustrated with the speed of negotiations.

Palace have been interested in several centre-backs since the January window when Marc Guehi was sold to Manchester City.

Among those have been Toulouse's Charlie Cresswell, Lyon's Ruben Kluivert and Trabzonspor's Chibuke Nwaiwu, who is also of interest to Fulham.

Sky Sports' Adam Bate:

Chelsea have not paid a transfer fee for a player aged 26 or over since the summer of 2022 with the ill-fated acquisitions of Raheem Sterling and Kalidou Koulibaly. But Crystal Palace's Maxence Lacroix is a player worth relaxing the policy for.

Far from a veteran, Lacroix, 26, is entering his prime after two strong seasons with Palace. Beyond Selhurst Park, perhaps the Frenchman has gone a little under the radar. But, particularly since Marc Guehi's exit, there is growing awareness of his key role.

Image: Lacroix's top speed for Crystal Palace in the Premier League

Oliver Glasner, who worked with him in both Germany and England, rather summed it up with his own verdict on the player recently. "There is Maxence Lacroix, who came from Wolfsburg, and many asked, 'Why did you sign this player?' I think he stepped up."

Few defenders boast his skillset. Lacroix ranks among the top five fastest centre-backs in the Premier League since his arrival from Wolfsburg in 2024. That recovery speed helps make him one of the most formidable one-on-one defenders in the competition.

The numbers back that up. In one-on-one situations, nobody is better than Lacroix at winning the ball back. He is the only player in the Premier League to have faced 50 or more such situations in the past two seasons and won the ball more often than not.

Image: Lacroix's one-on-one defending for Crystal Palace in the Premier League

At 6'4" tall, Lacroix is a robust physical presence who has adapted easily to the demands of the Premier League. He has all the stats to support that, ranking third for clearances and seventh for aerial duels won. But he can do more than defend his box.

Sports.title: DeChambeau reveals Open penalty frustration
Sports.content:
Bryson DeChambeau has spoken for the first time about the controversial two-shot penalty he believes cost him a shot at winning The Open.

DeChambeau was remarkably penalised in his second round after officials reviewed footage and ruled he had improved the area of his backswing by flattening some long grass on Royal Birkdale's fifth hole.

The penalty turned his bogey into a triple-bogey seven, which moved him from outright second to fifth in the standings at the midway point.

DeChambeau threatened to withdraw from the tournament in protest but played on, making it through to the weekend to end a run of three consecutive missed cuts in majors and avoid the 'Bryson Slam' of missing all four in a season.

But despite recovering with rounds of 69 and 72 he was left wondering what might have been after finishing six shots behind winner Ryan Fox.

"I made the cut," DeChambeau told a LIV Golf UK press conference.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Bryson DeChambeau was given a two-shot penalty after inadvertently improving his lie in thick rough on the fifth hole at The Open.

"It was a good fight. I wish I'd have given it more on Saturday and Sunday, it felt like I could have.

"Besides the fifth, being three over on it, and the 11th, that's six shots. That's tied for the lead right there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Scottie Scheffler defended Ryder Cup teammate Bryson DeChambeau after he was given a 2 shot penalty during the second round of the Open.

"Two holes and I'm right there for the Claret Jug."

World No 1 Scheffler defended DeChambeau over the rules controversy, insisting his fellow American is "not a cheater", while Rory McIlroy described the incident as "performative".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rory McIlroy spoke to the media after his third round of The Open and said he was not impressed with Bryson DeChambeau's actions that led to his two-stroke penalty after the second round.

"I won't pretend to be up here and defend Bryson," McIlroy said on Saturday. "I'm not particularly fond of him. I think a lot of it's performative. I think a lot of it's for attention.

"To hold the tournament hostage like that, and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn't feel like it was a great look."

Sports.title: Jürgen Klopp confirmed as Germany head coach for Euro 2028 and 2030 World Cup
Sports.content:
Jürgen Klopp is to return to the dugout after being appointed head coach of the Germany men’s national side until 2030. The 59-year-old takes over from Julian Nagelsmann in the job after Germany’s humbling last-32 defeat by Paraguay at the World Cup.

Klopp has been away from frontline management since leaving Liverpool at the end of the 2023-24 season, when he cited fatigue as his principal reason for stepping away after a hugely successful nine-season spell in which he won the Premier League and Champions League, among other trophies. He won two Bundesliga titles in charge of Borussia Dortmund in the early 2010s.

“It’s a great honour for me to be sitting here today,” Klopp told a press conference in Frankfurt on Friday morning. “This is ideally the high point of my career, of my life, my professional life. I will give it everything I have. The national team brings us Germans together like almost nothing else can. That’s what makes this task so special for me.”

Klopp added that he would be prepared to leave without any severance pay if the job doesn’t work out, and threatened to resign if the media doesn’t “leave my family in peace”.

Klopp was made Red Bull’s head of global soccer in October 2024, working in the background for the multiclub organisation. He also worked as a pundit for German TV during the World Cup in the US, Mexico and Canada.

“We’re very happy to be able to present Jürgen Klopp today as the new coach,” the German Football Association [DFB] president, Bernd Neuendorf, said. “We’ve had very intense discussions. He was our ideal solution from the start. We at the DFB were unanimous in saying he was the candidate we had to talk to. Our talks with Jürgen only strengthened our belief that he’s the right man at the right time.”

Neuendorf also thanked Red Bull for ending its contract with Klopp early. Klopp’s release was secured by the German FA making a €1m donation to the company’s Wings for Life foundation and agreeing to play three internationals in Leipzig, where Red Bull backs the city’s Bundesliga team, by 2030.

His first game in charge of the four-time World ⁠Cup winners will come away to their bitter rivals the Netherlands on 24 September in the Nations League. Klopp’s side will also face Greece and Serbia in Group A2 before preparing for their Euro 2028 qualifying campaign. His contract will run until the end of the 2030 World Cup in Morocco, Portugal and Spain. He will be assisted by Peter Krawietz, Pep Lijnders and former Germany international Sven Bender.

Klopp faces a daunting task in turning around the fortunes of the national side, which has failed to win a knockout game at a World Cup since beating Argentina in the 2014 final, after exiting at the group stages in 2018 and in 2022 before this year’s last-32 knockout. They showed promising signs of improvement in their home Euros in 2024 under Nagelsmann before losing to eventual winners Spain in the quarter-final.

The former Germany defender Per Mertesacker is also joining the national side set-up as the new managing director for sport, with a role overseeing the the men’s national teams and an emphasis on bringing players through youth national teams for the senior team. He will start the role in January and joins after eight years running Arsenal’s academy.

Sports.title: From Popp to Diani: 10 women’s transfers you may have missed during the men’s World Cup
Sports.content:
There were a host of big women’s football transfers which were hard to miss across June and July, despite the dominance of the men’s World Cup. Among them were Beth Mead’s move from Arsenal to Manchester City, Mary Earps and Georgia Stanway returning to the Women’s Super League with London City Lionesses and Arsenal, Sam Kerr leaving Chelsea to return to Gotham FC and, most prominently, Alexia Putellas’s game-changing switch from Barcelona to London City.

But here are 10 transfers you might have missed while attention was focused on the action in the US, Canada and Mexico.

Alexandra Popp to Borussia Dortmund

The three-time Champions League winner Alex Popp may be reaching the twilight of her playing career but her move to Borussia Dortmund, signing a three-year contract at the tier-three club, after 14 years with Wolfsburg shows she is not quite ready to hang up her boots. The 35-year-old has been prolific for club and country, scoring 112 goals in 219 games for Wolfsburg and 67 goals in 145 games for Germany prior to her international retirement in 2024. A Borussia Dortmund fan whose “heart beats for this club”, Popp couldn’t pass up the opportunity to assist the development of the women’s team, which was launched in 2020.

Kirsty Hanson to Tottenham

The 28-year-old was a top target for Spurs after a phenomenal fourth season at Aston Villa. Last year Hanson said she was working on adding more goals to her game – come the end of last season she was the third-highest top scorer in the WSL, finishing on 12 in 22 games, which was 43% of Villa’s total tally and only one goal behind second-place Alessia Russo. She heads to a focused Tottenham who are giving their manager, Martin Ho, the tools to push closer to, or even break into, the top four.

Ally Sentnor to Angel City

Sentnor, who was the first overall pick in the 2024 NWSL draft, was the subject of a blockbuster $850,000 (£635,000) trade between Kansas City Current and Angel City on 19 June. She then made her debut for her new side on 3 July, starting a 2-0 win against Orlando Pride. The USA women’s national team player has scored seven goals and provided three assists in 23 international games and, at just 22 years old, has a lot of football ahead of her.

View image in fullscreen Ally Sentnor (right) on the ball for Angel City in a 2-0 win against against Chicago Stars last weekend. Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/Shutterstock

Felicia Schröder to Real Madrid

Many clubs were circling but in the end Felicia Schröder completed a big-money move from Häcken to Real Madrid. Multiple Swedish outlets reported the deal for the 19-year-old forward was worth over 15m Swedish kronor (£1.15m). She attracted attention from across the world as she racked up 91 goals in 128 games for Häcken and starred in Uefa’s inaugural women’s Europa Cup competition, finishing as top scorer with eight goals, four of which came in the two-legged final against Hammarby.

Manaka Matsukubo to Chelsea

The versatile 21-year-old, who can play as a forward or attacking midfielder, joined Chelsea from North Carolina Courage for an undisclosed fee but, as one of the most exciting young talents in the women’s game, it’s unlikely she came cheap. The Japan international scored 11 goals, became the youngest NWSL player to score a hat-trick, and was named NWSL midfielder of the year in 2025. She was up to five goals in nine games in the 2026 season before Chelsea swooped earlier this month.

View image in fullscreen Manaka Matsukubo at her Chelsea unveiling. Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Johanna Rytting Kaneryd to OL Lyonnes

The 29-year-old won three league titles, two FA Cups and two League Cups with Chelsea, including a domestic treble in . Rytting Kaneryd is one of several attacking players to leave Chelsea this summer with Sam Kerr, Guro Reiten and Catarina Macario also having departed as they revamp their front line in an effort to reclaim their WSL crown after Manchester City ended their six-year title-winning run.

Noémie Mouchon to Everton

The loss of the forward Kelly Gago, who has signed for West Ham, has been tempered a little by the arrival of the French striker Noémie Mouchon from Leicester. Mouchon did not have the easiest time at Leicester after arriving from Reims with expectations high. The 23-year-old sustained an anterior cruciate ligament injury one month into her first season in the WSL and was ruled out for the remainder of the campaign. She made 16 appearances and scored two goals in the WSL last season but made only two starts. Everton will be hoping she can find the form that helped her to nine goals in 22 games for Reims in the 2023-24 season.

Denise O’Sullivan to Gotham (on loan)

The influential Republic of Ireland midfielder returns to the NWSL with Gotham after six months with Liverpool. The 32-year-old spent 10 seasons in the US before her January move to Liverpool, with Houston Dash and North Carolina Courage (albeit with a number of loan spells in Australia and England). She won the NWSL Shield in 2017 and again in 2018 and 2019 when Courage also secured the NWSL Championship, with O’Sullivan named the side’s MVP in both years. She has 22 goals in 132 games for Ireland.

View image in fullscreen Denise O’Sullivan (right) showing off her close control against Aston Villa last season. Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

Bethany England to Crystal Palace

Bethany England’s Tottenham departure was mourned by fans, with the former Chelsea forward having become the team’s record goalscorer in the WSL with 32 in three-and-a-half seasons, helping them to a first FA Cup final in 2024. The 32-year-old has signed a two-year contract with Crystal Palace, who earned promotion back into the top flight with a second-place finish in WSL2. After four WSL titles, two FA Cups and two League Cups with Chelsea, England brings a wealth of experience to Palace.

Kadidiatou Diani to London City Lionesses

The arrival of Alexia Putellas and Mary Earps has dominated the London City Lionesses transfer talk, while the acquisition of the France forward Kadidiatou Diani from Lyonnes for more than £500,000 has flown somewhat under the radar. The 31-year-old scored 41 goals in 93 games in three seasons for the Champions League giants following her stunning 92 goals in 168 games for Paris Saint-Germain. Michelle Kang, who owns both London City and Lyonnes, will be hoping she brings that edge up front to the ambitious WSL side. They finished sixth last season, their debut campaign in the top flight, nine points behind Tottenham, but they want more and are spending big to make progress.

Sports.title: Chelsea paid Aston Villa £117m for Morgan Rogers. Is he the right fit?
Sports.content:
It quickly became apparent this summer that Aston Villa would not be holding on to Morgan Rogers. Having helped the club finish fourth in the Premier League and win the Europa League, the 23-year-old was in demand.

Arsenal looked like his likeliest next destination, with the champions eager to strengthen the left side of their attack. The charm offensive came from many angles, with Martin Ødegaard, Mikel Arteta and the club’s England players trying to sell the idea to Rogers. But, with Arsenal reluctant to meet Villa’s asking price, Chelsea intervened and made Rogers the most expensive British player ever, surpassing the £116m that Manchester City paid Nottingham Forest for Elliot Anderson earlier this summer.

Xabi Alonso is new to Chelsea, so it is difficult to know exactly where Rogers will play. The versatile forward, who started out at West Brom before moving to Manchester City, Middlesbrough and then Villa, will probably be used in a variety of roles – often starting from the left but having opportunities to take up various attacking positions.

Alonso predominantly used a 3-4-3 formation at Bayer Leverkusen and a 4-2-3-1 at Real Madrid. If Chelsea play with three at the back, Rogers will be the left-sided No 10 in the team; if they use a four-man defence, he will start slightly wider but with the freedom to come inside – or he might even occupy the central role.

If Alonso goes with the style he used at Leverkusen, Rogers might not be the best fit. During Alonso’s two full seasons in the Bundesliga, the team averaged 62.1% (2023-24) and 59.6% (2024-25) possession. During their title-winning campaign in 2023-24, they went unbeaten all season while dominating the ball and moving up the pitch slowly.

They were set up to patiently build with lots of passes, win back possession quickly if they lost it and keep the ball as close to the opposition’s goal as possible. They made 367 high turnovers, which was 54 more than any other side. This system works best with attacking players who are tidy and intricate in tight spaces. However, Rogers is at his most effective when he can use his pace and gallop into space.

His dribble completion rate last season was 34.2%, which was nothing to shout about. And his completion rate for passes under pressure was 73.4% – again not exceptional. Of the 161 forwards and midfielders who attempted at least 300 passes under pressure last season, Rogers ranked 143rd. The statistics suggest he is not particularly effective in close-quarters engagements.

With space to attack, Rogers is a threat. He made 223 progressive carries last season, the 10th highest among Premier League forwards, wingers and attacking midfielders. Only Cody Gakpo (41) and Matheus Cunha (35) had more carries that ended in shots than Rogers (30). He also created 16 chances for teammates after a carry: only 11 players created more. Rogers’ combined 46 chances created and shots taken following carries put him behind just Jérémy Doku (58), Gakpo (57) and Bukayo Saka (56). Alonso’s passing style may not bring the best from Rogers.

There are reasons for optimism though. Rogers is frequently on the move and that makes him difficult to track. Only four players made more off-ball runs in the league last season; his 160 off-ball runs ending in the box was the eighth highest in the division.

View image in fullscreen A mural of Jude Bellingham and Rogers in Birmingham. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

He also has the potential to form a good relationship with João Pedro. The Brazilian will probably be the focal point of the team and he is not a conventional No 9. He likes to drop deep, link with teammates and be a creator almost as much as a finisher. With Pedro dropping back, there will be room for Rogers to exploit beyond him: he made 258 runs in behind last season, the 12th highest in the league.

Rogers’ strong relationship with Ollie Watkins bodes well for Chelsea. He created 20 open-play chances for Watkins last season, which was the second most from one player to another in the league. Wherever he has played, Rogers has developed an understanding with his teammates. He already has a close friendship with Cole Palmer after their time together in the Manchester City academy.

Rogers’ other great attribute is his ball-striking ability. Since he made his Premier League debut in February 2024, Rogers has scored 21 non-penalty goals from 14.7 non-penalty expected goals. His overperformance of +6.3 is the 10th highest in the league.

Rogers has a great strike on him and it could be a gamechanger for Chelsea, particularly when they play teams employing a low block. His five league goals from outside the box since his Villa debut is bettered by only six players. Few players are as accurate when shooting from distance. It was his shot against Norway that led to Jude Bellingham’s winning goal in the World Cup quarter-final.

Chelsea have paid an incredible amount of money for Rogers and there are reasons to wonder if the move will work tactically. But Rogers has a habit of making an impact regardless of the context. He’s not a right winger but he still made his presence known for England against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final, setting up Anthony Gordon’s opener from the right.

Is he a £117m player? Perhaps not. Will he succeed playing the same way he played at Villa? Perhaps not. But it’s hard to imagine him not making a significant impact at Stamford Bridge.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Elliot Anderson lauds City as ‘kings of Manchester’ after £116m Forest transfer
Sports.content:
Elliot Anderson has called Manchester City the “kings of Manchester” after completing his £116m move to the club from Nottingham Forest.

The 23-year-old was a key part of England’s third-place finish at the World Cup, having been an ever-present for Forest in the Premier League last season. Before Morgan Rogers’ £117m transfer to Chelsea from Aston Villa on Tuesday, Anderson’s fee was the record for a British player.

The midfielder is taking a three-week break after his exploits in North America but is clearly relishing the prospect of playing for City, picking out the first Manchester derby of the new season on 13 September as a standout fixture. He may well be in line for a hot reception from the Old Trafford faithful given his claims about City’s superior status.

“It’s one of the biggest derbies in the world and for as long as I’ve known Manchester, City have been the kings of Manchester,” Anderson said in an interview on City’s website. “It’ll be a great fixture and I can’t wait to be involved in something like that.

“They’re winners, they’re relentless, and that’s the sort of team I want to be a part of – champions and people who win trophies,” Anderson said of his reason for signing for City.

“Over the last 10, 12 years, they’ve dominated, so that’s why I wanted to join. It’s happened quite quick, but I think I always believed I could get to this point and this is where I want to be. Now that I’m here, I’ll keep pushing and try to take this club forward.” Anderson’s rise has been rapid, with his England debut coming as recently as last September, in a 2-0 victory over Andorra.

The Tyneside-born player, who began his career at Newcastle before joining Forest for £35m in July 2024, believes there is much more to come. “I’m only 23, so I’ve got plenty of time to get to my best levels and I definitely think I’m not there yet,” he said.

The deal was agreed three weeks ago but finalised this week after the player’s return from the World Cup. Anderson has signed until 2031 and is City’s first major signing since Enzo Maresca succeeded Pep Guardiola as manager. He is looking forward to working with the Italian. “I’ve watched his teams over the past couple of years and spoke to a few of the lads from Chelsea and they all rate him very highly,” Anderson said.

“I like to be intense when I play and use lots of energy around the pitch and get the fans going. So, I think that’ll be good.”

Kevin De Bruyne, who departed City two summers ago, is an idol for Anderson. “Growing up through the academy at Newcastle, I’ve always wanted to play like him,” Anderson said. “I’ve watched him all the time and to be sat here in the team that he was doing it for is so special.”

Anderson led the Premier League last season in most touches (3,300), most duels won (297) and winning possession (306). “I think I bring a bit of everything. I bring quality, physicality, energy,” he said. “I’d like to think I’d get them [the City supporters] excited, get them off their feet and bring energy to the team.”

Anderson spent half a season on loan at Bristol Rovers in 2022 and became known as the “Geordie Maradona” among supporters. “They started that and it sort of stuck everywhere I’ve been,” he said. “It makes me happy and it gives me real confidence.”

Reflecting on the World Cup, Anderson added: “It was disappointing, but I loved it personally. We had the whole country behind us and we’ve done so well but just fell short. From a personal point of view, I thought I did pretty well.”

Sports.title: Aston Villa seal loan signing of Alejandro Garnacho from Chelsea
Sports.content:
Aston Villa have confirmed the loan signing of the Chelsea winger Alejandro Garnacho, as a summer of change continues at Villa Park.

The deal for Garnacho’s season-long loan includes a conditional obligation to buy a player who joined Chelsea last August from Manchester United in a deal worth £40m. Villa will be expected to pay a similar fee for the 22-year-old, who struggled to impress at Stamford Bridge despite featuring in 43 games in all competitions and scoring eight goals.

Garnacho has been allowed to depart Stamford Bridge after being informed he was not guaranteed regular playing time under the club’s new manager, Xabi Alonso. He did not report for duty when Chelsea players returned for pre-season, as arranged.

It was agreed he would stay away from the training ground while any departure was completed. Named in Argentina’s initial 55-man selection, he missed out on this summer’s World Cup.

Unai Emery, Villa’s manager, said: “We are delighted with Alejandro. He is so talented, young and he ⁠showed us his wish to help our ​project. We are ‌really happy.”

Villa’s third signing of the summer, to follow the arrivals of Johan Manzambi and João Gomes, comes via a familiar trade route. The £117m deal that took Morgan Rogers to Stamford Bridge this week continued a run of transfers between the two clubs, incorporating Carney Chukwuemeka’s and Omari Kellyman’s sale to Chelsea in 2022 and 2024, Ian Maatsen heading in the reverse direction in 2024 and Axel Disasi’s brief 2025 loan to Villa.

Another former Chelsea charge, Jadon Sancho, spent last season on loan at Villa from United and, despite becoming a free agent, he was not signed. Youri Tielemans has also departed Villa for Manchester United this month after his £35m release clause was triggered as the Europa League champions rebuild as a Champions League club, though one under Uefa sanction.

Earlier this summer Villa received a partly suspended £19.4m fine by Uefa for a “significant breach” of the squad cost ratio rule for 2025. Depending on the club significantly decreasing their squad cost ratio in 2026, £12.9m is suspended, with the club restricted on the registration of new players on their squad list for the coming Champions League season.

Sports.title: ‘Don’t become the protagonist’: Andoni Iraola on the secret of Spain’s success and his role at Liverpool
Sports.content:
Over coffee in Liverpool’s plush hotel in Chicago, Andoni Iraola presents his theory for the phenomenal success of Basque and Spanish coaches. It is a theory that will shape his entire approach to life as the Liverpool head coach and his attempts to bring the connection, the joy and the belief back to Anfield. It centres on the power of the collective.

The Champions League, the Premier League, the Europa League, the FA Cup, the League Cup, the European Championship and, as of Sunday, the World Cup: all currently in the hands of Basque and Spanish coaches, even if Pep Guardiola has since taken his leave from Manchester City. Next season, four men from the small Basque region of Gipuzkoa will manage four of the Premier League’s main contenders, Iraola included, alongside Mikel Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Unai Emery. There is, Iraola believes, a simple explanation for the rise of the guys from Gipuzkoa and for Spanish dominance across a global stage.

“They ask me why a lot of Basque managers especially have arrived to this level and why Spanish teams are winning a lot of things,” Iraola explains. “I always say that a sense of collectiveness is very important. Spain has never had the best athletes. If you analyse in swimming, boxing, track and field, Spain don’t normally win medals. But in collective sports they are very good. In football, basketball, handball, hockey, normally they have good teams. We always put the team first. An example is someone like Rodri. He didn’t score or make an assist but at the end they won the World Cup and he won best player of the tournament. Team-first was always integrated in how we were raised.”

Iraola, warm and friendly despite the jetlag at the start of Liverpool’s pre-season tour of the US, then gives an immediate example of how he embodies those values. He is asked about a letter he sent to Liverpool in January 2014 when, as captain of boyhood club Athletic Club, he rejected the opportunity to sign for Brendan Rodgers’s team. By all accounts courteous and apologetic, as well as highly unusual, the letter provides a telling insight into Iraola’s character. It is an open goal of a question to a new head coach wanting to win over a new fanbase. But Iraola declines to shoot.

Following a lengthy pause, he says: “I don’t know if I want to tell this story so early in my career here. I would like to win some games first. It is a nice story but if you remember me in some months, then you can ask me again. I don’t like to do this from the beginning. I just don’t want to. It will look like I am selling myself. We need some time, and to win some games.”

Iraola’s outlook is refreshing – “Don’t become the protagonist,” he says of his role – and one that Liverpool can easily identify with. Continuing with the theme of Spain’s collectiveness, he adds: “I think there has to be something in society. It cannot only just be about football. I think things work when we are not just selfish, no? When, in the end, you prioritise the situation of the one who has less. That happens also in football. The ones that don’t play, the ones who come from the academy, the ones who earn less. You can compare it with society.”

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola will hope to inspire Jeremie Frimpong this season after his disappointing debut campaign at Anfield. Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

But, and it is a “but” that needs saying given what Iraola hopes to achieve, there were few signs of togetherness at Liverpool last season as Arne Slot’s reign unravelled amid acrimony in the dressing room and in the crowd. The power of the individual took over, and the power of the team appeared secondary. Mohamed Salah’s frequent attempts to undermine his former, title-winning coach was not the only example of that last season.

“I cannot change the personality of the players,” says Iraola, who will manage for the first time as Liverpool head coach on Saturday against Sunderland in Nashville. “Some players are very different to me but they are great players. I don’t want to change everyone and what they think is the best way. But I think we need to think collectively in this game. As a player you are always selfish. You always want to play, you always want to get your stats, you always want to play all the minutes, but I think there has to be an understanding that this is not going to always happen and still I have to be helpful with my teammates and with the team.

double quotation mark I always say we are assistants to the players. They are the main part Andoni Iraola

“The first thing we have to do is try to play well, but it’s not just only about playing well. Supporters have to identify with what they see on the pitch. Sometimes it’s not about just putting one ball in the top corner. A lot of the time, the ones watching the game, OK, they cannot do that but they can run, they can fight for the balls, they can press, they can fight until the last line for every situation and when they see this from the players of their team it’s easier to get behind that team. I will encourage my team to give them these things.”

Iraola never came close to signing for Liverpool 12 years ago despite the best efforts of Michael Edwards, until recently the chief executive of football for the club’s owners, Fenway Sports Group. “I never really wanted to leave Athletic Club,” their former right-back admits. “For me, Athletic Club was the place to be. The only way of leaving was to go to the MLS [with New York City FC] and try something completely different. I didn’t want to become a problem for the club.”

The 44-year-old, however, does see parallels between his boyhood club and his new one. He explains: “This is one of the biggest clubs in the world and, in some way, the comparison to Athletic Club probably isn’t fair, but in a lot of ways I see a lot of similar things. This sense of belonging, of being a little bit different. This connection, also, with players from the academy. The atmosphere of Anfield.”

At his official unveiling in Liverpool last week, Iraola said he intends to immerse himself in the city and “take some pictures” of the tourist spots. The truth is he has already done so. He visited the city a few times during his playing days with Athletic and for a very simple reason. “It had the best flight connections,” he laughs. “The best connections were Manchester and Brussels and sometimes we only had two or three days so the main thing was to go somewhere quick. I remember the first time I went to Liverpool it was already the Christmas market so it was probably around the November international break. We had no kids at the time so we are talking about a lot of years ago but it was a lovely time with my wife.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There has been no holiday this summer for Iraola and his family, now extended by two children. “I went home for one week in the half-term for the kids at the end of May,” he says. “That was once the season had ended. I have mostly been in Bournemouth but I also had some trips to Liverpool to sort the schools and the housing. This is the stuff I wanted to do before I started working officially.”

Iraola describes the process of leaving Bournemouth after three impressive years as “very, very clean” and claims he only started considering his next step once last season had ended with the club in Europe for the first time. The process of becoming Slot’s replacement “was actually quite fast”. He says: “Honestly. It was true that I was talking with some clubs [Milan, Bayer Leverkusen and Crystal Palace all made approaches]. I think it was the first or second week after the season ended. But it happened fast. They contacted me, and it didn’t take a lot [to say yes to Liverpool this time].”

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola answers questions in the US before Liverpool’s opening pre-season game against Sunderland on Saturday. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

It hasn’t taken long for Liverpool fans to create a song in honour of their new head coach. Sung to the tune of Christy Moore’s Viva la Quinta Brigada, written about Irish volunteers who fought against Franco’s fascist forces in the Spanish civil war, the song went viral within days of Iraola’s appointment in June. He is genuinely astonished when told, almost spluttering over a second cup of coffee.

“A new one?” Iraola asks incredulously. “For me it is a strange situation because I always understand that football is about the players. At the beginning when I arrived in England, I remember the first few games I didn’t go with the players to clap the supporters after games. Tommy and Shaun [Elphick and Cooper, Bournemouth assistants who have followed Iraola to Liverpool] said I should join in. In Spain, normally you leave it to the players; they are the ones who have played the game and we are the ones who stayed behind. In England, managers are the ones who go to the fans, so I have done it every time.

Quick Guide Liverpool and Newcastle plan Keegan tributes Show Newcastle and Liverpool are in discussions over a tribute to Kevin Keegan before the clubs meet for their opening fixture of the new Premier League season at St James' Park on 23 August. Keegan rose to prominence at Liverpool, later becoming a folk hero on the pitch and as manager on Tyneside. The former England striker's death at the age of 75 was announced on Monday, and Newcastle have confirmed that both clubs are talking about a shared tribute. 'The opening Premier League match of 2026-27 sees Newcastle United hosting Liverpool – where Kevin made 323 appearances between 1971 and 1977,' a statement on the club website said. 'To ensure his memory is marked fittingly before the game, the club is in communication with Liverpool and will work closely with supporter groups ... and the Premier League, to shape tributes.' Newcastle will hold a minute's silence before their friendly at Gateshead on Saturday, while during their trip to Bristol City, Keegan’s image will be shown on the stadium’s screens in the seventh minute, a reference to the shirt number he wore during his distinguished career. In addition, the club will consult Keegan’s family 'at the appropriate time' as they consider options for a permanent memorial. PA Media Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

“These are the cultural things you have to learn when you arrive in a new league. But I always say we are assistants to the players. They are the main part. Our main thing is to help them and they are the only ones who can give us success. We are not as important as they are, that is pretty clear.”

The Kop may dispute that theory, but not Iraola’s take on the power of the collective if restored to full working order.

Sports.title: Socceroos star Cristian Volpato allegedly tests positive for cocaine during roadside test
Sports.content:
Socceroos forward Cristian Volpato has allegedly tested positive for cocaine after being stopped while driving at almost 50km/h over the speed limit in Sydney.

Volpato was one of Australia’s breakout stars of the 2026 World Cup but is now back in the spotlight after allegedly driving a BMW Coupe at 109km/h in a 60km/h zone across Anzac Bridge about 1.10am on Friday.

The 22-year-old was subjected to a roadside drug test which allegedly returned a positive result for cocaine. A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis, while NSW police confirmed it will continue its inquiries.

Volpato was reportedly issued an infringement notice for speeding and has had his international driver’s licence suspended for six months, meaning he cannot drive in New South Wales. He has not been charged with a criminal offence.

Police allege that Volpato was also stopped two hours earlier on Anzac Bridge, west of Sydney’s CBD, and issued an infringement notice after allegedly driving more than 20km/h over the speed limit.

He was subjected to a roadside alcohol breath test at about 11.05pm Thursday, which returned a negative result.

Football Australia has been contacted for comment.

Volpato plays football for Italian club Sassuolo and represented Italy at at under-19 and under-20 level before switching his international allegiance to Australia on the eve of the World Cup.

He made three appearances for the Socceroos at the tournament and provided an attacking threat as the side progressed from the group stage as runners-up before being knocked out by Egypt in the last 32.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Australia Sport Get a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports desk Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Volpato was born and raised in Sydney and played junior football at Sydney United 58, Sydney FC and Western Sydney Wanderers before moving overseas to join Serie A club Roma.

He left Roma after two seasons to join Sassuolo where he has scored seven goals in three seasons, before making his mark with the Socceroos and shaping up as a key to the national side’s future.

Sports.title: Norway considers filing Fifa ethics complaint over Trump role in World Cup red card saga
Sports.content:
Donald Trump’s role in clearing Folarin Balogun from a mandatory one-game ban at the World Cup is set to provoke a formal complaint to Fifa ethics investigators.

The Norway soccer federation said Thursday its board of directors will consider filing the complaint at its next meeting, likely on 6 August.

“We need our leader in Fifa to say that this was an error,” Norwegian federation president Lise Klaveness told the Times in an interview published Thursday.

After Trump called Fifa president Gianni Infantino, a one-game ban for Balogun’s red-card tackle against Bosnia and Herzegovina was deferred so he could play against Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake.

Belgium beat the US 4-1 after a chaotic 36 hours at the World Cup. The Belgium players were seemingly fired up by one of the all-time controversies in tournament history.

Trump called the referee’s red card for Balogun after video review a “horrible” call and took credit for getting Fifa to review what should routinely have been a one-game ban.

“We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process,” Klaveness told the Times of the Fifa ruling that was unprecedented in the past 60 years at World Cups. “When you bend a rule like this, you’re on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk,” said the former Women’s World Cup player for Norway, who is an elected member of European soccer body Uefa’s executive committee.

Klaveness is a lawyer and judge who has positioned the Norwegian federation as a conscience in world soccer since her election in 2022. “It is a worry for the game when you compromise fundamental rules of the game,” she said Thursday about not enforcing Balogun’s ban.

Norway previously joined a London-based NGO’s complaint to the Fifa ethics committee alleging Infantino breached a statutory duty of political neutrality, including by creating a peace prize to award to Trump at the World Cup draw in December.

The close personal and political ties between Trump and Infantino include the US president believing the soccer official could be a good pick as next secretary general of the United Nations, the New York Post reported this week.

The human rights NGO, FairSquare, also has filed an ethics complaint about the Balogun incident to the International Olympic Committee, where Infantino is an elected member, about breaching its rules on political neutrality.

Fifa and the IOC rarely acknowledge or provide updates on potential cases before their ethics bodies. The independence of Fifa’s process to handle complaints alleging unethical conduct has been questioned since the lead investigator and judge both were replaced in 2017, in the second year of Infantino’s presidency. Fifa has yet to publish documents explaining how its disciplinary judges reached verdicts about Balogun or other World Cup players.

Sports.title: Per Mertesacker lands new job immediately after Jurgen Klopp appointment
Sports.content:
Per Mertesacker lands new job immediately after Jurgen Klopp appointment

Per Mertesacker has been named the German FA's new managing director for sport.

The former Arsenal defender's appointment follows Jurgen Klopp's arrival as national team boss.



3 Mertesacker has landed a new role with the German FA following Klopp's arrival Credit: Getty

Klopp has succeeded Julian Nagelsmann in the dugout following Germany's round of 32 exit at the World Cup.

He has signed a four-year deal through to the end of the 2030 finals.

It marks Klopp's first managerial role since leaving Liverpool in 2024, having served as Red Bull's head of global soccer since the start of last year.

The 59-year-old is not the only familiar face to have joined the national team set-up, though.



Mertesacker's new job

Mertesacker has also signed a deal through until the summer of 2030.

He will succeed Andreas Rettig as the DFB's managing director for sport from January 1.

Rettig's contract expires at the end of December following three years in the role.



Mertesacker's arrival will follow the upcoming Nations League campaign.

Germany are set to face the Netherlands, Greece and Serbia across September, October and November.



However, he will assume the role prior to the start of Euro 2028 qualifying.

3 Mertesacker was a member of Germany's 2014 World Cup-winning squad Credit: Getty

As a player, Mertesacker scored four goals in 104 caps for Germany and was part of the 2014 World Cup-winning side.

Having retired in 2018, the 41-year-old spent eight years as Arsenal's academy manager.



His new role marks his first job since leaving the Gunners at the end of last season.

Speaking following his appointment, Mertesacker explained: "I’m really looking forward to this new role and the responsibility that comes with it.

"I have always remained in contact with the DFB, even after my international career ended, so returning in this role is something very special for me. German football has enormous potential.

"With humility, a willingness to work hard and the necessary patience, we want to develop talented players and people who can make the difference.



3 Klopp has been appointed as Germany manager on a four-year deal Credit: Getty

"Together, we want to create an environment in which players can take responsibility, grow through challenges and fulfil their potential, from grassroots level all the way through to the national teams.

"It’s an honour for me to have the opportunity to help shape the DFB’s future and contribute to its continued development."

Klopp's backroom team

As well as confirming the appointment of Mertesacker, the DFB have also announced three members of Klopp's coaching staff.



His former Liverpool coaches Peter Krawietz and Pep Lijnders will serve as assistants.

They will be joined in the same role by former Borussia Dortmund and Germany midfielder Sven Bender.

The two-time Bundesliga champion made 181 appearances for Dortmund during Klopp's time as manager.

Sports.title: Pep Guardiola rejects immediate return to management after international offer
Sports.content:
Pep Guardiola has turned down the opportunity to become the next Italy head coach.

The former Manchester City boss was the first-choice candidate to succeed Gennaro Gattuso who left the role in March following Italy’s failure to qualify for a third successive World Cup.

4 Pep Guardiola bid farewell to Manchester City in May after a decade at the club Credit: Getty

Italian Football Federation (FIGC) technical director Paolo Maldini had sounded out Guardiola as the man to help rebuild the national team.

Maldini and his advisor Leonardo flew to Barcelona last weekend to hold talks with Guardiola in the hope of luring him into his first international role.

Not the right time

However, the Spaniard has opted against accepting the offer as he wants to dedicate time to his family.

The 55-year-old is determined to take extended leave from football management to recharge before making a comeback in the future.

An instant return to football following a decade in charge at the Etihad Stadium was always likely to be a difficult hurdle to overcome in negotiations.

There were also Guardiola’s reported salary demands of around £17million a year.

The figure was at odds with the FIGC’s budget of £8.5m a year although one senior figure said there could be salary exceptions for managers of a certain level.

The news comes as a huge blow to the FIGC who had hoped to transform Italy’s flailing fortunes under Guardiola.

The Spaniard's decision could see Maldini turn his attention to Carlo Ancelotti in a bid to fill the void while former Italy midfielder Andrea Pirlo is another option.

The legendary Italian is contracted to Brazil until after the 2030 World Cup; however, the mood around his position with the Selecao has worsened following their premature World Cup exit.

4 Brazil boss Carlo Ancelotti remains on Maldini's list of options Credit: Getty

4 It's back to the drawing board for Leonardo and Paolo Maldini in their search for a new manager Credit: Getty

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Maldini said had hoped to confirm a new manager by the end of the week.

“The ideal would be to have the coach by the end of this week, but perhaps even more ideal would be to wait for the person we really want,”

“There is a certain hurry, but not a hasty one.

“We cannot deny that we also spoke to Carlo Ancelotti before talking to Pep, and it felt only right to start with those we considered to be the best in the world. So we needed to get a general idea of their availability.”

According to Italian daily La Gazzetta dello Sport, Guardiola told the FIGC that he had seriously considered the offer but the timing was not right for him to take the job.

The report claims that Guardiola still sees himself as a day-to-day coach on the training pitch rather than one that adopts a part-time role.

4 Guardiola's need for the day-to-day responsibilities of coaching may have led to his decision to turn down the job Credit: Getty

Maldini and Leonardo previously claimed that it could take eight to ten years for Italy to return to the top of international football, a timespan that may have further deterred Guardiola from the position.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp makes Germany quit threat just minutes after being announced as manager
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp makes Germany quit threat just minutes after being announced as manager

Jurgen Klopp vowed he will be 'gone' as Germany manager if the media 'don't leave my family alone'.

The 59-year-old made the sensational threat shortly after being unveiled as the new boss of Die Mannschaft.



1 Klopp's contract with Germany runs until 2030 Credit: Getty

"On the day you no longer want this, say so. And I'm gone. No severance pay," Klopp said.

"If you say tomorrow that I'm crap, I'm gone. Not just individuals — it would have to be more than that.

"If the DFB says I'm crap, I'm gone. If you behave out of line and don't leave my family alone, I'm gone."



Klopp's warning came after he brought an end to a two-year stint as the head of global soccer for Red Bull.

He recently shared his knowledge and expertise as a football pundit with during the World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico.



During his time away from the dugout, Klopp has been linked with various club roles including the previously vacant position at Real Madrid.

But managing his country is one role that Klopp could not turn a blind eye to and German Football Association president, Bernd Neuendorf shared his delight at securing the former Liverpool boss.



“We’re very happy to be able to present Jürgen Klopp today as the new coach,” Neuendorf, said.

The German football chief also thanked Red Bull for agreeing to an early termination of Klopp's contract.

The German FA were required to make a €1m donation to the Red Bull's Wings for Life foundation as part of Klopp's exit.

They have also agreed to play three internationals matches in Leipzig by 2023, the city whose football team is backed by Red Bull.



Klopp’s first game in charge of Germany will be a baptism of fire against long-time rivals the Netherlands.

The Nations League clash, scheduled for September 24, will now take on extra significance due to Klopp’s arrival.

The new UEFA calendar will see the 59-year-old take charge of three further matches within an extended international break lasting three weeks throughout the back end of September and early October.

His first home match in charge will come in Greece’s visit to Germany before another home fixture against Serbia and the return clash in Greece.



Klopp knows he has a difficult task in turning around Germany’s fortunes following a disappointing showing at the World Cup.
