Sports.title: Golf news: Rory McIlroy sends invite to Bryson DeChambeau as star withdraws from 3M Open
Sports.content:
Golf news: Rory McIlroy sends invite to Bryson DeChambeau as star withdraws from 3M Open

Golf news as Rory McIlroy reaches out to Bryson DeChambeau and major winner suffers another setback

View 3 Images Rory McIlroy has had plenty to say about Bryson DeChambeau (Image: Peter Byrne/PA Wire)

The golfing world continues to spin following an eventful Open Championship. Ryan Fox kept his head while all around him were losing theirs to make his major breakthrough at the age of 39 with a birdie at the last for a one-shot victory at Royal Birkdale.

‌



The New Zealander was one of only three players in the final 12 groups to shoot under par on a chaotic final day. The son of former All Blacks star Grant became his country's second Open champion after Sir Bob Charles in 1963.

‌



The Open also made the headlines for Bryson DeChambeau's conduct and Rory McIlroy's damning comments about the American. While McIlroy enjoys a break from the game, DeChambeau has stayed in the UK to play in the LIV Golf UK event at the JCB Country Club.

‌



Meanwhile, the PGA Tour continues with the 3M Open, where world number one Scheffler is part of the field. Here's a round-up of the latest golf news…

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

McIlroy sends DeChambeau invite

McIlroy has sent a surprise invitation to DeChambeau despite his brutal comments about his conduct at The Open. The Masters champion let rip at DeChambeau after the LIV Golf star was docked two shots for a rules violation during his second round.

‌



Incensed by the punishment, DeChambeau requested to be driven out to the scene of the incident on the fifth hole, where he spent a lengthy period remonstrating with officials before returning to the scoring compound for further discussions.

Bryson DeChambeau controversy at The Open costs LIV Golf star more than £200,000 READ MORE :

The saga delayed the publication of the third-round tee times until around 11pm and prompted criticism from several players, including McIlroy, who accused DeChambeau of holding the tournament "hostage" and called his antics "performative." He also dropped in that he was "not particularly fond" of the 32-year-old.

Despite those words, McIlroy insists DeChambeau would be a welcome his addition to the field at September's Irish Open, which will be held at the Donald Trump-owned Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg.

‌



DeChambeau is friends with Trump and reportedly threatened to call the US President amid his spat with R&A officials at Birkdale. Therefore, there is speculation that he could make an appearance at the Irish Open, which would be welcomed by defending champion McIlroy, who said: "I mean, I think that would be great for the tournament, absolutely. Having someone like Bryson at the Irish Open, yeah, it would be great for the tournament."

View 3 Images DeChambeau could play at Donald Trump's course in Ireland (Image: Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)

Day withdraws

Former world number one Jason Day has been forced to pull out of the 3M Open due to an ongoing back injury. The Australian, who missed the cut at The Open, withdrew during the first round of the US Open with a similar issue.

‌



He was replaced in the field at TPC ⁠Twin Cities in Minnesota by Charley Hoffman. Meanwhile, Scheffler made a strong start with a six-under par first round to sit three shots off the lead.

View 3 Images Jason Day's injury woes have continued (Image: Getty Images)

Scheffler, who finished tied fourth at Birkdale, began on the 10th and reached the turn at two under before picking up four more birdies in a blemish-free 65, holing 134 feet of putts in his first appearance at the tournament.

Article continues below

American Ben Kohles finished with an eagle three on the 18th to end two shots clear at the top of the leaderboard at nine under. Emiliano Grillo, Jackson Koivun and Gary Woodland, who hit rounds of 64, are in a share of second place.

Sports.title: Argentina president goes on rant as calls for country to be banned from World Cup grow
Sports.content:
Argentina president goes on rant as calls for country to be banned from World Cup grow

The fallout from the World Cup final continues, with Argentina's president Javier Milei busy posting on social media amid a backlash against his country after defeat by Spain

View 3 Images Javier Milei has been active on social media since the World Cup final (Image: Tomas Cuesta/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Argentina president Javier Milei has suggested that others are jealous of his country after a petition calling for them to be banned from future World Cups attracted over 23 million signatures.

‌



Argentina have been on the receiving end of a barrage of criticism following the shameful scenes after the final whistle in New Jersey. Spain overcame Lionel Messi and Co in extra time thanks to Ferran Torres' strike, but their victory was overshadowed by what followed.

‌



Midfielder Leandro Paredes kicked and punched as he shoved Eric Garcia to the ground and grappled with Gavi, while Nahuel Molina appeared to have instigated the altercation by throwing a punch at Rodri. FIFA are investigating the ugly scenes, which could prompt suspensions and fines.

‌



Argentina have been widely criticised for their behaviour, which came at the end of a match in which they mustered just two shots, committed regular fouls and had Enzo Fernandez sent off. An online petition calling for them to be banned from all future World Cups has now racked up 23,316,108 signatures from around 170 countries.

Argentina FA intervene as World Cup final conspiracy theories emerge after Spain win READ MORE :

Furious Argentina fans launch petition to replay 'corrupt' Spain World Cup final READ MORE :

But the backlash has only served to create a siege mentality in the South American country, with a rival petition launched arguing the match should be replayed due to a "corrupt" referee.

‌



Now right-wing leader Milei has amplified the feeling of injustice against his country through some posts on Instagram. The 55-year-old has shared a succession of posts which appear to defend the team.

"Do you have enemies? It means you once defended something. We defend Argentina," one reads. Another says: "The problem with Argentina is that we are conspicuous, we don't go unnoticed, people are jealous of us, and we are good at almost everything."

Milei also shared an AI image of him ripping open his suit to reveal an Argentina shirt with the caption "Long live Argentina, damn it!"

‌



View 3 Images Leandro Paredes was at the centre of the post-match fighting (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The nationalist rhetoric follows the semi-final win over England, which sparked more controversy after Argentina's players were shown celebrating with a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas", which translates as "The Falklands are Argentine".

The feeling has been echoed by many of Lionel Scaloni's squad, including arch villain Paredes, who refused to apologise for his behaviour after the final. "Thank you, Argentina! I love you today and always. Today, I write with a heavy heart, having been unable to bring our country the joy it so richly deserves," he wrote.

‌



"But with a chest full of pride for having given everything we had and for flying our flag at the very top once again! Thank you to everyone who was part of this national team.

View 3 Images Argentina celebrated with this banner after defeating England (Image: Paul ELLIS / AFP via Getty Images)

"To this group of players who gave their all to represent this jersey, fighting for it until the very last second of every match! It was an honour to be part of the best Argentine national team in history."

‌



Paredes managed to avoid a red card for his actions, but along with team-mates Molina and Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala, could face disciplinary proceedings from FIFA.

World football's governing body has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at MetLife stadium. Those involved are facing suspensions, while the Argentine Football Association (AFA) can expect a hefty fine for failing to control players and staff.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.

"Obviously the nation was hurt massively, but in terms of the current group of players I don't think they're dwelling too much on that hurt.

"To be honest, we're just riding the wave of the confidence we've got as a group - which I think this young group deserves - from the last two games and we're looking forward to Thursday night and then see what comes after that.

"But to see how the nation is feeling now is incredible and we've got a duty to try and make them even happier."

Image: Troy Parrott's goals inspired Ireland to stunning wins over Portugal and Hungary that secured a play-off spot

Ireland are only in Prague because they backed up a scratchy Group F victory over Armenia with an unexpected 2-0 win against Portugal in Dublin before going to Hungary and coming out on top in a five-goal thriller in which Troy Parrott scored the decisive goal with the last kick of the game.

Coleman is one of only two players - 34-year-old Robbie Brady is the other - in the current squad to have been to a major tournament, and the experience they had in earning their trip to Euro 2016 in France could prove invaluable this time around.

Image: Coleman and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson are bidding to lead Ireland to World Cup qualification for the first time since 2002

Martin O'Neill's team reached the finals by beating Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1 on aggregate in a play-off after a hard-fought 1-1 draw in Zenica in the first leg.

Coleman said: "Maybe two years ago it would have been a lot for the young lads to take.

"But everyone now has stepped up and are prepared for what's to come and we absolutely, no doubt about it, understand it's going to be a tough game for us, but it's also going to be a tough game for them as well."

Head coach Hallgrimsson, who is without suspended defender Liam Scales and injured midfielder Josh Cullen, as ever exuded calm as he fulfilled his media duties on Wednesday morning, simply asking for more of the same from his players.

He said: "We all know by now why we got good results and good performances, and that's the key, not be over-ambitious tomorrow, stay on point, focus on why we are here and trying to improve that, not only this game, continuously."

Czech boss says Soucek still key player despite not being captain

Image: West Ham's Tomas Soucek is no longer captain of his country

Czech Republic boss Miroslav Koubek said "full-fat" Tomas Soucek remains a key player for his country despite being stripped of the captaincy.

The 31-year-old West Ham midfielder has been replaced as skipper by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci after being removed from his position amid the fall-out from the 2-1 defeat by the Faroe Islands in October.

However Koubek, who himself took over from Ivan Hasek as head coach in December, still counts Soucek among his most important players ahead of Thursday night's World Cup play-off semi-final against the Republic of Ireland in Prague.

He said: "Tomas Soucek is an outstanding player with a great career. He doesn't have the captain's armband at this moment for reasons you all know, but nothing changes.

"It does not mean he will lose his value. He is still a 'full-fat' player, if I can use these words."

Image: Miroslav Koubek's first game in charge of the Czech Republic is against Ireland

Soucek's removal as captain has prompted speculation in the Czech media that he could even lose his place in the team, although Koubek remained coy over his team selection.

The 74-year-old said: "I don't read the newspapers, so I don't know. You will see tomorrow."

Koubek's side will welcome Ireland to the Fortuna Arena, the home of domestic champions Slavia Prague, knowing they will have to find a way to stop in-from striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in his country's last two qualifiers against Portugal and Hungary to get them to the play-offs.

Asked about his analysis of Heimir Hallgrimsson's team, he said: "One thing I noticed: they put a lot heart into their game. Ireland will definitely be a very tough opponent.

"But we will have a similar mindset, it will be a hard match, definitely.

"As for Parrott, he is outstanding, he is doing great. He is very fit, we know how he works. We do have some information, so now it will all be about eliminating him in a smart way. We will just have to stop him."

Krejci, however, has little doubt that it will be he and his team-mates who ultimately fight it out with either Denmark of North Macedonia for a trip to the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

He said: "We will make it. We will reach our goal. We will qualify for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Former boxing world champion Adrien Broner sued over sexual battery and assault allegations
Sports.content:
Former multi-division world champion boxer Adrien Broner is facing a lawsuit alleging sexual battery, assault and intentional infliction of emotional distress following a series of June incidents in California.

According to a civil complaint obtained by TMZ, a woman named Havana Saint alleges that Broner pressured her into unwanted sexual acts, exposed himself and doused her with ice water during a live stream after she rejected his advances.

The court filing details that the trouble began after a June 2 after-party, where Saint claims Broner encouraged her to drink heavily.

After staying at the residence because she was unable to drive home, Saint alleges Broner attempted to force himself on her, ignoring her repeated refusals and explicit statements that she was not interested in men.

Days later, on June 8, Saint encountered Broner again at a live-stream content house in Los Angeles County, where she claims he physically pulled her from the venue and forced her to come to his Encino home.

The lawsuit alleges that after she again refused to have sex with him, Broner doused her with ice water the following morning during a live stream, causing her severe humiliation and emotional distress.

Former world champion boxer Adrien Broner is facing a lawsuit alleging sexual battery, assault and intentional infliction of emotional distress

According to a civil complaint, a woman alleges that Broner pressured her into unwanted sexual acts, exposed himself and doused her with ice water after she rejected his advances

Saint further alleges that Broner and fellow live-streamer Nurideen Shabazz, known online as 'DeenTheGreat,' made defamatory statements during subsequent broadcasts by falsely claiming she had engaged in sexual relations with people at the content house.

The lawsuit names Broner for sexual battery, assault, defamation and emotional distress, while also naming Shabazz for defamation and targeting the streaming platform Kick for negligence.

Broner, who won world titles across four weight classes during his professional boxing career, has not yet publicly responded to the allegations or the lawsuit.

Back in September, Broner was kicked off rapper Cam'ron's popular podcast after ignoring the host's warnings to stop flirting with his on-air co-host.

Sporting a greying beard and speaking in an increasingly raspy voice, the 36-year-old Broner repeatedly interrupted the interview to make passes at Treasure 'Stat Baby' Wilson, who co-hosts 'It Is What It Is' with Cam'ron and Ma$e.

At one point, Broner responded to a question about boxing's welterweight division by telling Wilson: 'Stat, I love you.'

Things ultimately boiled over during a discussion about Sunday's NFL action when Broner appeared to stop himself from making another comment about Wilson: 'I can't talk… You told me to stop.'

Cam'ron took the moment to end his interview with Broner.

A native of Cincinnati who won the WBO Super Featherweight title at just 22 in 2011, Broner enjoyed a meteoric rise in the boxing world

Back in September, Broner was kicked off a podcast after repeatedly flirting with one of a host

'Hey, we going to have to ask you to go, my n*****,' Cam'ron said before pulling a stack of cash out of a small bag to give to his guest.

'I don't have no problems with you, but I'm gonna pay you for your time,' the rapper said, adding: 'You can't violate, bro.'

Cam'ron went on to explain that Wilson's boyfriend was on set.

A native of Cincinnati who won the WBO Super Featherweight title at just 22 in 2011, Broner enjoyed a meteoric rise in the boxing world before his career was derailed by a series of arrests, upset defeats and mental health issues.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's bouts are fights in name only - their opponents are merely useful punchbags who'd be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners: JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
It will be possible to be at ringside to watch Tyson Fury box in Thailand this Friday evening and then attend Anthony Joshua’s fight in Saudi Arabia on Saturday night.

The Gypsy King will prove that by flying from Bangkok to Riyadh soon after his encounter with the veteran Mariusz Wach in time to see AJ take on somebody called Kristian Prenga.

It is safe to presume that precious few, if any, of their respective thousands of fans will join Fury on that journey or pitch up at either occasion. And not only because many of them will have sacrificed a year or two’s wages, perhaps their mortgages, maybe their marriages on England’s ill-fated World Cup expedition.

Even the rich boys on tour are likely to jib at forking out another small fortune to attend distant events which are fights in name only. Joshua’s flight booking gives the game away, as does the choice of venues. No capital cities this time. Fury goes through the motions in the notorious Thai beach resort of Pattaya. Joshua at Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah-on-sea.

Of course these are by way of preparation for them fighting each other in that forever awaited box-office boomer later this year. But to be honest these match-ups are not so much warm-ups as water-treaders. These opponents would be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners.

Describing Poland’s Mariusz Wach as a ring veteran is actually an understatement of his decline since he went into a world heavyweight title fight against Wladimir Klitschko as 27-0 unbeaten challenger. He not only lost that night in Germany 14 years ago but failed a drugs test which interrupted for two years his descent into today’s 39 wins, 13 defeats record.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

Tyson Fury is fighting Mariusz Wach in Bangkok on Friday as he prepares to secure a long-awaited bout with Joshua

The longer he drags on, as he approaches his 46th birthday, the more he becomes a useful punch-bag, given his masochistic capacity to absorb punches for several rounds. A painful service he has provided to a number of British heavyweights, Dillian Whyte, Frazer Clarke and Hughie Fury among them. This is so patently a mismatch that it is not being televised anywhere in the world, but being saved by Netflix to help promote Fury v Joshua when that finally comes around,

Two years ago Wach was flattened in as many rounds by our world heavyweight champion-in-waiting Moses Itauma. That mercifully swift ending made for more comfortable viewing than some of the pointless beatings he has taken down the years. Make it quick, Tyson.

Kristian Prenga is a virtually unknown entity outside his native Albania. He has passed almost equally unnoticed on undercards mostly around New York, New Jersey, Philadelphia and across the Canadian border since he emigrated to the US.

At least he is ten years younger than Wach and has 20 knock-out wins on his record against one points defeat. Not that you are likely to recognise any of the names on that dance card. Try Joey Dawejko, Aldo Callendar, Tim Chemelli, Willie Jake Jr, or the only man to beat him Giovanni Auriemma. Me neither. Most of them appear to have other jobs, such as barmen, bouncers or cab drivers.

Prenga, a pleasant enough feller, made the right noises at his London press conference: ‘A J and his team have made a mistake. They’ve overlooked my knock-out record. They’ve forgotten that he can no longer take a big punch like mine. Get ready for the world-wide shock which will change my life forever.’

He seems not to have noted that AJ is a former Olympic gold medallist and two-time world heavyweight champion. Nor that he is stepping into an altogether higher realm. Nor that Joshua is highly motivated emotionally by this being his first fight since his two close friends and team members were killed in a car crash in Africa which he was lucky to survive. ‘This is for them,’ he says. Get it done early, AJ. before he has a chance to land.

Fury is set to fly from Bangkok to Saudi Arabia to watch Joshua a day after his own fight

Then you can invite Fury to join you in the ring – ‘but don’t forget Tyson I’m the landlord for this one’ – so they can start the big sell.

November is the likely month for Fury v Joshua 1. Wembley the stadium of choice but only if Brent Council agree to lift their usual 11 pm curfew and permit it to be transmitted live to the American TV audience at somewhere between 2 am and 4 am London Sunday time.

So enormous will be the difference from this weekend that Fury is about to entertain no more than a thousand or so locals in a small, screened-off hall. He is donating the revenue from those tickets to good causes in Thailand, of which he has become fond as a training camp. It will be charity all-round. What with Wach and Prenga picking up probably the biggest purses of their lives for their roles as fall guys. But what if the inconceivable did happen?

Not only would the gigantic pay-days of Fury’s and Joshua’s last hurrah go down the drain but at least one or maybe both their careers would be terminated.

Don’t dare mention it.

*Fury v Wach this Friday night will be for private screening only.

*Joshua v Prenga will be televised live on DAZN pay-per-view this Saturday night

*Fury v Joshua is expected to be televised live to Netflix subscribers in the early hours one Sunday morning in November

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua refuses to talk about Tyson Fury clash ahead of comeback fight against Kristian Prenga - with bout versus the Gypsy King on the cards if both stars win this weekend
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua shut down talk of Tyson Fury and insisted there is 'no future' beyond Saturday night unless he first gets the job done against Kristian Prenga in Jeddah.

The long-awaited Battle of Britain showdown with Fury is edging ever closer, with both heavyweights taking interim bouts this weekend before an expected blockbuster collision later this year.

Fury boxes Mariusz Wach in Thailand on Friday before Joshua makes his return against the heavy-hitting Albanian less than 24 hours later.

But despite the frenzy surrounding what could finally become one of British boxing's biggest-ever fights, Joshua made it clear he has no interest in looking past the man standing across the ring from him.

'Look, respect my opponent here,' Joshua said when questions during Thursday's press conference turned towards Fury.

'We don't want to talk about Tyson Fury. Respectfully, I have done all the media that I can about what the future holds but you know our focus is him and his team.

Anthony Joshua (left) is refusing to entertain talk of a clash with Tyson Fury ahead of his comeback fight

'We have been working since January, working hard, keeping my head down, aligned all my stars and I am fully focused.'

Joshua acknowledged the excitement surrounding what could await him if he comes through unscathed, but stressed that those conversations count for nothing unless he delivers in Saudi Arabia.

'I understand there is a big picture. The goal is to conquer the universe, right? But first we must conquer earth. My target is here.'

It is a mindset forged by the toughest period of his life.

Saturday marks Joshua's first appearance since stopping Jake Paul in Miami last December, just days before tragedy struck when close friends Latif 'Latz' Ayodele and Sina Ghami were killed in a car accident in Nigeria.

The devastating loss forced Joshua away from boxing as he grieved, with serious doubts over whether he would ever fight again.

Instead, he eventually returned to training and rebuilt towards what could become the defining final chapter of his career.

Victory over Prenga is expected to pave the way for the fight fans have demanded for more than a decade, but Joshua insists he cannot afford to think beyond the immediate task.

Fury (pictured) and Joshua are expected to clash this year but must first both win this weekend

'When you speak to me about what may lay ahead or I sit down in an office with Eddie (Hearn) and he presents to me what may lay ahead, it is a great opportunity for me to understand where this checkpoint takes me and what it leads me on to,' Joshua said.

'The reality of the matter is there is no universe, there is no future unless I get past this checkpoint on Saturday night.'

Prenga arrives in Jeddah with 20 knockouts to his name, although the Albanian has never shared the ring with an opponent anywhere near Joshua's calibre.

For the 35-year-old, however, Saturday represents the opportunity he has spent a lifetime chasing.

'I work all my life for this, I waited all my life for this and I hope I am going to show the world on Saturday who I am,' Prenga said.

Sports.title: 'I never considered walking away': ANTHONY JOSHUA opens up on his return to boxing in wake of car crash tragedy that killed two of his best friends - and reveals how the power of prayer spurred him on
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua never considered walking away.

Not after the darkest chapter of his life. Not after the unimaginable tragedy that left the boxing world reeling and forced him to confront grief far greater than any defeat inside the ring. And certainly not now, as he prepares to step through the ropes for the first time since the car accident that changed everything.

The crash near Lagos, Nigeria, late last year claimed the lives of Joshua's childhood friends, Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, both 36. The pair had been part of his inner circle for decades, with Ghami serving as his strength coach and Ayodele as his personal trainer.

On Saturday night, Joshua returns to the ring in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, against Kristian Prenga. It is, in many ways, the beginning of a new chapter.

It is his second fight under Oleksandr Usyk's team, but the first after a full training camp together and the first real opportunity to showcase the technical improvements those around him insist have transformed his game. And, perhaps most importantly, it represents the first step towards the blockbuster showdown with Tyson Fury that British boxing has craved for years.

But before any of that, Joshua had to decide whether he even wanted to fight again.

That decision was never really a decision at all.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

He beat Jake Paul in Miami in December, but within days had lost two friends in a car crash

'I never considered walking away, because boxing is my purpose,' Joshua explains ahead of his comeback. 'It's not just about competing. Boxing is therapeutic as well. It gives me purpose.

'As fighters, that's what it gives us. When I'm boxing, I know I'm where I'm supposed to be. It's where I'm most comfortable.

'It gives me direction in life, and that's why I never really thought about walking away. I'm content. This is where I belong.'

Joshua speaks calmly. There is no bravado, no attempt to create headlines. Instead, there is a noticeable sense of perspective from a man who has spent the past year processing an experience no person should ever have to endure.

He is careful when discussing loss, and even more careful not to make himself the focus of it.

'Everyone deals with it differently,' he says. 'For me, I have to put my own emotions to one side because I focus on the parents.

'My emotions can come later, but I look at what the mums and dads are going through because that's what must be hardest.

'I don't make it about me. I make it about them. You have to keep your own emotions under control. That's not how everyone deals with it, but it's the best way for me. I need to be a good soldier. At the end of the day, it's not about me. It's much bigger than me.'

The 36-year-old says he never intended to walk away from boxing because it is his purpose

Daily Mail Sport's Charlotte Daly caught up with Joshua ahead of his return fight

Another source of strength has come from an unlikely place.

Joshua's move to train alongside former undisputed heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk has inevitably led to questions about technical improvements, but the biggest lesson he has taken from the Ukrainian has nothing to do with slipping punches or throwing combinations.

'The importance of prayer,' Joshua says without hesitation while speaking to The Daily Mail in Jeddah. 'Even if you're not deeply religious or don't follow one particular faith, prayer is important. It's something you can take into every training camp.'

Inside Usyk's camp, Joshua insists every aspect of his game has evolved, but one lesson stands above the rest.

'We'd be here all day talking about everything they've added to my game.

'The biggest thing is my relationship with hard work. You can be in one environment and think you're working hard, then you go into another environment and realise what you thought was hard actually isn't hard enough. It isn't good enough.

'So it's really changed my relationship with hard work. I want more from myself. I've put myself in an environment where I know I'll get more out of boxing because I've given more of myself to boxing. These guys push me harder than I was ever pushed before.'

Those working closest to Joshua believe his defence has improved dramatically since arriving in camp. Watching him spar, they see a more patient, more rounded heavyweight than the explosive Olympic champion who first burst onto the scene over a decade ago.

Joshua pictured moments after the tragic crash took place on a major road outside Lagos

Joshua pictured with friends Latif Ayodele (centre) and Sina Ghami who both died in the crash

Saturday offers the first glimpse of whether those improvements translate under the bright lights.

If Joshua comes through against Prenga, attention will inevitably turn to Fury.

The long-awaited Battle of Britain has flirted with becoming reality for years before collapsing at the negotiating table. Now, with both men rebuilding, it feels closer than ever.

Joshua knows Fury will be watching.

Asked what he wants his rival to think after seeing him back in action, Joshua smiles before delivering an answer that perfectly captures the confidence still burning beneath his measured exterior.

'This guy is a f***ing killer. He's a beast. He's strong. He's quick. He's got good footwork. He's got good defence and it's gonna be hard work trying to beat this guy. That's what I'd want him to think.'

Yet for all the excitement surrounding a potential meeting with Fury, Joshua refuses to place it above the moments that have already defined his career.

'It's a huge fight, but it's not for a world title, if I'm being completely honest,' he says.

Sina Ghami had worked with Joshua for years as his S&C coach and sports rehabilitation specialist, while Latif 'Latz' Ayodele became his PT after years of friendship

'It's a great achievement if I beat someone like Tyson Fury, but for me, nothing compares to becoming a world champion.

'You can beat great fighters, but it's different when you're beating them to become a world champion.'

In an era where some of boxing's biggest stars openly question the value of championship belts, Joshua remains unapologetically old school.

He points to changing financial realities, with fighters now earning fortunes outside the traditional title picture, but believes the sport's history still matters.

'There's a lot of talk nowadays about fighters saying belts don't matter anymore,' he says. 'People's attitudes are changing because there are different opportunities now. But personally, the heritage and history of boxing still means everything to me. You can't beat becoming a world champion, in my opinion...

'Unless someone dangles a big enough carrot in front of me... then f*** the belts.'

It draws a laugh, but the message is clear.

For now, Fury can wait. So can championship ambitions.

Joshua's focus is fixed solely on Prenga and proving that, after everything he has been through, he is still exactly where he believes he belongs.

Back in the ring. Back with purpose. And determined that the next chapter of his career is defined not by the tragedy behind him, but by the fights still to come.

Sports.title: Revealed: Shocking arrest history of man detained over death of boxer Hannah Rapp... after driver 'REVERSED into her'
Sports.content:
The man arrested for manslaughter over the death of boxer Hannah Rapp has a long history of arrests including for gun and driving offenses, it has emerged.

The American boxer died after she was hit by a car in Texas on Saturday, with the Brazos County Sheriff's Office saying the 26-year-old was cycling on a highway when she was passed by a car which suddenly came to a stop and then reversed into her.

Rapp was treated at the scene before being taken to hospital where she later passed away from her injuries.

The driver, who authorities have named as 31-year-old Charles Medina, has been arrested on charges including manslaughter.

NBC reports that, according to the probable cause statement, Medina told officers he believed the cyclists were 'trying to flag him down' so he 'stepped on his brakes which caused them to lock up before coming to a stop.'

He also claimed that, while reversing at 15mph, he did not see Rapp 'until the last moment before he hit her.'

But, as first revealed by ESPN, jail records show that Medina has a long history of run-ins with the police dating back to his teens.

The Texas man arrested over the death of boxer Hannah Rapp has a long history of arrests

Rapp received treatment at the scene before she later passed away in hospital in Texas

Charles Eric Medina

He was first arrested in Brazos County in 2012 for reckless driving and evading arrest. Medina reportedly pleaded guilty in both cases.

Since then, the 31-year-old has been detained a dozen times including in 2014 - for reckless driving - and 2020, when he was accused of hit and run. It is not immediately clear how those cases ended. Medina was arrested again in 2024 for deadly conduct in the discharge of a firearm. According to reports at the time, the authorities responded to reports of a man - identified as Medina - 'chasing vehicles with an axe and a knife.' Officers are said to have found him in his yard with a handgun. Medina then fired several shots into the air. After what the sheriff described as a 'short standoff,' he was taken into custody. That case reportedly remains open.

Following Rapp's death, the authorities released a statement on the tragedy. 'Investigators learned that the driver of the vehicle... had passed two bicyclists traveling along FM 159. After passing the bicyclists, Mr. Medina stopped his vehicle, reversed, and struck one of the cyclists,' the Sheriff's Office statement said.

'Despite lifesaving efforts, she later passed away at the hospital. At this time, investigators believe this was an isolated incident.'

Rapp had enjoyed a burgeoning career in the ring and challenged for the WBC women's featherweight title on June 13, losing to Tiara Brown in Orlando. Her professional record read eight wins, one draw and one loss.

Jake Paul, her promoter, tweeted: 'Gone too soon. Condolences to her entire clan. RIP warrior, Hannah Rapp.'

WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman said in a statement: 'She was an exceptional boxer, but above all, an invaluable member of our boxing family.'

Rapp's former rival Brown labelled her the 'best dance partner I have ever faced as a pro' and revealed how Rapp had asked for her autograph before their bout.

'It filled my heart because we were getting ready for war, yet she was still asking for my autograph,' said Brown. 'We fought a great fight. It was my honor to share the ring with her.'

Jake Paul, Rapp's promoter, tweeted: 'Gone too soon. Condolences to her entire clan'

Rapp, from Indiana, turned professional in 2024 and had competed in athletics before turning her attention to boxing. During training, she maintained a full-time job as a fire and life safety inspector.

A GoFundMe has also been launched to help her family cover the costs of funeral expenses.

'A beloved daughter to Angie and James, sister to Tanner and Maggie, a friend to everyone she met, and an inspiring boxing athlete,' the tribute read.

'Hannah was resilient. She was brave and insightful, always pushing others to do their best. She loved her family so incredibly much, and moving from Indiana to Texas meant distance for her friends and family.

'Hannah was an inspiration. Even on her hardest days, she continued to bring love, laughter, and light into the lives of others.'

The GoFundMe page has already received more than 230 donations totaling more than $22,000.
