World.title: Merz ally challenges Germany’s far-right firewall ahead of crucial state elections
World.content:
With those comments, Kretschmer stirred up tensions that Merz has stubbornly sought to avoid.

Merz rules out cooperation with the far right — invoking the country’s Nazi past — but the political realities of eastern Germany are piling on the pressure for a rethink. Polls show that the AfD has a chance of winning an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 and is poised to perform well in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin later that month.

At the national level, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the AfD as the single most popular party with 28 percent support, with the Christian Democrats on 22 percent.

For now, however, Merz is sticking to his line that Germany has a special historic responsibility that means it cannot follow the course of other EU countries where the far right has worked with the centrist mainstream.

“If a far-right party were to enter the government in Germany, it would have a completely different significance than if that were to happen in another country,” he told reporters at a press conference. “This is also tied to our history, and that’s why, for me, it’s neither a benchmark nor an example, nor something to learn from. It is, quite simply, something different. I will do everything in my power in Germany to prevent it.”

Instead, Merz said the government’s goal had to be to seek to create a climate where the far right could be defeated.

World.title: French PM’s office meets banks to try resolve far right’s financing problem
World.content:
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has often struggled to secure a loan despite heading one of the most popular parties in France, with banks wary of perceived reputational damage that comes with financing the far right.

“It’s essential that all the candidates, whatever their political creed, can access French funding to finance their campaign,” said the aide from the prime minister’s office.

Lecornu’s initiative aims to avoid the interference of a “foreign financing network.” In the past, the National Rally has obtained loans from Russian and Hungarian banks.

A person close to Lecornu, also granted anonymity to speak freely, however, said that the prime minister’s office was not “negotiating on behalf” of the far right.

“It’s as false as it is absurd. We are opponents, and there have been no discussions between the PM’s office and the National Rally on the subject,” the person said. The initiative would also benefit other smaller candidates.

Victor Goury-Laffont contributed to this report.

World.title: 'All paths appear closed': Iranians weigh prospect of US invasion of their country
World.content:
US military planners have drawn up options for a ground operation in Iran, and US President Donald Trump has not ruled it out, a prospect that has opened a sharp and deeply personal debate inside the country about whether foreign boots on Iranian soil would be a liberation or a catastrophe.

 

Iranian army spokesperson Brigadier General Mohammad Akrami-Nia warned recently that any US entry onto Iranian territory would trigger a military response. "If the Americans set foot on one of our islands, we will definitely target them on our own soil," he said.

Lawmaker Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani went further, warning that Tehran could launch ground operations against US allies in the Gulf, including Kuwait and Bahrain, if US forces entered Iranian territory.

Trump has repeatedly warned that Washington is prepared to go further if Tehran does not change course, and has threatened the Islamic Republic with an unprecedented "massive attack" in another escalation of rethoric after the interim deal between the two sides failed earlier this month, leading to renewed fighting.

Euronews spoke to five Iranians about the prospect of a US ground operation — whether they believe it is coming, whether it could topple the Islamic Republic, and whether they would fight to resist it or welcome it.

Their names have been changed to protect their safety.

'Most people I know are against war'

Ali, 36, a construction worker from Karaj, does not believe the US will send ground forces into Iran.

"I don't think America will enter Iran with ground forces. Even if it wanted to do so, it would not be able to seize the islands or the southern parts of Iran," he told Euronews.

He said he opposed war because ordinary Iranians would pay the heaviest price. "People in Iran are already under pressure. War would only increase that pressure."

Asked whether he would prefer continued sanctions and maritime restrictions or a war that might produce political change, he said, "I would choose lifting the maritime blockade, in any way possible."

Ali said opinion among those around him had shifted after the initial 40 days of the war war failed to bring down the Islamic Republic.

"Most people I know are against war. Before the 40-day war, some supported military action because they believed it could lead to the collapse of the system," he said.

"But when that did not happen, many changed their minds. They now believe this government will not fall because of war, and that ordinary people will only suffer. I personally do not think this regime will collapse through war."

On speculation about Iranian ground operations against Gulf states, Ali was dismissive. "The era of ground warfare is over. Their military technology is more advanced than ours. If our forces entered Kuwait, they would be targeted from the air and would achieve nothing."

'Occupation would be a humiliating defeat for the regime'

Jamshid, 44, runs a newsstand in Tehran. Unlike Ali, he believes a US entry into southern Iran or its islands is a genuine possibility — though he says it would come at a heavy cost for Iranians regardless of their politics.

"As an Iranian I didn't want things to get to this point, because if the entry of the US army into Iran involves hitting infrastructure, bridges, primary resources, bases and petrochemical plants, Iran will suffer a great deal," he told Euronews.

"In that situation it is no longer only to the detriment of the Islamic Republic; the Iranian people will suffer as well."

Women sit in the outdoor dining area of a cafe in central Tehran on Wednesday 22 July 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi) AP Photo

He said he could support intervention under narrow conditions. "If the entry of American forces does not mean destroying the country's infrastructure, and if it leads to the fall of the Islamic Republic or forces it into an agreement with the United States — allowing Iran to become something like China after Mao — then I would prefer American forces entering Iran."

Jamshid argued that any territorial loss would weaken the government politically. "If part of Iran is occupied, this would be devastating and humiliating for the Islamic Republic and could increase the possibility of its collapse."

But he said he did not know anyone who would fight alongside US soldiers. "I don't know anyone who says they would fight with the American army. But America does not need ordinary people to fight for it."

'Perhaps an occupation would force a deal'

Laleh is a high school sociology teacher in Tehran. She believes the US could occupy parts of Iran's southern coast or its islands — and that the Islamic Republic would be unable to retake them.

"I think America could occupy parts of the islands or southern Iran. If that happens, I don't think the Islamic Republic would have the ability to retake those areas," Laleh told Euronews, adding that she does not believe occupation would bring the government down, but thinks it would eventually force talks.

"An occupation would not necessarily bring down the Islamic Republic. The government could justify it to its supporters. But ultimately, it would have to negotiate in order to recover the occupied territories."

Parichehr, 46, is a lawyer. She told Euronews she did not expect a ground operation — "I do not believe the US government would send its army into a country as large as Iran" — but when asked directly whether she would support it, she gave an unexpected answer.

"At this moment, I personally support the presence of American forces in Iran," she said.

She was cautious about drawing conclusions from Afghanistan and Iraq. "When we speak with Afghans, many are unhappy with the period of American presence in their country, although a minority are satisfied. I cannot make a definitive judgment based only on their experience," Parichehr said.

According to her, decades under the Islamic Republic had pushed some Iranians toward a position they would not previously have considered.

"For almost 50 years, Iranian people have experienced life under the Islamic Republic," Parichehr said.

"We have tried different ways to improve the situation, but when all paths appear closed, people begin to think perhaps another option should be tested," she added.

"Even if you do not know all the consequences of a new path, you may still prefer not to continue on the same road."

'My family and I would fight'

Morteza, 38, is a mechanic in Tehran. He said a ground invasion was impossible, but described what he thought would follow if it happened.

"In my view a US ground attack is impossible. At most, the United States might bomb Tehran with missiles like in the days before the New Year. It won't raise the level of war beyond that," Morteza told Euronews.

"But if it did enter by land and occupy parts of southern Iran, then Iran would hit Kuwait and Dubai with missiles in such a way as to cause extensive damage and destruction," he said.

He said he would take up arms regardless of his views on the government. "Iran is our home and we know this country better. It is like someone entering your house by force. You try to remove them by any means," Morteza said.

"If American forces enter Iran, I would join the Iranian military to defend my country and my family. We know our equipment is not enough, but we would fight to prevent our country from being occupied."

Asked whether the Islamic Republic should remain in power, he said: "Given the current economic situation, I think it is better for the Islamic Republic to remain for now. If it collapses, nobody knows who will take control of the country."

World.title: Uzbek economy grows 8.5% as services and investment expand
World.content:
Uzbekistan's economy grew 8.5% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to official figures presented at a meeting chaired by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, as the country posted its strongest credit rating upgrades in years.

 

Investment reached approximately €24.6 billion in the six-month period, with exports at around €12.7 billion. Services expanded by 16.9%, construction by 13.8%, industry by 8% and agriculture by 4.7%.

Moody's upgraded Uzbekistan's sovereign credit rating from Ba3 to Ba2 in June, while Fitch kept its BB rating but shifted the outlook from stable to positive. Both moves reflect growing confidence among international investors in the trajectory of reforms launched after 2017.

Mirziyoyev called on regional and sector leaders to extract more value from existing investment, industrial and export projects.

"To improve the living standards of our 40 million people, economic growth of 9% to 10% is essential," Mirziyoyev said.

From agriculture to industry

The ministry of economy and finance attributed the first-half figures to a structural shift that has reshaped Uzbekistan's economic base since 2017, when the government launched a programme of foreign-exchange liberalisation, trade opening, privatisation and monetary reform.

Saidkhonov Saidislombek, a department head at the ministry, told Euronews that agriculture's share of gross value added was reduced from 27.3% in 2017 to 17.3% in 2025, as faster growth in industry and services changed the composition of the economy.

Industry's share rose from around 22% to nearly 27% over the same period, while services climbed from 43.7% to 48.6%.

Exporting company in Uzbekistan Euronews

Gross fixed capital formation reached €41.3 billion by the end of 2025, up from approximately €12.3 billion earlier in the reform period. The investment-to-GDP ratio rose from 19.5% to about 32%. Exports increased from roughly €10.6 billion in 2017 to €29.9 billion in 2025.

Koba Gvenetadze, the IMF Resident Representative in Uzbekistan, said the reforms included a new central bank law that had "strengthened credibility and independence" at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan.

He said greater exchange-rate flexibility was a necessary condition for the shift toward inflation targeting and for making the economy more resilient to external shocks.

The presidential review examined whether investment agreements were being converted into actual output and exports. Agreements reached during 52 high-level visits cover 1,617 investment projects worth approximately €187.3 billion.

The presidency said implementation was uneven and instructed officials to address barriers in certification, working capital access, logistics and market entry abroad.

Employment formalisation a gradual process

Regional employment agencies have been tasked with expanding vocational training and linking infrastructure programmes more directly to job creation. Officials were told to focus on household incomes for the remainder of 2026.

Andrin Fink, programme officer at the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, said he had observed "a lot of reforms and a lot of efforts" to formalise employment but cautioned against expecting a rapid transition.

"It is of course a very big transition," he told Euronews, adding that it would require "a big effort and maybe a little bit of time." Formal employment gives workers access to social insurance, pensions and other protections.

Programme Officer at the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation Euronews

Switzerland and Uzbekistan's employment ministry have developed an online commentary on the Labour Code adopted in 2023, intended to help workers and employers understand how the legislation applies outside the country's largest cities.

Regional proposals on risks across industry, infrastructure and exports are due by 15 August, and will feed into Uzbekistan's budget, investment and export planning for 2027.

World.title: Charli XCX - 'Music, Fashion, Film': Euronews Culture's review and verdict
World.content:
I confess that from the get-go, Charli XCX's 'Music, Fashion, Film' rubbed me up the wrong way.

 

Not because I was desperate for 'Brat 2.0' or that anything but another era-defining follow-up would be dismissed as an disappointment. If anything, the thought of a new direction following one of the most critically acclaimed albums of the past five years was not only enticing but artistically necessary, as trying to recapture the zeitgeist in the same way would have seemed both foolish and desperate.

I just wasn't sold.

First, there was lead single 'Rock Music', featuring distorted guitars and some frankly terrible lyrics like “Me and my friends, we go out / We take pictures and make stuff together / And sometimes we cry / We kiss each other, real incestuous vibes” and “I think the dancefloor is dead / So now we’re making roooooock music”.

The self-awareness and sarcastic / meta humour weren't landing, and the phrase "real incestuous vibes" came off as a performative provocation that just felt desperately thirsty for attention.

The accompanying video for the single didn't help. It looked like staged edginess, with Charli's cigfluencer antics feeling like grating posturing featuring the social media crutch-prop du jour. Even as someone who fully endorses the Chandler Bing school of thought which states that "The bottom line is smoking is cool and you know it", the whole 'smoking = rebellion' isn't unruly or hedonistic. It's try-hard and uninspired in the extreme.

Then there was the album cover which, in keeping with the title, features founding Velvet Underground member John Cale, fashion designer Marc Jacobs and legendary filmmaker Martin Scorsese – with each figure representing the three ‘aspects’ of the album.

Impressive to have gotten all three icons in the same room for the Aidan Zamiri photo shoot, but the whole thing felt too on the nose.

Regardless, I wanted my first impressions to be wrong when listening to Charli's seventh album in full, having been a fan since 2014's 'Sucker', a champion of 2019's 'Charli', and pleased as punch that the British pop star had achieved hard-won universal acclaim in 2024.

Charli XCX - Music, Fashion, Film Aidan Zamiri / Atlantic Records

The new and very lean 30-minute LP starts off with 'Rock Music' - an inauspicious beginning which is rapidly redeemed by 'SS26', the sound of a polished apocalypse that is arguably the strongest song on the album.

From then on, it's a frustrating downhill slide during which Charli addresses her relationship with identity, self-worth, and the pressures of post-'Brat' fame. All promising avenues to explore, but the ideas are muddled - as if the existential crisis needed a bit more time to mature before being expressed.

This is mirrored in the tracks themselves, with most of them clocking in at a scant two-minutes. Plenty are inessential (the vapid '2007' and the minimalist nothing of a song 'Yeah' both stand out for all the wrong reasons), but the ones that actually register (the grunge-aping 'Card Declined' and the promising 'Camera') are over before they've had a chance to develop. Or matter.

On 'Camera', the solid hook is merged with a decent stab at self-reflection: "I don't feel embarrassed even if I suck / I'm always craving an experience that feels dangerous / And maybe this is it, maybe it's what I need / 'Cause it's the only way to feel like I'm not actually me." Frustratingly, the song ends there, leading to the impression that 'Music, Fashion, Film' is a hastily released sketchbook of half-baked ideas and songs.

The initial promise of Charli's state-of-mind vignettes leading to hollowness is epitomised in the song 'Wink Wink'.

Far less demo-feeling than some of the other tracks, it contains flashes of earworm brilliance which are undone by a semi-stream of consciousness culminating in grating punchlines.

"I used to lick cream off strawberries in the summer..." Good for you. Real upper-class British summer vibes, but do keep going – it's a delicious pastime.

"And maybe I fucked your dad..." Oh, how risqué of you. What will the landed gentry think now?

"Just kidding, I'm only saying that for effect..." Ah, a pivot to self-awareness suggesting a 'cool girl' archetype takedown, showing that you're so very in on your own joke.

"But my point is I think people can change." True, but that's not as profound as you think it sounds.

The self-referential flip-flopping culminates with, "I'm not a bad girl anymore / Wink, wink", at which point you're reminded of that insufferable person who says something needlessly insulting or unpleasant during conversation and defends themselves with a smirk and the pithy refuge: "Can't you take a joke? It's just banter!"

Incidentally, anyone guilty of that retort or fond of using the term 'banter' needs to come to terms with the fact that the passive-aggressive and accountability-dodging term only masks the trivialisation of bullying. Stop it. Get some help.

In Charli's defence, 'Music, Fashion, Film' has its fleeting moments, and following up 'Brat' was never going to be an easy task.

Pivot too hard, and you alienate the fanbase; do more of the same, and you're coasting. But when the follow-up to your global juggernaut barely registers – despite 'SS26', the genuine gut-punch of 'I'm Afraid', and album closer 'No One Lasts Forever' featuring the impressive inclusion of director David Cronenberg – something's gone wrong.

And when your existential questioning makes you seem more self-indulgent than profound or even ironically witty, the letdown only confirms that first impressions are often irretrievable.

'Music, Fashion, Film' is out now.

World.title: EU finds TikTok failed to shield the privacy of children's accounts from adults
World.content:
The European Commission said on Friday it had found TikTok did not adequately protect children's privacy on its platform, after allowing adults to view the accounts of minors.

 

The Commission said the failure exposed children to cyberbullying, unwanted contact and predatory behaviour.

The finding is the latest in a series of crackdowns on Big Tech by Brussels, which has led the world in regulating major technology firms, including Meta and Apple.

TikTok can now defend itself and reply to the findings.

If the Commission is not satisfied with the Chinese firm's response, it could issue a so-called non-compliance decision and a possible fine worth up to 6% of the company's total annual revenue.

The Commission has been investigating TikTok's compliance with the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU's sweeping rulebook for online platforms, since February 2024, when the company was designated a Very Large Online Platform under the law.

This is not the first time the investigation has produced adverse findings for TikTok.

In February, the Commission found the platform had breached another part of the DSA over its "addictive design," pointing to features such as autoplay and infinite scroll that it said could harm the physical and mental health of users, particularly minors.

TikTok rejected those findings at the time, calling the Commission's assessment "categorically false".

TikTok has also faced scrutiny beyond the DSA.

Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined the company €345 million in 2023 for breaching EU data protection rules by allowing accounts for children under 13 and failing to adequately safeguard their data.

TikTok was separately fined €530 million by the same regulator over its transfer of European user data to China, a decision upheld by Ireland's High Court this year.

World.title: Podcast | Brussels eyes political reshuffles in London and Budapest
World.content:
Former British Prime Minister Harold Wilson's quote stating that "a week is a long time in politics" feels particularly apt for Hungary and the United Kingdom (UK) at the moment.

 

Hungarian President Tamás Sulyok, widely considered a loyalist to former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, signed an amendment to the country's constitution on Saturday, 18 July, ending his presidency.

Meanwhile, in the UK, Keir Starmer stepped down as prime minister on Monday after months of a decline in his popularity. He was replaced by Andy Burnham, formerly the mayor of Greater Manchester.

How is the political reshuffle in Budapest being viewed by Brussels? And will Burnham continue the thaw in the EU-UK relationship?

Euronews’ weekly podcast Brussels, My Love? explores these political reshuffles with Andrea Renda, director of research at the Brussels think tank CEPS; Teresa Küchler, Svenska Dagbladet’s European correspondent; and Euronews reporter Sandor Zsiros.

The end of a yes-man

Removing the president was central to the campaign of Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party ahead of the April elections. After the centre-right party won a parliamentary supermajority, the National Assembly managed to pass a constitutional amendment ending Sulyok's term.

"Sulyok was not active at all politically during his presidency," Euronews' Sandor Zsiros said. "As a president, he was invisible, and this was the reason why Orbán appointed him, because he wanted an extremely weak personality who does not object to his plans."

This was echoed by Renda: "He never challenged Orbán or the many violations of the rule of law his administration perpetrated. He was basically a yes-man. The division of powers did not work."

The decision to remove Sulyok, a move Zsiros notes is "extremely popular" among Hungarians, was criticised by some NGOs. Human Rights Watch warned it risks halting advances to restore the rule of law, which Magyar pledged to do upon entering office.

Küchler questioned whether, in the long term, Magyar's approach risks being seen as "too aggressive", citing one diplomat who told her "one thing Magyar cannot do is start behaving like Orbán himself."

Zsiros rebuffed that argument, pointing to three big differences: "He shut down the toxic propaganda, broke the extremely close ties with Russia and China and is conducting a pro-European foreign policy.

"I asked the Commission many times how it felt about the removal of the president, and there was no comment."

Renda believes the matter is being closely watched by Brussels. "It's very important that this is an initial bending of the rule of law, because it is seen as a one-off, and will not become a sort of stretching of the rule of law."

The parliament has until mid-August to find a replacement. Magyar put forward world chess champion Judit Polgár, but she turned down the offer to become the next head of state.

"What Magyar wants is somebody above party politics, who represents the whole of Hungary, and somebody well-known even outside of Hungary. That's why he proposed Polgár. [...] Magyar is behaving like an influencer; he likes sensation, so I expect that he might propose somebody with a similar profile," Zsiros said.

Renda and Küchler stressed Sulyok's replacement should act as a type of antagonist and hold the head of government to account.

Rapprochement with EU?

This week, Brussels was also eyeing a political shuffle in the UK, where Andy Burnham became the seventh prime minister in office since 2016.

His move into 10 Downing Street comes at a time when strengthening cross-Channel ties was top of the agenda both in Brussels and London, an effort initiated by Starmer.

Hours after entering his role, Burnham spoke with European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, in which the importance of stronger EU-UK ties was underlined.

But for now, Burnham's priorities seem to be mainly domestic.

Renda, who was in the UK on Monday, spoke with various high-level figures involved in the new administration. "They see a big emphasis on growth and on the devolution of powers towards a local level, and the reindustrialisation of areas where a lot of discontent has emerged," he said. Those living in these de-industrialised areas were also more likely to vote "Leave" in the 2016 referendum.

"But even if Burnham's new programme is not directly aimed at bringing the UK closer to the EU, the actual result of re-industrialising and finding new prospects for the local dimension can actually bring people closer to more inclusivity and, gradually over time, be closer to the European Union going forward."

Küchler emphasised that the result of the referendum carries weight and should be respected, but noted that geopolitically, now is a good moment for closer ties.

"We saw how [US President] Donald Trump disrespected Keir Starmer and humiliated him on the international arena," she said. "I think many voters in the UK right now would say, 'This is a very good point for us to make sure that we stay on good terms with our European friends', because it has been proven politically volatile to depend too heavily on Washington."

For more on that, make sure you keep following Brussels, My Love?, and listen to the full episode in the player above or wherever you get your podcasts.

World.title: Wildfire emergency near Madrid forces over 10,000 to flee as Spain sounds alarm
World.content:
Dramatic footage filmed overnight on 23 and 24 July 2026 in San Martín de Valdeiglesias and Chapinería, south-west of Madrid, shows firefighters confronting towering flames, Civil Guard officers responding to the advancing fire, and displaced residents sheltering in an emergency centre.

 

Locals described flames and thick smoke surrounding San Martín de Valdeiglesias, forcing residents, including many elderly people, to flee their homes.

Spain declared an unprecedented national emergency over wildfires on Thursday night as rapidly spreading blazes near Madrid and in neighbouring Ávila province drove more than 10,000 residents from their homes. The emergency affected Villa del Prado, San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Pelayos de la Presa and Aldea del Fresno, while Chapinería alone sheltered more than 150 evacuees, according to Mayor Lucía Moya. Several municipalities also reported homes damaged or destroyed.

The declaration placed firefighting operations under the direct control of the Interior Ministry, allowing additional resources to be deployed. More than 270 emergency personnel and 40 ground units, supported by Spain's Military Emergency Unit and water-bombing aircraft, have been mobilised despite strong winds and extreme heat complicating efforts to contain the flames.

The fires come during one of Spain's most severe wildfire seasons in recent years. According to the European Forest Fire Information System, more than 104,000 hectares have burned across the country since the beginning of 2026. Earlier this month, wildfires claimed at least 13 lives, including in a deadly blaze in Almería. The latest outbreaks around Madrid add to a series of major fires in Guadalajara, Aragón and Andalusia, further stretching Spain's firefighting resources at the height of the summer fire season.

World.title: Jürgen Klopp confirmed as new German national team coach
World.content:
Jürgen Klopp has been officially confirmed as the new coach of the German national football team.

 

The German Football Association (DFB) unveiled the 59-year-old at its headquarters in Frankfurt on Friday morning. His appointment follows the departure of previous head coach Julian Nagelsmann.

After Germany's disappointing showing at the World Cup, Klopp will be tasked with leading the Germans back to winning ways.

The charismatic former Liverpool boss has long been the preferred choice of many fans and officials to take the reins.

High expectations

Fans will hope Klopp's hugely impressive club record and high-energy approach will be the key to changing the fortunes of the national side.

But he will face some major challenges, and he has some big decisions to make after yet another early World Cup exit for Germany.

Klopp will have to decide whether Joshua Kimmich should remain as captain and who will replace veteran goalkeeper Manuel Neuer following his retirement from international football. He will also need to work out what to do with older players such as Antonio Rüdiger and Leon Goretzka while finding opportunities for younger players looking to break into the side.

Klopp is expected to take time to speak with the team's leaders before making his first sporting decisions.

Former Liverpool coach Jürgen Klopp congratulates France's Kylian Mbappe (10) after France defeated Morocco in the World Cup quarterfinal soccer match. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

A trusted coaching team

Klopp is bringing several long-time companions with him into the job.

Peter Krawietz will once again work as his assistant, while Pepijn Lijnders, with whom Klopp enjoyed many successful years at Liverpool, also joins the coaching staff. Former Germany international Sven Bender will further strengthen the team.

Klopp does not have much time to get prepared, however.

On 24 September, he will make his debut on the touchline in a Nations League match against the Netherlands, with games against Greece and Serbia to follow soon after.

From Mainz coach to global star

Klopp began his coaching career in 2001 at 1. FSV Mainz 05, leading them to the Bundesliga for the first time.

In 2008, he moved to Borussia Dortmund, winning the German league title twice and guiding BVB to the Champions League final.

He went on to become a club legend at Liverpool, winning the Champions League in 2019 and ending a 30-year title drought by lifting the English league title in 2020.

After leaving Liverpool, Klopp initially moved into a leadership role in international football before now taking on the challenge of coaching the national team.

His contract with the German FA runs until after the 2030 World Cup.

World.title: From housing to healthcare: What are Europeans worried about in 2026?
World.content:
Europe is facing challenges centred on geopolitical security, economic strain, and environmental pressures, many of which are causing concerns for citizens, too.

 

A YouGov survey across six European countries suggests there is no single issue dominating public opinion across the continent. Instead, national concerns vary on local priorities, with the economy high on the list for most.

Where does the economy top the list?

Economic concerns remain at the forefront in some of Europe's largest economies.

Almost half of French respondents (47%) and 44% of Germans ranked the economy among the two biggest issues facing their countries. Immigration also came second in both countries, cited by 27% of respondents in France and 26% in Germany.

These findings come as the eurozone's two largest economies face persistent economic pressures. In Germany, a recent uptick in industrial production has offered limited reassurance, as output remains below pre-pandemic levels and experts report that recovery remains fragile.

The country's export-led economy has faced pressure as a result of weaker demand from both the US and China, particularly its automotive industry — once a key driver of economic growth.

In France, first quarter data shows that economic growth has stalled as the Iran war weighed heavily on energy prices. Political deadlock has also complicated the country's efforts to pass reforms to improve public finances.

Respondents in both countries also expressed little optimism about the year ahead, with around 68% of French respondents saying they expected the economy to worsen over the next 12 months, compared with 58% in Germany.

Housing the biggest concern in Spain

In Spain, concerns centre around a different hot-button issue: housing.

Nearly half of respondents (49%) ranked housing among Spain's two biggest concerns, making it the highest rated issue across all six countries studied. Healthcare and the economy followed, both selected by 25% of respondents.

These findings reflect a housing crisis that has dominated political debate in Spain over the past year, with figures from Spain's National Statistics Institute (INE) showing house prices rose by almost 13% year-on-year at the end of 2025. This was the fastest increase in Spain in years and was among the fastest increases in Europe as a whole.

People hold a banner, top left, reading in Spanish: "Homes for those who live in them" during a protest in Madrid, Spain, Sunday, May 24, 2026. AP Photo

In 2025, data suggested that a worker would have to devote the equivalent of 8.4 years of their average salary to have a chance of purchasing an 80-square-metre home.

The issue is particularly pronounced in certain parts of the country, with the Balearic Islands and Madrid among the most expensive regions for home ownership, whilst short-term lets in cities such as Barcelona have long sparked locals' anger over the lack of affordable housing.

Italians worried about healthcare

Italy, meanwhile, was the only country surveyed where healthcare emerged as the biggest concern, with some 43% of respondents ranking health and the healthcare system among the country's two biggest issues, ahead of the economy and immigration.

This comes as Italy's public health services continue to face mounting pressure from staff shortages and an ageing population. Euronews previously reported that the country is short of an estimated 175,000 nurses, with low pay, heavy workloads and limited career prospects contributing to an exodus of trained medical professionals to other European countries.

Denmark stands apart

Denmark was the only country where the economy, housing, or healthcare did not top the list of concerns.

Instead, international terrorism or aggression and climate change were jointly ranked as the country's biggest issues, with both cited by 27% of respondents. Immigration followed at 24%, while healthcare and the economy ranked lower.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey: What chances does Ozel's new opposition party have?
World.content:
After being removed as head of Turkey's main opposition CHP in May, Ozgur Ozel has announced the formation of a new party. Dozens of lawmakers have followed him, but will he be able to challenge President Erdogan?

In the early morning of May 24, shocking images of Ankara were broadcast around the world. After a court ordered that Ozel be ousted as head of the center-left Republican People's Party (CHP), the country's largest opposition party, its headquarters in the Turkish capital were surrounded by special forces.

The party leader and his allies had barricaded the doors with tables and chairs, but hours later they stopped resisting. "We want to avoid an escalation and are leaving of our own free will," a visibly shaken Ozel said. "Our only crime is to have defeated the ruling party."

Indeed, under his leadership, the CHP had managed something it had not succeeded in doing in 22 years. It had defeated the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) in a nationwide election.

In the local elections of March 2024, the party emerged as the strongest and took over control of city councils in 14 major cities. That included Istanbul, whose mayor, Ekrem Imamoglu, quickly became so popular that he established himself as a serious challenger to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in the next presidential election, which is scheduled for 2028.

The arrest of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu triggered protests across the city Image: Umit Bektas/REUTERS

But soon Imamoglu was arrested, alongside several other mayors and their staff. They are accused of corruption and fraud. And then in May, Ozel was removed from his position.

Two months later, he announced the formation of the Yeni Parti, or "New Party," submitting formal registration to the interior ministry. With 91 lawmakers, it is set to become the second largest party behind the AKP in Turkey's 600-seat parliament.

CHP, a divided opposition party

Founded in 1923 by the founder of the Republic of Turkey, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the CHP is Turkey's oldest political party, standing for the separation of church and state, patriotism and republicanism.

Ozel, who came from the pro-reform faction and became head in 2023, was able to open up the party to voters beyond its core base, placing more emphasis on the values of social democracy. He met with success, as the election results showed.

But after Ozel was ousted, Kemal Kilicdaroglu, the old party leader under whose watch the CHP had lost every election for two decades, returned. Kilicdaroglu was considered to be Erdogan's preferred opponent.

Why did the CHP split?

There has been much speculation as to why the party accepted the court ruling and agreed to the party being divided. Experts believe that behind the scenes, political calculations that benefit Erdogan are at play. The split will allow him to eliminate dangerous opponents ahead of the next presidential election.

The conflict within the CHP dates back to 2023: After the defeat of Kilicdaroglu, who was party leader at the time, by Erdogan in the presidential election, the reformist faction led by Ozel and Imamoglu pressed the 75-year-old to step down. They prevailed at the party convention in the autumn of 2023.

But in May 2026, a court declared the party convention null and void due to alleged irregularities. As a result, Ozel and other leaders were removed from their posts, and Kilicdaroglu and his allies returned.

What Ozel said upon leaving CHP

Ozel was less willing to accept the ruling; he and his faction fought to the very end to remain, but they were forced out because the country's judiciary has become increasingly less independent under Erdogan.

In his farewell speech on Tuesday, Ozel called on his supporters to follow him: "We will walk together on a new path," he said. "We will march to power. Let's walk friends, let's walk friends!"

Dozens of lawmakers followed Ozel from the CHP to his new party Image: ANKA

And follow him they did. The mass exodus to Ozel's Yeni Parti will leave the CHP with 44 seats in parliament, making the CHP the fourth largest in Turkey.

Can Ozel be a serious challenge to Erdogan?

Seren Selvin Korkmaz, the director of the Istanbul-based think tank IstanPol, said that Ozel's Yeni Parti had good chances of succeeding, considering it had so much support from former CHP supporters.

However, she warned against taking voters for granted. She said that a recent poll the think tank had conducted showed voters did not just want the CHP with a different name but a party that built upon its legacy while also moving beyond it.

According to the IstanPol poll, around 30% of respondents would vote for the new party or at least consider it. Another 19% said their decision would depend on the party's program, candidates and leaders.

She concluded that there was a "broad but conditional potential" for support of almost 49%, explaining that this was fueled both by sympathy for Ozel as well as hostility toward the judiciary interfering in party politics. She said that generally opposition voters were open to a new party.

Korkmaz suggested that the new party could make inroads among supporters of the nationalist conservative IYI party and the pro-Kurdish DEM, as well as certain voters of the ruling AKP party and some of the supporters of its coalition allies from the ultranationalist MHP. She added that the biggest challenge would be to unite the at times conflicting expectations of these different segments under a common umbrella.

She predicted that the party could be successful if it was able to avoid being too ideologically limited or bland and centrist. He said that it was clear from Ozel's rhetoric that he wanted to establish an inclusive center, with a republican and socio-democratic backbone.

No future in Turkey? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It remains to be seen whether Ozel will be able to establish party structures in at least 41 of Turkey's 81 provinces by the time of the next presidential election in 2028. This is a prerequisite for being eligible to run.

Ozel's Yeni Parti does not have access to the same funds as the CHP, which will make the process even more difficult.

World.title: Why Trump's 'forced labor' tariffs leave the world puzzled
World.content:
After the US Supreme Court struck down Donald Trump's emergency tariffs, the White House has turned to another trade law linked to alleged human rights abuses. DW explains the new tariffs and the debate surrounding them.

Which countries will face Trump's new tariffs?

The Trump administration on Thursday announced new tariffs on 60 economies, including the European Union, citing their handling of imported goods made with forced labor.

In a statement, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) said it had investigated major trading partners and found that they failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods made through modern slavery.

The tariffs cover more than 99% of US imports and replace a temporary 10% global tariff that was due to expire.

A 10% tariff will apply to countries like Argentina, India, Pakistan and the UK that have adopted or committed to forced-labor import restrictions.

Trump hits Canada with 50% tariffs in major trade escalation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland will face tariffs of either 10% or 12.5%, depending on the product.

Goods from 38 other countries will be subject to the higher tariff of 12.5%, including China, most of the Middle East, much of Latin America, Australia, New Zealand and Russia.

Exemptions include steel, aluminum, automobiles, civilian aircraft, rare earth minerals and goods covered by the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

The new tariffs took effect just after midnight Eastern Standard Time on Friday, July 24.

Are Trump's new tariffs really about forced labor?

The USTR noted that the US has banned imports made with forced labor for almost a century, adding that despite international consensus, "the prevalence of forced labor persists worldwide and has even escalated in recent years."

Washington argues that foreign producers gain an unfair price advantage from the practice and that US workers cannot compete with forced-labor wages.

In reality, many critics and analysts see the move as a legal workaround for US President Donald Trump's broad tariff program, announced on "Liberation Day" April 2, 2025, which the US Supreme Court struck down in February.

At that time, Trump invoked the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) of 1977 to impose the tariffs without congressional approval, but the court ruled that the law does not authorize presidents to impose tariffs on their own.

The new forced labor tariffs were introduced under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a more established trade law that many analysts believe will be harder for courts to overturn.

Does the EU really have a problem with forced labor?

Compared with parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America, forced labor isn't a major issue within the 27-member EU, due to comprehensive labor laws and strong enforcement.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) defines forced labor as work performed under the threat of penalty and without voluntary consent.

While labor protections in the EU are comparatively strong, many imports still contain raw materials or components linked to forced labor elsewhere.

In December 2027, Brussels will introduce one of the world's strictest import bans, when no product tainted by forced labor will be allowed to enter, circulate or leave the EU market.

Reacting to the new tariffs, the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, compared the bloc's labor laws to those of the United States, noting that EU workers have paid vacations and other better working conditions.

Why do critics see the tariffs as a legal workaround?

Some analysts argued that the new tariffs don't keep to the spirit of the Supreme Court ruling and could be challenged.

"These new tariffs would represent another case of presidential overreach," Alan Wolff, a former deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization (WTO), wrote in a blog post ahead of the announcement.

"The world has become accustomed to higher US tariffs. There is no evidence that changing the US rationale for them will materially reduce forced labor in other countries," Wolff added.

Others said Trump was using forced labor concerns as a pretext, when the share of imports linked to forced labor from most advanced economies is negligible compared with China.

If tackling forced labor is critical, trade experts question why the Trump administration hasn't singled out China Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

"The tariffs use real concerns about China's labor practices not as the basis for tariffs against China, but for broad tariffs against most of the world," Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank, wrote on X.

Chad Bown, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, also thinks the tariffs "divert US and allied attention from the trade war we should be fighting", which he said was cutting reliance on Chinese goods and building "resilient alternative supply chains."

Trade partners echoed those criticisms, with Brazil calling the tariffs "unjustified" and Australia labeling them "absurd."

Could Trump use Section 301 for more tariffs?

The administration is already using Section 301 for another investigation into excess manufacturing capacity in 16 major trading partners, including China and the EU. Trade experts expect it could lead to additional tariffs.

During his first term, the same legislation allowed Trump to impose tariffs on China over intellectual property theft and technology transfer. These were expanded under the Biden administration.

MAGA moves to meddle in European politics To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump's team continues to maintain existing national-security tariffs on steel, aluminum, automobiles and other products, under Section 232 of the same Act.

Trump's first administration imposed 25% duties on steel and 10% on aluminum in 2018, after the US Commerce Department found the low-cost imports threatened US national interests.

During his second term, Trump restored, expanded and increased many of those rates, while adding new tariffs on vehicles, auto parts and copper.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: Ousted Turkish opposition leader forms second-largest party
World.content:
With 90 lawmakers defecting alongside him, Ozgur Ozel's New Party has automatically become the second-largest group in Turkey's parliament. He leaves behind deep devisions and judicial challenges against the CHP.

The ousted leader of Turkey's opposition Republican People's Party (CHP), along with 90 other lawmakers, broke away under a new banner on Friday.

Ozgur Ozel founded the Yeni Parti, or "New Party," and has vowed to lead the fight against Turkey's longtime President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

"May it be beneficial to our country, our nation, our party, and all of us," Ozel said.

New party becomes second-biggest in parliament

With 91 lawmakers in total, the New Party becomes the second-largest party in Turkey's 600-seat parliament, after Erdogan's Justice and Development Party (AKP) which holds 277 seats.

Meanwhile, the CHP had until now been the second-largest with 135 seats, but Friday's exodus leaves the party with just 44 lawmakers — including some Ozel backers among them.

That relegates it to fourth place, behind the pro-Kurdish opposition DEM party, which has 56 seats.

"The new party we are about to establish will become the main opposition force in the Grand National Assembly by a wide margin," Ozel told lawmakers on Tuesday.

The CHP was established in 1923 by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, who founded modern Turkey as a secular republic and served as the country’s first president.

The Kemalist party was the main challenger to the ruling conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP), which has been in power for six consecutive terms since 2002.

CHP mired by division, legal troubles

Ozel's breakaway party was founded after deep divisions within the CHP.

He had won the CHP's leadership election in 2023 and reversed the party's fortunes with major gains at municipal elections the following year.

Turkey's Ozel launches new party to challenge Erdogan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2025, Ozel gained an even higher profile when he became the face of mass protests to free Istanbul mayor and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who faces a prison sentence in excess of 2,000 years on charges of corruption and terrorism. He was widely seen as viable challenger to Erdogan's two-decade rule.

However, in May of this year, a court annulled the election over allegations of vote buying. The court stripped Ozel of his title and appointed his unpopular rival, Kemal Kilicdaroglu, in his place.

Critics have described the legal challenges against Imamoglu, Ozel, the CHP and its supporters as politically motivated and undemocratic.

The government denies these claims and maintains that the judiciary is independent.

After the New Party filed formation papers with the Interior Ministry on Friday, defecting Ankara MP Murat Emir told reporters: "We are leaving an occupied party behind."

World.title: Fighting wildfires is getting harder — these tips could help
World.content:
With Spain declaring a national emergency, France seeking EU assistance and Canada dealing with more than 900 hot spots, wildfires are out of control. How can we stop our forests from burning?

Intense, relentless heat waves and prolonged drought have triggered another severe wildfire season across Europe this summer, with crews battling massive blazes in France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, the UK and even Norway.

Similar conditions have also fueled fires in the United States and Canada. For weeks, hundreds of wildfires have ripped throughout the vast boreal forest stretching from the Yukon in the north to Newfoundland in the east. As of July 24, they've wiped out at least 3.3 million hectares (8.1 million acres — an area larger than Belgium.

As toxic smoke shrouded major cities, also in the US, President Donald Trump accused Canada on social media of "not properly maintaining their Forests" and deliberately neglecting "basic Forest Management and Debris Removal."

Smoke worsened air quality and cast an eerie light over cities in Canada and the US, including Toronto Image: Cole Burston/AFP

'No one-size-fits-all' solution

While eliminating flammable fuel is part of the job for fire experts, effective management goes beyond just clearing debris. And in Canada, clearing brush from such an extensive, remote area would be impossible.

"There is no one-size-fits-all" solution, said Amy Duchelle, a senior forestry officer with the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

Frequent extreme heat waves and extended droughts linked to human-caused climate change are drying out trees and undergrowth. That's fueling high-intensity fires more likely to burn out of control, said Duchelle — even in places previously too humid to burn.

Tropical forests like the Amazon region or Southeast Asia didn't evolve to coexist with fire — no thick, resistant bark or plants suited to germinate after a blaze. Here, it's crucial to stop deforestation linked to mining and agriculture, preserve the canopy and vegetation that creates the humid, fire-resistant habitat, and train people to immediately respond to any fire risk.

Heat waves fuel wildfires across southern Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Europe, management solutions can include cross-border monitoring and protection, and prioritizing fire-resistant vegetation instead of highly flammable conifers. That also means bringing back diverse tree species that contribute to more resilient forests, which have dwindled due to farming and exploitation over the centuries.

Fighting fire with fire

In some places, fire itself is key to preserving forests.

"Our boreal forest is a fire-dependent forest — it needs fire for health," said Amy Cardinal Christianson, an Indigenous Metis fire specialist in western Canada. She said a certain number of blazes are part of a natural cycle, creating natural firebreaks, stimulating fresh plant growth and restoring ecosystems — all of which can slow the spread of wildfires.

Research has shown that certain forests have evolved to live with periodic fires, which act as a sort of reset. The flames can clear the way for smaller plants struggling to compete with unchecked undergrowth, for example, and burned material also releases nutrients that enrich the soil.

Some fires help forest landscapes to thrive Image: Ondrej Hajek/CTK/picture alliance

But Canada's wildfire season is now accelerating the normal, healthy cycle — starting earlier, lasting longer and becoming harder to control.

It's also adding to Canada's carbon emissions: the 2023 record fire season, which wiped out five times the annual average of forestland, added 23% to the world's annual wildfire emissions. Some of the pollutants even made it as far as western Europe.

Christianson, a former research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service and now director of fire stewardship with the Indigenous Leadership Initiative , said older forest management practices ideas introduced by Europeans to support the timber industry — strict regulation, complete suppression and a focus on fast-growing monocultures — don't fit into the Canadian context.

"By excluding fire, we've actually accelerated the risk," she said, adding that periodic controlled burns can actually help reduce the risk of out-of-control infernos.

Global fire hub aims to share knowledge

Duchelle told DW how skilled pros who've dealt with forest fires for decades are now seeing blazes even they can't control — "the fire is moving too fast, the flames are too high, the heat is too intense."

Faced with these challenges, the focus has shifted from suppressing fires to reducing risk, preparing for changing conditions and building post-fire resilience. In 2023, the FAO set up the Global Fire Management Hub to help countries confronting wildfires to train and work together, sharing their knowledge.

A major focus is using new technology and data to direct monitoring and response, along with a digital platform to share information, and developing international interoperability and community-based management.

Christianson has worked with the Fire Hub to develop a network focused on Indigenous knowledge and practices, after setting up an independent network of more than 200 local guardians in Canada to help manage wildfire response.

Wildfires on the rise: Rethinking prevention across Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

That includes cultural burning — small, low-intensity deliberate blazes adapted to specific landscapes which help eliminate decaying organic matter in a controlled manner, protect wildfire and biodiversity and preserve local cultures.

Prescribed burns, which are generally done by government agencies, are also beneficial and have been employed for years. But they tend to be larger, and don't always take the local environment into account. They may also be done in the summer when conditions are drier, to speed up the process, increasing the risk of escape.

Cultural burning usually happens in early spring or late fall, based on snow and other environmental factors. But climate change has also shifted that schedule, and Christianson said it helps to be familiar with the landscape to notice those changes. "We usually would burn in April or May," she said of her property. "This year, I burned a bunch in February."

'Healthy landscapes' key to living with fire

Christianson regularly carries out cultural burning on her land — and has introduced her daughters to the practice Image: Indigenous Leadership Initiative

Speaking with DW from her home in Rocky Mountain House, Alberta, Christianson said while the same burning practices can't always be applied across diverse cultures, they've still been able to share proven ideas and techniques internationally.

"The really cool thing about Indigenous cultural burning practices is that there's a lot of overarching similarities, a responsibility that we all feel to steward the landscape, and that fire is one of those important ways that we can do that," said Christianson, who has also introduced the practice to her daughters.

"The overall goal for most Indigenous folks that I've talked to is achieving healthy landscapes."

That means looking at the bigger picture — restoring wetlands to make an ecosystem more resilient in the face of fires, or reintroducing native species like the bison in Canada, which once numbered in the millions and help control fires by grazing on vegetation encroaching on grasslands and forests.

The practice has also recently been reintroduced in Europe, with horses and European bison in Spain and Portugal.

"A healthy landscape […] can more easily adapt to these fire events that we're seeing," said Christianson.

Amazon forest fires at historic low in 2025

One country that has seen recent success in tackling forest fires is Brazil.

"Brazil's been quite effective in bringing down not only their deforestation rate, but also the incidence of fires in the Amazon," said Duchelle, crediting cooperation between state, municipal and federal agencies and a national policy on integrated fire management. "[This success] didn't happen by accident."

Tropical forests like the Amazon aren't adapted to intense wildfires Image: Christian Braga/Greenpeace

In 2025, forest fires across South America's largest nation hit a historic low, burning around 12.7 million hectares, an area roughly the size of Greece.

New data from environmental monitoring network MapBiomas showed just under a quarter of the total burned area was in the Amazon rainforest, the world's largest and a key regulator of global climate. That's an 80% drop compared with 2024, and around 56% lower than the 40-year historical average.

The Cerrado savanna in central Brazil, however, where fire is part of the ecosystem, continued to burn at similar rates, due in part to prolonged drought. Experts have warned that the incoming El Nino weather pattern could bring even drier weather, amplifying the fire risk.

Brazil's $125 billion plan to save the world's rainforests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: How vanilla's history is not so … 'vanilla'
World.content:
Long before "vanilla" meant bland, the bean's fandom spanned Mesoamerican elites to European courts. But it owes its ubiquity to a 12-year-old, enslaved boy.

Vanilla is almost everywhere — in ice creams, cough syrups, cleaning products and perfumes.

Its ubiquity, thanks to the cheaper and widely available synthetic vanillin, has over time earned it synonymity with "ordinary" or "plain" in the English language.

Yet natural vanilla is one of the most labor‑intensive crops on earth and one of the most chemically complex, containing more than 200 aromatic compounds. As the world's second most expensive spice after saffron, it sells between $100 and $600 (€90 to €550) per kilogram.

And its history is anything but "vanilla."

It involves, among others, a stingless bee, colonial machinations, as well as the ingenuity of a 12‑year‑old enslaved boy named Edmond Albius — whose discovery enriched colonial coffers and altered the bean's global trajectory.

Today synthetic vanillin lends its aroma to diverse products Image: Mungo & Maud/dpa/picture alliance

From Aztec tribute to colonial 'discovery'

Vanilla's origin story is generally situated in ancient Mesoamerica, where the creeping orchid vine — Vanilla planifolia — grew wild in tropical forests.

Early written records show that different communities had their own names for it: the Mexica called it "tlilxochitl," the Totonacs "xanath," and the Maya "sisbic." Vanilla was a valuable commodity among these civilizations — used in medicine, in ritual, to perfume temples, in cacao drinks and as tribute.

The Totonac people who lived in what is now Veracruz, Mexico, were the first to cultivate the vine, which they prized for its scent. When the Aztecs conquered them, they demanded vanilla as tribute and used it to flavour "xocolatl," a cacao‑based sacred beverage reserved for elites and warriors — and precursor to modern-day chocolate.

Europe developed a taste for vanilla after the Spanish brought it over from Mexico Image: KHARBINE-TAPABOR/IMAGO

In 1519, Aztec Emperor Moctezuma Xocoyotzin served this drink to Spanish forces led by Hernan Cortes, shortly before Spain established colonial rule in central Mexico.

The Spanish later introduced vanilla to Europe, where it first circulated in the Spanish royal court through the chocolate preparation they had adopted in Mexico. Vanilla soon reached French and English court kitchens, where it began to serve as the sole flavor in certain sweets and pastries.

A bee stumps Europe

The orchid was cultivated in botanical gardens in France and England, but try as they might, the Europeans could not get the flowers to fruit.

Colonial administrators even shipped vines across their empires — to India, Java, the Philippines and the French colony island of Reunion. The vines climbed and the flowers opened, but produced no vanilla pods. A puzzle that persisted for nearly three centuries.

The tiny Melipona bee was once the only natural pollinator of the vanilla orchid Image: Sunbird Images/imageBROKER/IMAGO

Growers were stumped as to why until 1836, when Belgian horticulturist Charles Morren identified the stingless Melipona bee as vanilla's natural pollinator — an insect geographically native only to Mexico. Morren did manage to manually pollinate vanilla in a lab, but his method was time-consuming and non-scalable for colonial plantations.

Until 12‑year‑old Edmond Albius, an enslaved boy on Reunion Island, cracked the code.

Edmond Albius and his 'uncannily simple' invention

In 1841, Edmond discovered how to pollinate the vanilla flower by hand.

Using his thumb and a small splinter to lift the tiny flap inside the flower that keeps the pollen and stigma apart, he pressed them together. And voila, the orchids produced vanilla pods soon after.

Edmond Albius' ingenious hand pollination method is used to this day Image: piemags/IMAGO

Historian Eric T. Jennings, the author of "Vanilla: The History of an Extraordinary Bean" (2025), has attempted the technique himself: "Like many brilliant inventions, his seems uncannily simple after the fact. Putting the male and female parts of the vanilla into contact is easier said than done," he tells DW.

Reunion Island briefly dominated the global vanilla market. But by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, French colonial administrators spread Edmond's hand-pollination method to their other colony, Madagascar, which is still the world's largest vanilla producer. The beans grown in these French colonies became known as Bourbon vanilla — named after Reunion's former colonial name, Ile Bourbon.

Present-day Reunion Island was previously known as Ile Bourbon, lending its name to the vanilla grown there Image: KHARBINE-TAPABOR/IMAGO

A footnote in vanilla's history?

Edmond's technique is the now the universal standard in the global multibillion dollar vanilla industry. It remains a slow, delicate and intensely labor‑driven endeavor, as each vanilla flower opens for a single day, and is quickly pollinated by hand.

Yet, Edmond never profited from the industry built on his ingenuity. He died in poverty in 1880, while French colonial coffers swelled from the method he'd devised aged 12.

Jennings, whose research took him to Reunion, tells DW that there are two monuments in Edmond's honor — a plaque and a statue — in his native town of Sainte-Suzanne on Reunion Island, and a couple of schools are also named after him. "But his story is still relatively unknown, it seems to me," says Jennings.

Natural vanilla is one of the world's most labor-intensive crops Image: Depositphotos/IMAGO

This despite Edmond's discovery having reshaped Reunion's agricultural future: "He not only brought prosperity to Reunion Island by making it the world's top vanilla producer within 30 years of his discovery, but he also helped rediversify the island's crops, which up until his discovery was tracking toward the monoculture of sugar. That, in turn, was starting to drain and exhaust the island’s rich soils," Jennings points out.

While Jennings agrees that the lack of proper credit or monetary compensation for Edmond's discovery also lies in the fact that he was an enslaved teen, he points out that Edmond was nevertheless recognized as the inventor of a new method, since a rival white botanist at the head of Reunion's main garden tried to take credit for the discovery and failed.

"Indeed, the reason we know the details we do about Edmond Albius stems from the rebuttal that his former owner and acquaintances launched against this rival claim," Jennings explains.

The widespread use of synthetic vanillin in many consumer goods has reduced vanilla to mean 'ordinary' Image: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

Anything but plain

But vanilla's story continued evolving after Edmond's breakthrough. Chemists isolated vanillin — the compound behind much of its aroma — in 1858 and synthesized it in 1874.

Cheap and easy to mass produce, synthetic vanillin quickly became standard in ice creams, soft drinks, perfumes, baked goods and processed foods, turning a once-coveted spice into a flavor few of us think twice about.

Jennings says this substitution transformed the flavor's meaning. As synthetic vanillin democratized vanilla's consumption between 1880 and 1960, it became less exclusive, more widespread — even boring. Its "sheer evenness, the complete flatness of the synthetic produces a numbing effect," Jennings says of its association with being "plain."

Yet the real bean, layered with more than 200 compounds, was never bland — and neither was its history.

Vanilla - more valuable than gold To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

World.title: Klopp named new head coach of Germany men's football team
World.content:
Germany has turned to Jürgen Klopp to lead a new era for the four-time world champions after their disappointing World Cup exit, with hopes of building toward future international tournaments.

The German Football Association (DFB) has appointed Jürgen Klopp as the new head coach of the national team on Friday, ending speculation about who would succeed Julian Nagelsmann.

DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said the association's governing bodies had unanimously approved Klopp's appointment, describing him as the "ideal choice" for the role.

"It is a great honor to sit here today," Klopp said at the press conference announcing his appointment, adding he was "delighted."

What else do we know about Klopp's appointment as Germany head coach?

Klopp emerged as the federation's preferred candidate after Nagelsmann stepped down following Germany's penalty shootout defeat to Paraguay in the World Cup round of 32.

In a statement released by the DFB, Klopp was quoted as saying: "The national team can unite us Germans like almost nothing else. That is precisely what makes this role so special to me."

He said he was looking forward "to this special challenge in German football, which we will tackle together with humility and patience." He wanted to build a team "that fights for one another, that enjoys playing football, and behind which the people of our country can rally with complete conviction."

The real Jürgen Klopp To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The former Liverpool manager held talks with DFB officials in New York while working as a television analyst during the tournament, and the federation announced on July 11 that the two sides had reached agreement on the essential terms of a contract.

His contract starts on August 15 and continues until the summer of 2030, with the next World Cup tournament.

His first match as Germany head coach will be against the Netherlands in Amsterdam on September 24 in Germany's opening Nations League fixture.

This is Klopp's first coaching job since he left Liverpool in 2024 citing fatigue.

The DFB also announced on Friday that Per Mertesacker will be its managing director, after his predecessor Andreas Rettig steps down at the end of the year.

Klopp's star-studded coaching career

After spending much of his career as a player for Mainz, Klopp as coach took the club to the Bundesliga for the first time.

Then, as Borussia Dortmund's coach, he took the team to back-to-back Bundesliga titles, taking the club to the Champion's League final in 2013.

His more recent coaching career saw him shine with England's Liverpool, which he coached for nine years, delivering a first league title in more than a quarter of a century and glory in the 2019 Champions League final.

Klopp was awarded the highest civic award in Germany as a result of his outstanding contribution to democracy and his impact on the football world. He was credited with becoming a role model, a football ambassador and someone who has improved the image of Germany around the world, particularly in the United Kingdom.

This is Klopp's first coaching job since he left Liverpool in 2024 citing fatigue Image: Florian Wiegand/dpa/picture alliance
