World.title: Armenian rights lawyer files ECHR complaint over Ruben Vardanyan’s 20-year jail sentence in Baku
World.content:
ECHR complaint over Vardanyan case

Human rights lawyer Siranush Sahakyan has filed a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) over the case of Ruben Vardanyan, the former state minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. She said she would represent Vardanyan before the court. Sahakyan has represented Armenian detainees at the ECHR for many years.

“The application sets out in detail violations of eight articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, supported by comprehensive legal and factual arguments,” Sahakyan said in a statement shared with the media and posted on social media.

Vardanyan is one of 19 Armenians still held in Azerbaijani prisons. In February 2026, a military court in Baku sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

According to Sahakyan, the defence was only recently able to obtain the court’s written judgment, which was required before an application could be submitted to the ECHR. She said Azerbaijan had withheld the ruling until then, which is why the complaint was filed only on 19 July.

The court found Vardanyan guilty of a number of serious offences, including waging war, financing terrorism and deportation.

Armenian rights groups, however, have described the trial in Baku as “political rather than legal”. Vardanyan himself called the proceedings “a farce” and “a mockery of justice”. During the hearings, he instructed his lawyer not to present arguments in his defence.

“It is impossible to protect rights in a system that fundamentally denies the right to a fair trial. That is why Ruben Vardanyan decided to continue his fight for justice through international legal mechanisms,” Sahakyan said.

Details of Vardanyan case

In her statement, Sahakyan disclosed further details of the case. She said the military court in Baku did not read out the full verdict. Now that Vardanyan’s family has passed the written judgment to his lawyers, it has become clear that he was convicted on 41 counts under 21 articles of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code.

According to Sahakyan, the judgment does not substantiate Vardanyan’s personal criminal responsibility with facts or evidence.

“Instead, the court concluded that the ‘criminal organisation’ – the leadership of the self-proclaimed Republic of Artsakh – had been operating in Nagorno-Karabakh since 1988. It also found that Vardanyan joined this ‘organisation’ in December 2020, although he was living in Moscow at the time.”

She also said the court treated Vardanyan’s appointment to a civilian administrative post as a violent seizure of power. His commercial and charitable activities were classified as illegal entrepreneurship and financing terrorism, while his entry into Nagorno-Karabakh via the Lachin Corridor was deemed an illegal crossing of Azerbaijan‘s state border.

Sahakyan said Vardanyan had not appealed against the verdict because he regarded the trial as staged and pre-planned, and considered all domestic legal remedies ineffective.

Background

On 17 February, a military court in Baku sentenced Russian-Armenian businessman, billionaire and philanthropist Ruben Vardanyan to 20 years in prison. His case was heard separately from those of the former leadership of Nagorno-Karabakh.

A month after the verdict, Vardanyan’s family said he had tried to raise concerns with Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner, Sabina Aliyeva, during a phone call with relatives, but the call was cut off.

The family has repeatedly appealed to the international community, saying that neither Vardanyan nor the other Armenian detainees in Azerbaijan have access to institutional protection. They argue that the country lacks independent human rights protection mechanisms. They have also noted that the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had facilitated contact between detainees and their families, has ceased operations in Azerbaijan.

On 5 February, two weeks before Vardanyan’s sentence was announced, an Azerbaijani court handed life sentences to several other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders, including former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, his deputy Davit Manukyan, former parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and former Foreign Minister Davit Babayan. Former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison.

All of the detainees faced a range of serious charges, including terrorism and genocide. Ghukasyan and Sahakyan received lighter sentences because they are over 65, and Azerbaijani law does not allow life imprisonment for people above that age.

Independent media and human rights observers were not allowed to attend the trials. Information about the proceedings was published by Azerbaijani state and pro-government media.

World.title: New report reveals what triggered SA's catastrophic algal bloom crisis
World.content:
After more than 18 months of uncertainty surrounding South Australia's most catastrophic algal bloom crisis, a long-awaited report has been released by the SA government shedding light on the environmental conditions that fuelled the marine event.

The report has concluded that floodwater, a coastal upwelling and a marine heatwave all contributed to the conditions that led to the devastating event, but that there was no "single trigger".

The preliminary investigation was conducted by the South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI) into potential drivers of the bloom, and its release was foreshadowed in February, when authorities blamed the bloom on a "convergence" of events — including comments on the nutrient load from River Murray flooding as one of the main factors.

A full report was released today following what the SA government described as an independent peer-review process.

The algal bloom was first detected in March 2025, and is characterised by foamy and discoloured water. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Report released late

But the date on the report dated back to May 15 this year, which has been questioned by some, including Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, who slammed the state government for not being up-front on the matter from the beginning.

"We know from the beginning they [SA government] were too slow to act and asleep at the wheel," she said.

" The South Australian government has tried to downplay the impact of the toxic algal bloom on South Australians and on our environment, so I am unsurprised that a peer reviewed report has been sitting on the desk for months. "

Sarah Hanson-Young says the SA government has downplayed the impact of the toxic algal bloom. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

When asked why the report was made public late, South Australia's Primary Industries Minister Clare Scriven said it needed to go through the processes, including being peer-reviewed.

"It needed to go to the Algal Bloom Taskforce, and be analysed by my office and the taskforce," Ms Scriven said.

"It was reviewed by independent reviewers from Tasmania and the United States."

But ecologist Faith Coleman, who resigned from SA HAB (Harmful Algal Bloom) Scientific Advisory Committee and SA Algae Bloom Reference Group earlier this year, said the report did not need to be peer reviewed and should not have taken that long.

"It shouldn't have needed to gone off and spend all the time from April to now being peer-reviewed, that is a lot of months," she said.

But she welcomed the transparency from the government saying the findings will be useful going forward.

Faith Coleman has asked the state government to release more data. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The findings

The report found that there were three major contributing factors that triggered the ideal conditions for the bloom to develop, including floodwater, a coastal upwelling and a marine heatwave.

It was found that the bloom developed and intensified during an unprecedented marine heatwave.

The report stated that while temperature alone may not explain bloom initiation, the associated calm conditions, reduced wind mixing and enhanced water-column stratification were considered a key enabling factor, favouring motile dinoflagellates such as Karenia.

It said that multi-decadal analyses show that the bloom developed following a period of prolonged environmental pre-conditioning.

SARDI's executive director Professor Mike Steer said a comprehensive amount of research had gone into finding these out.

"There's not a single smoking gun, there wasn't one particular environmental factor that was the culprit for this algal bloom, in fact it was a convergence of many different things," Professor Steer said.

"This is really important information to understand because if we're going to develop a forecasting index for harmful algal blooms for SA or Australia in the future then we really need to understand these fundamental drivers."

Mike Steer says there are notable gaps in the data collected. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

He admitted there were still gaps in the data they have collected and analysed.

"Now there are notably gaps in those data, but we'll seek to fill them as we go forward," he said.

But Professor Steer said he was surprised how quickly the team was able to pull together the report.

"I thought it was going to take us a lot longer to get where we are at, but the foundation that we have set is really promising," he said.

Ms Scriven said while nothing could be done to stop the algal bloom from occurring, the research helps to be more prepared.

Clare Scriven says nothing can be done to prevent a harmful algal bloom from occurring. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

But Ms Coleman has asked the state government to release more data.

"It's not a rigorous review of the science that we would've liked to see at this point," she said.

" It is a good technical report, I'm looking forward to seeing a huge pile of data to go with it, rather than just the dot points. "

"I'd like them to release the data about all of the other hazardous species that have occurred, not just Karenia."

Ms Coleman said she also hopes the government will change conversations around the Murray River — which was persistently blamed as one of the main contributing factors.

"That has been a major issue for us all the way along is the comment that it is the River Murray, because that impacts how we manage the biggest most regulated river in the nation," she said.

There's gap in the data

Professor Steer said there was still a lot that is not known and that it was going to take time to look at some of the knowledge gaps.

The algal bloom devastated South Australia's coastline, resulting in the deaths of significant numbers of marine life. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"One of the challenges in science is that in answering one particular question you generate ten more," he said.

" There is an incredible complexity of issues that are happened within a marine environment and the complexity within the harmful algal bloom community dynamics is just next level. "

Professor Steer said the report is a strong foundation for the new office to continue their research in collaboration with national and international jurisdictions.

This includes looking at topics such as, "The different biochemicals are produced by the harmful algal bloom species, the role the environment plays in persisting algal blooms, and understanding the impact on key recreational commercial fisheries and marine ecosystems," he said.

Going forward, Professor Steer said the algal bloom crisis and the report will set down precedent on how to deal with similar crisis in the future.

" We don't want the legacy of the bloom, our response to the bloom being our legacy, we want the preparedness for future blooms to be something that we'll work towards. "

"Our focus now is on improving our science and understanding it so we're better prepared in the future."

World.title: Police officer shot while responding to call on the Fraser Coast
World.content:
A police officer has been shot while responding to an incident on the Fraser Coast.

Officers were called to an incident on Horizon Court in Yengarie, west of Maryborough, just after 3pm following reports of a disturbance.

Police say one of the officers was shot in the leg while officers attempted to engage with a man at the property.

It is understood the officer is in a stable condition and has been transported to hospital.

An emergency declaration has been made under the Public Safety Preservation Act in relation to the incident.

An exclusion zone is in place for multiple streets in Yengarie. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

The exclusion zone encompasses Lake Drive, Meadow Drive, and Mary View Drive along the Mary River in Yengarie.

Ergon has cut electricity to the suburb as the police operation continues.

Residents are being urged to stay indoors, and members of the public are being urged to avoid the area.

In a statement, the Queensland Police Union said a 36-year-old constable had sustained a gunshot wound.

"He is receiving expert medical care, and the QPS is taking responsibility for notifying his immediate family," the statement read.

It said the QPU Critical Incident Team was also assisting.

World.title: Youth rehab provider's social media follows questioned in parliament
World.content:
Concerns about the social media conduct of a publicly funded youth rehabilitation provider have been raised in Queensland parliament.

The Yabun Panjoo Aboriginal Corporation is one of nine service providers contracted to deliver the Crisafulli government's $50 million regional reset program.

It was tasked with providing a 12-month intensive rehabilitation program for at-risk young people, some as young as eight, in Townsville and Mount Isa.

The corporation received $1.43 million last year to deliver the program in each service location, over four years.

The Labor spokeswoman for Youth Justice, Di Farmer, questioned whether the taxpayer-funded provider's social media use was appropriate, during parliamentary budget estimates.

Di Farmer questioned the delivery of the government's youth justice programs in budget estimates. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"The Yabun Panjoo Facebook page follows twelve people," she said.

"About 70 per cent of them are adult content creators, including OnlyFans creators."

"Is it appropriate that taxpayer-funded contractors who work with troubled young people almost exclusively follow profiles promoting adult content?"

Ms Farmer later withdrew the question.

Laura Gerber fronted estimates on Friday. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber said providers of the government's early intervention program were delivering.

"They're there to be able to deliver a reset to youth that otherwise would be following down a life of crime," she said.

The director of Yabun Panjoo, David Boye, was contacted for comment.

The Department of Youth Justice's director-general, Michael Drane, said suppliers must comply with the department's social media code of conduct.

Questions over government's rehabilitation programs

The heated budget estimates hearing continued into this evening with questions about the delivery of the government's youth rehabilitation programs, including the canning of a previous provider.

The Mara Way was contracted to deliver an early-intervention program in Mareeba in Far North Queensland, but had its funding pulled last month.

Speaking to the ABC in June, the organisation's chief executive Crystal Williams said it was meeting its obligations, but the terms set by the Youth Justice Department were unworkable.

Ms Farmer questioned Mr Drane over the funding cancellation.

"I would submit that if The Mara Way were unclear about the commitment, then they shouldn't have executed the contract," he said.

"The Department remains clear that they failed to execute the requirements under the contract that they were funded to deliver."

Ms Farmer asked if the same degree of monitoring was being applied to Yabun Panjoo Aboriginal Corporation.

"Yes, it is the case that the Department routinely monitors the performance and delivery of all contracted service providers," Mr Drane said.

"There are some 61 organisations delivering over 105 services funded by the Department of Youth Justice and further grant providers."

"Their performance is routinely monitored."

Queensland parliamentary budget estimates will continue next week.

World.title: Hundreds attend memorial for murdered mum Jana Armstrong
World.content:
Up to 1,000 people have attended an emotional candlelight vigil in Toowoomba to honour the life of 30-year-old Jana Armstrong.

As the sun set and candles sparkled, Faith Isaacs told the crowd she hoped her sister's death would encourage domestic violence victims to speak up.

"If sharing her story can save even one life then her legacy will continue to make a difference," Ms Isaacs said.

Family, friends and strangers gathered to pay their respects. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

The vigil was attended by Toowoomba Mayor Geoff MacDonald and his wife Lisa, Prevention of Domestic and Family Violence Minister Amanda Camm, local federal member Garth Hamilton, senior police officers and the police chaplain.

They were joined in the civic square lawn area adjacent to City Hall by friends and colleagues of Ms Armstrong's, as well as strangers who wanted to pay their respects to the young mother who was killed two weeks ago.

Faith Isaacs has pledged to love and care for her nephew as if he were her own. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

Ms Isaacs and her husband Michael are caring for Ms Armstrong's four-month-old son. The couple cradled the baby during the hour-long vigil.

"No family should have to go through what ours has. Domestic violence doesn't just take one victim, it leaves children without parents, families with unimaginable grief and communities heartbroken," Ms Isaacs told the crowd.

"We hope Jana's story encourages people to speak up, seek help if they are experiencing domestic violence, and to look out for those around them.

" We miss you, Jana, every single day. We will always love her, always remember her and will never stop saying her name. "

Faith Isaacs says the family misses Jana "every single day". (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

State Treasurer and local member David Janetzki told the crowd that too many women lived with the scourge of family violence.

"Every 11 days a woman is killed by someone she trusts in our country," Mr Janetzki said.

He named two other Toowoomba women who were allegedly the victims of domestic violence in the past 18 months.

"These are women we have gone to school with, they are women we have worked with, we have played sports with, we share our everyday lives with them," he said.

David Janetzki made an emotional speech at the vigil. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

On either side of the stage was a picture of Ms Armstrong and the words "Jana, never forgotten".

Ms Armstrong's aunt, Kathy Sweedman, urged the crowd never to turn a blind eye to domestic violence.

"If you are experiencing any form of domestic or family violence please speak up … please don't ever think you are alone," she said.

Kathy Sweedman urged people not to ignore domestic violence. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

Amanda Dalton, the chief executive of domestic violence charity Protea Place, said the vigil was an opportunity for people to wrap their arms around Ms Armstrong's family.

"It is very much community-focused. It is very much from the heart, to allow people that safe space to come and to gather," Ms Dalton said.

She said more women had come forward to seek support since Ms Armstrong's death.

"It hits home, the reality of it … it does raise that awareness that 'I think I might need some help,'" she said.

Jana Armstrong's family were in the front row at the service. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

Partner charged with murder

Ms Armstrong was last seen alive on the afternoon of July 7 at her home in Newtown. Earlier that day, she had met Ms Isaacs for brunch at a cafe.

Jana Armstrong is being remembered as a loving mother, sister and community member. (Supplied)

At 6am on July 8 Ms Armstrong's car was found 500 metres from her home, but she was nowhere to be found.

Taxi driver Dharminder Singh was found at Ms Armstrong's home that morning with their baby.

What we know about the alleged murder of Jana Armstrong The search for Toowoomba mother Jana Armstrong ended in tragedy. Here's what police say happened to the young mother.

Police and the SES conducted searches at Black Gully Reserve, near her home, and along Tabletop Drive at Rangeville.

Family and friends held searches at Preston, where Ms Armstrong's car had been spotted on the evening after her disappearance.

Ms Armstrong's body was discovered at 10:39pm on Sunday, July 12 in steep bushland off Esk Hampton Road at Redbank Creek, about 60 kilometres from her home, by two men out pig hunting.

Dharminder Singh was arrested at a property in Harristown in Toowoomba early the next morning and charged with her murder and with arson. He appeared in court the next day and was remanded in custody.

Family and friends searched for Jana Armstrong at Preston. (ABC News: Dan McCray)

Outside court his lawyer, Ramli Salehkon, said Mr Singh asserted his innocence and that the matter would be defended.

Ms Armstrong's funeral will be held on August 7 in Millmerran on the Western Downs. She will be buried alongside her parents and grandmother.

Almost $75,000 has been donated to a fundraiser for the family.

World.title: Woman allegedly makes antisemitic comments at Bondi attack site
World.content:
A woman will face court after allegedly making antisemitic comments to a group including Jewish leaders and Sydney Swans players at the site of the Bondi Beach terror attack.

Officers were called to Archer Park on Wednesday afternoon after a 67-year-old woman allegedly confronted the group and made abusive comments.

Executive Council of Australian Jewry Co-CEO, Alex Ryvchin was with one of the victims who was shot during the targeted December attack on a Jewish event, which claimed 15 lives.

He said the woman made comments directly to them, including "Evil Zionist".

"Which is deplorable at the best of times, but to do so in that place, at that time, in the presence of a survivor, was something which we're not going to stand for," Mr Ryvchin said.

He said the incident was also confronting for the Sydney Swans team who were visiting the site to show solidarity.

"It's grossly insensitive, it's more than that, it's inhuman and it gave them a real life example of what the Jewish community has to deal with on a daily basis," he said.

In a statement on the day of the incident, police said officers patrolling the area as part of Operation Shelter had attended the park, but that no further action would be taken.

'Not going to stand for it'

The alleged incident happened at Archer Park, the scene of the December Bondi terror attack. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Ryvchin said the survivor of the mass shooting went to police to make a complaint.

"We see what happens in our society when incitement and hatred and vilification goes unchecked," he said.

" We're not going to stand for it, we're not going to live with this, and we're not going to allow the desecration of a sacred site with that sort of language and that sort of abuse. "

Police on Friday issued the woman with a court attendance notice and said she was charged with offensive language.

"We're very grateful for it, we think it's the right move by the police and sends a strong signal throughout the country," Mr Ryvchin said.

The woman is expected to face Waverley Court in September.

World.title: Friends turned millionaires take tech company shares battle to court
World.content:
The millionaire co-founder of an Australian video tech company behind some of Hollywood's biggest blockbusters has told the Federal Court a decade of hostility by fellow shareholders has unfairly barred him from selling his lucrative stake in the billion-dollar business.

Peter Barber is suing the company he helped establish, Blackmagic Design, and co-founders Grant Petty and Douglas Clarke over claims he has been denied dividends for years, access to information about the business, and the ability to sell his shares.

Mr Barber, now based in Singapore, also alleges Mr Petty sabotaged an attempted investment in the company that valued Blackmagic at as much as $1.5 billion.

Lawyers for Peter Barber told the court he effectively has around $98 million in assets locked up in the company. (LinkedIn: Peter Barber)

Blackmagic has grown rapidly since it was founded in Melbourne in 2001 by Mr Barber and Mr Petty, old high school friends who grew up in Shepparton, and Mr Clarke, whom Mr Petty reportedly met at an Apple user group.

Last financial year the company generated more than $550 million in revenue and now operates 10 offices worldwide.

The tech juggernaut is in high demand by both amateur content creators and US production houses which used its video editing software, DaVinci Resolve, for box office smash Avatar, the recent Peaky Blinders film and hit television series Grey's Anatomy and Yellowstone.

The company's hardware was also behind 2019's The Lion King and Avengers: Age of Ultron.

Blackmagic Design's video editing software DaVinci Resolve Studio was used for post-production on Yellowstone. (Paramount)

Selling shares would 'destroy the place'

Court documents seen by the ABC show Mr Barber first floated the idea of selling his 28 per cent stake in the company a decade ago when his professional relationship with Mr Petty broke down.

A statement of claim filed by Mr Barber alleges Mr Petty said he would "fight back" against shares sold to a third party, and promised to be "the most hostile f***ing agent you can possibly imagine".

"[I'm] not gonna assist in any way your selling your shares," Mr Petty allegedly told Mr Barber in a 2016 phone call.

"I'm simply not gonna do that because it's gonna f***ing destroy the place."

A few months later, Mr Barber was ousted from Blackmagic's board of directors when the company told corporate watchdog ASIC the 56-year-old had failed to perform his executive duties.

He says that since then, he has not received a salary and that dividends have gone unpaid without explanation since 2022 while the company's remaining directors and other key personnel have been compensated millions of dollars each year.

Lawyers for Mr Barber told the Federal Court on Thursday their client effectively has around $98 million in assets locked up in the company.

Peter Barber is asking the court to order Mr Petty and Mr Clarke to buy out his share, facilitate the sale, or wind up the company. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

According to the documents, venture capital firm Five V Capital had expressed interest in investing in Blackmagic after assessing the company at between $900 million and $1.5 billion.

It pulled out after being told Mr Petty would not entertain a sale.

Mr Petty, Blackmagic's CEO, and Mr Clarke have been contacted for comment through their lawyers who are due to file a defence to the claims next month.

The court heard the pair were considering making an application that could require Mr Barber to set aside a sum of money to pay their legal costs should his case fail.

Mr Barber was last year appointed CEO and managing director of Atomos, another Australian video tech outfit, which on Friday responded to media reporting about the proceedings.

"[The proceedings] have no impact on Atomos, its operations, strategy, financial position or governance, and no impact on Mr Barber's ability to perform his duties," Atomos said in an announcement to the ASX.

Mr Barber is asking the court to order Mr Petty and Mr Clarke, who each own 35.8 per cent of Blackmagic, to buy out his share in the company, facilitate the sale to a third party, or wind up the company entirely.

The matter will return to court next month.

A Daly Cherry-Evans match-clinching field goal and a treble from James Tedesco propelled the Sydney Roosters to a thrilling 23-22 win over an injury-smashed Newcastle. In one of the games of the season, the host Knights were brave throughout, while losing Origin back-rower Dylan Lucas to a dislocated and suspected broken left ankle in the first period, and star half Dylan Brown to a worrying knee injury early in the second. Loading If the title favourites Penrith have wobbled over the weeks around State of Origin, the high-flying Roosters have been building, and Friday night’s win was their fifth in a row – the competition’s best record in that period. Tedesco was brilliant for the victors in a wonderful return from the Origin series and concussion.



Newcastle, who were already without injured skipper Kalyn Ponga, have now lost their last three games and remain sixth on the ladder. That streak aside, they were in this match right until the dying stages and will not be overawed come the big games in September. The Roosters celebrate a James Tedesco try. Getty Images The game started at breakneck speed worthy of a finals match, and it took 15 minutes for Tedesco to open the scoring with a brilliant stepping try through the heart of the Newcastle defence. The Knights bounced back within 10 minutes when Francis Manuleleua, who was immense for his side, burst onto a peach of a Brown pass 30 metres out to power over for his first NRL try.



Undeterred by the injury to Lucas, Newcastle took the lead approaching the half hour mark when hulking middle forward Mat Croker pushed off Tedesco and Reece Robson to score. The Knights then dominated possession in the next 10 minutes and led 10-6 at the break. Trainers assist Dylan Lucas. Getty Images The second term began with more drama when Egan Butcher was placed on report for a shoulder to the head of Manuleleua, who was forced from the field for a head injury assessment. Tedesco had a double shortly after but when Sam Walker missed the conversion things were all locked up.



Nat Butcher joined his brother on report when an errant swinging arm caught Tyson Frizell on the nose, sending the veteran for a HIA. Newcastle responded again, Fletcher Hunt sending Dom Young over as the momentum see-sawed once more before Brown’s injury, only for Tedesco to nab his third try, backing up a break from Nat Butcher. Billy Smith put the Roosters in front in the 68th minute but the Knights would not go away and when Manuleleua again burst into the backfield before unleashing Bradman Best, the scores were level with six minutes remaining. Enter the game’s most clutch field goal kicker to seal the win as veteran Cherry-Evans kicked the 31st field goal of his career in the 77th minute. The Roosters weren’t without their injury woes either, losing Egan Butcher with a calf problem and Daniel Tupou with a shoulder complaint in the second half. AAP

World.title: Brisbane’s ritziest food festival shows that hospitality still has a major gender problem
World.content:
Perspective Eating outFood Brisbane’s ritziest food festival shows that hospitality still has a major gender problem It’s jarring in 2026 that an event should have an all-male chef line-up, but here we are. Still, it’s time we tackled the industry’s sausage fest issue. Sarah Baldwin July 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You might have heard: James Street Food and Wine Trail returns this Sunday. Now in its 13th year, this one-day festival brings Brisbane’s ritziest precinct alive with events, activations, chef demonstrations, long lunches and after-hours activities. It’s a potent reminder that there’s more to James Street than just The Calile and high-end retailers. One event stuck out on social media: the James Street Food and Wine Trail Chef Stage, featuring demonstrations and showcases from some of this city’s very best chefs. The issue? All of them were men. Chef demonstrations, long lunches and after-hours activities are all on the food and wine trail program. In 2026, it felt jarring.



I wasn’t the only one to notice. A number of women in hospitality commented publicly on the post, questioning the absence of female chefs. I reached out with a private message: “Adding a woman to this line-up for next year will be an A+ inclusion.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Not long afterwards, comments on the post were disabled and those who had raised concerns were addressed privately by James Street Initiative, which promotes the precinct. The response was much the same for all of us: the event had been pitched to James Street tenants, and the final line-up reflected who those tenants had put forward. Related Article What to eat, see and do at James Street Food and Wine Trail 2026 Initially, I was frustrated – I thought it was a conversation worth having publicly – but it’s understandable that JSI’s priority was promoting the event. As JSI director Marie-Louise Theile told me later: “We had a schedule, and we wanted to push forward with that.” That’s fair. But it got me wondering, where do we have these conversations, if not in public? We can’t keep having them behind closed doors.



Most head chef positions in James Street’s kitchens are held by men, and those are the people who were put forward for the event. But then that’s simply a reflection of the wider hospitality industry, which in 2026 continues to be dominated by men. Just this week, a major annual award announced its nominations for Chef of the Year. All were male. The ritzy strip in Fortitude Valley is closed off for the annual festival. Hospitality is ruthless, and no more so than in the kitchens of our best restaurants. The hours are long, the job often unglamorous. The kitchen brigade system was adapted from the military to apply a rigid hierarchy to restaurant operations. Built by and for men, it normalised long hours and stress. In the years following #MeToo and the investigative reporting that unearthed a misogynistic culture at Sydney restaurant groups such as Swillhouse and Merivale, it felt like the industry was finally ready to change. But somewhere over the past two years, that appetite seems to have been lost.



Hospitality relies on diversity to remain dynamic and engaging for both diners and the people who work in it. But it also relies on curators, talent searchers and media outlets to accurately represent the industry. These people influence who the public sees as successful. This affects the way our guests interact with us, controls the opportunities presented to us, and trickles down to our suppliers. As Jade Tareha, co-owner of Humble on Duke in Sunshine Beach, points out, these people affect how we operate our own businesses. Related Investigation Sex, sleaze and hospitality I’ve experienced it firsthand: radio silence from a supplier I’m trying to work with, until I appeared on an article or list of award nominations. That’s just one example, but I think there needs to be a greater understanding of the responsibility that comes with influence. Obviously, the James Street Food and Wine Trail Chef Stage wasn’t deliberately excluding women. And there is real diversity there, such as Sushi Room chef Shimpei Raikuni collaborating with fishmonger Mitsu Sakurai on a tuna carving demonstration. But the systems we have inherited are naturally producing male-dominated line-ups, unless we consciously work to disrupt them.



I reached out to JSI after the emailed response and Theile agreed to speak to me about the event. In that conversation, she conceded this year’s line-up could have been more diverse. Sarah Baldwin at her Joy restaurant in Fortitude Valley. Paul Harris “It was an oversight for us not to push harder, but at the end of the day, everyone was given an opportunity,” she said. She suggested looking beyond the faces of the Chef’s Stage, noting that some were representing businesses owned by women, such as Anyday, which put forward chef and culinary director Ben Williamson but is co-owned by Bianca Marchi. This is a systemic problem, but systemic problems aren’t solved in private. As a chef who’s a woman, I’ve been the one to fill a quota. OzHarvest, for example, asked me to join the CEO Cook-Off, and was up-front about how it would help them achieve a diverse line-up. And perhaps that’s an approach we can adopt: reminding the women you’re asking what impact they will have by saying yes.



Diversity shouldn’t be seen as taking anything away from anyone who deserves it. It’s about adding more and taking a moment of reflection to ask: “Who else deserves to be seen?” Related Article Brisbane’s cafes and bakeries aren’t what they used to be. They’re better New York restaurateur Will Guidara said one of my favourite things about our industry: “Service is black and white, but hospitality is colour.” Hospitality is colourful because of the diversity of identities it has become a safe space for, and stories become more exciting when all of these identities are included. Don’t we want the rest of the world to see how exciting, progressive and interesting a career in hospitality can be? Don’t we want every young person to be able to see a version of themselves on stage? We cannot stop talking about this, we cannot stop questioning, or the momentum will slow to a stop.

World.title: 40-storey office tower to be built next to Brisbane’s GPO
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane development 40-storey office tower to be built next to Brisbane’s GPO William Davis July 24, 2026 — 8:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A new 40-storey office tower will be built in the heart of Brisbane’s CBD with a large and unusual public “city room” on the ground floor. The building will replace the existing 10-storey Edison Exchange at 280 Elizabeth Street, next to the back section of the General Post Office and opposite St Stephen’s Cathedral. It will include more than 38,000 square metres of office space, an internal gym and a cafe on the ground floor. An artist impression of the new Cbus Property building planned at 280 Elizabeth Street in Brisbane, as seen from the steps of Saint Stephen’s Cathedral. “[This will] reinforce the character of Elizabeth Street, while enhancing connectivity, workplace amenity and the quality of Brisbane’s public realm,” a development application lodged with the council said.



Artist impressions show the first 10 storeys will be clad in white concrete, with the remaining being a more conventional glass design. The ground level will comprise a large atrium-like space called a “City Room” with pedestrian access through to Edison Lane. Early demolition work on the Edison Exchange at 280 Elizabeth Street had begun on Thursday afternoon. William Davis Just six car parking spaces are planned, but there will be room for 192 bicycles. Cbus Property bought the existing building in 2026, and is developing the tower.



It said significant effort had gone into making the building’s design blend with its heritage-listed surroundings, which includes the post office. The building was designed by Hassell, and Richards and Spence. Hutchinson has been contracted to build it. An impression of how the new building at 280 Elizabeth Street will look from the front on the heritage-listed GPO building. This masthead has contacted Cbus Property for comment on when it expected work to begin. Early demolition work on the existing building had already started on Thursday afternoon.



The Edison Exchange building was developed in 1963 by the federal government for telecommunications, and used for years by Telstra. Cbus Property was also the developer behind the tower at 205 North Quay, completed in 2024. The building will replace Telstra’s existing 10-storey Edison Exchange at 280 Elizabeth Street. According to a JLL report in 2025, vacancy rates in Brisbane’s CBD office market were the least volatile in the country during the past decade. World.title: Captain, commentator, coach: The life Tiana never could have seen for herself during her HSC
World.content:
A rugby sevens career split her HSC across two years, but with support,Tiana Penitani Gray was able to do it all.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Tiana Penitani Gray sat her HSC more than a decade ago, never could she have foreseen where she would end up 13 years later. It’s not becoming a professional athlete that would have shocked her, she says – after all, she became the youngest player to represent a senior Australian rugby team when she was selected for the rugby sevens team for the 2013 World Cup aged 17 and still at Maroubra’s South Sydney High School – but everything else that has followed has been a surprise. “I started playing rugby sevens professionally at the age of 17, so that was my first year of year 12, and that obviously required me to travel around the world a handful of times a year and be in training camps down at the Australian Institute of Sport,” Penitani Gray says of her high school experience. “I sat down with my deputy principal and my year adviser and basically came to the decision to take up pathways, which split year 12 over two years, just so I wasn’t missing too much school, and that essentially halved the workload for me over a couple of years. So, I did the first year at school, and then they did the second year by distance.” Thirteen years on from her HSC, Tiana Penitani Gray is the Sharks NRLW captain and a NSW and Australian representative player. Steven Siewert Any alternative wasn’t an option, says Penitani Gray. She always knew she wanted to give football her all.



“I was quite determined. I just remember really not accepting anything other than being a professional athlete, that was always on my radar, and I never really kind of looked outside of that,” she says. Related Article NRL 2025 From playground to playmaker: The schools that make NRL stars It’s certainly paid off. The 30-year-old is the captain of the Cronulla Sharks NRLW team, she’s been part of four NSW teams that have lifted the Women’s State of Origin shield, played in two NRLW grand finals and was part of the Jillaroos squad to play in Las Vegas last year. However, she loved school, and her favourite subjects during her HSC were PDHPE and legal studies. If football hadn’t worked out, a career in sports science or criminology and law is something she would have explored. A 17-year-old Tiana Penitani at South Sydney High School in Maroubra when she was first photographed by the Herald in 2013 ahead of the 2013 World Cup. Kate Geraghty Tiana Penitani-Gray in action for NSW last year. Getty Images



But life is full of surprises, and even with the NRLW still part-time, Penitani Gray has managed to make rugby league a full-time career – as a coach at Endeavour Sports High School and a sideline commentator for Fox Sports. “I didn’t gravitate towards journalism. I wasn’t interested in being on TV,” she says. Related Article HSC They topped the HSC decades ago. Where are they now? But it comes with the territory. Since starting her career as a teenager, she’s done hundreds of interviews for newspapers, television and radio, and that’s given her invaluable experience and exposure in the media. “I got a bit of practice in front of the camera, and I feel like I can string a sentence together, and that’s helped me along the way,” she says. “I’ve been so fortunate to have people see something in me and give me opportunity over the years, and it’s definitely like springboarded me into broadcast.” Tiana Penitani Gray interviews her brother Talanoa Penitani in her sideline commentary role for Fox. NRL Images

World.title: Brisbane’s ritziest food festival shows that hospitality still has a major gender problem
World.content:
Perspective Eating outFood Brisbane’s ritziest food festival shows that hospitality still has a major gender problem It’s jarring in 2026 that an event should have an all-male chef line-up, but here we are. Still, it’s time we tackled the industry’s sausage fest issue. Sarah Baldwin July 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You might have heard: James Street Food and Wine Trail returns this Sunday. Now in its 13th year, this one-day festival brings Brisbane’s ritziest precinct alive with events, activations, chef demonstrations, long lunches and after-hours activities. It’s a potent reminder that there’s more to James Street than just The Calile and high-end retailers. One event stuck out on social media: the James Street Food and Wine Trail Chef Stage, featuring demonstrations and showcases from some of this city’s very best chefs. The issue? All of them were men. Chef demonstrations, long lunches and after-hours activities are all on the food and wine trail program. In 2026, it felt jarring.



I wasn’t the only one to notice. A number of women in hospitality commented publicly on the post, questioning the absence of female chefs. I reached out with a private message: “Adding a woman to this line-up for next year will be an A+ inclusion.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Not long afterwards, comments on the post were disabled and those who had raised concerns were addressed privately by James Street Initiative, which promotes the precinct. The response was much the same for all of us: the event had been pitched to James Street tenants, and the final line-up reflected who those tenants had put forward. Related Article What to eat, see and do at James Street Food and Wine Trail 2026 Initially, I was frustrated – I thought it was a conversation worth having publicly – but it’s understandable that JSI’s priority was promoting the event. As JSI director Marie-Louise Theile told me later: “We had a schedule, and we wanted to push forward with that.” That’s fair. But it got me wondering, where do we have these conversations, if not in public? We can’t keep having them behind closed doors.



Most head chef positions in James Street’s kitchens are held by men, and those are the people who were put forward for the event. But then that’s simply a reflection of the wider hospitality industry, which in 2026 continues to be dominated by men. Just this week, a major annual award announced its nominations for Chef of the Year. All were male. The ritzy strip in Fortitude Valley is closed off for the annual festival. Hospitality is ruthless, and no more so than in the kitchens of our best restaurants. The hours are long, the job often unglamorous. The kitchen brigade system was adapted from the military to apply a rigid hierarchy to restaurant operations. Built by and for men, it normalised long hours and stress. In the years following #MeToo and the investigative reporting that unearthed a misogynistic culture at Sydney restaurant groups such as Swillhouse and Merivale, it felt like the industry was finally ready to change. But somewhere over the past two years, that appetite seems to have been lost.



Hospitality relies on diversity to remain dynamic and engaging for both diners and the people who work in it. But it also relies on curators, talent searchers and media outlets to accurately represent the industry. These people influence who the public sees as successful. This affects the way our guests interact with us, controls the opportunities presented to us, and trickles down to our suppliers. As Jade Tareha, co-owner of Humble on Duke in Sunshine Beach, points out, these people affect how we operate our own businesses. Related Investigation Sex, sleaze and hospitality I’ve experienced it firsthand: radio silence from a supplier I’m trying to work with, until I appeared on an article or list of award nominations. That’s just one example, but I think there needs to be a greater understanding of the responsibility that comes with influence. Obviously, the James Street Food and Wine Trail Chef Stage wasn’t deliberately excluding women. And there is real diversity there, such as Sushi Room chef Shimpei Raikuni collaborating with fishmonger Mitsu Sakurai on a tuna carving demonstration. But the systems we have inherited are naturally producing male-dominated line-ups, unless we consciously work to disrupt them.



I reached out to JSI after the emailed response and Theile agreed to speak to me about the event. In that conversation, she conceded this year’s line-up could have been more diverse. Sarah Baldwin at her Joy restaurant in Fortitude Valley. Paul Harris “It was an oversight for us not to push harder, but at the end of the day, everyone was given an opportunity,” she said. She suggested looking beyond the faces of the Chef’s Stage, noting that some were representing businesses owned by women, such as Anyday, which put forward chef and culinary director Ben Williamson but is co-owned by Bianca Marchi. This is a systemic problem, but systemic problems aren’t solved in private. As a chef who’s a woman, I’ve been the one to fill a quota. OzHarvest, for example, asked me to join the CEO Cook-Off, and was up-front about how it would help them achieve a diverse line-up. And perhaps that’s an approach we can adopt: reminding the women you’re asking what impact they will have by saying yes.



Diversity shouldn’t be seen as taking anything away from anyone who deserves it. It’s about adding more and taking a moment of reflection to ask: “Who else deserves to be seen?” Related Article Brisbane’s cafes and bakeries aren’t what they used to be. They’re better New York restaurateur Will Guidara said one of my favourite things about our industry: “Service is black and white, but hospitality is colour.” Hospitality is colourful because of the diversity of identities it has become a safe space for, and stories become more exciting when all of these identities are included. Don’t we want the rest of the world to see how exciting, progressive and interesting a career in hospitality can be? Don’t we want every young person to be able to see a version of themselves on stage? We cannot stop talking about this, we cannot stop questioning, or the momentum will slow to a stop.

World.title: 40-storey office tower to be built next to Brisbane’s GPO
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane development 40-storey office tower to be built next to Brisbane’s GPO William Davis July 24, 2026 — 8:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A new 40-storey office tower will be built in the heart of Brisbane’s CBD with a large and unusual public “city room” on the ground floor. The building will replace the existing 10-storey Edison Exchange at 280 Elizabeth Street, next to the back section of the General Post Office and opposite St Stephen’s Cathedral. It will include more than 38,000 square metres of office space, an internal gym and a cafe on the ground floor. An artist impression of the new Cbus Property building planned at 280 Elizabeth Street in Brisbane, as seen from the steps of Saint Stephen’s Cathedral. “[This will] reinforce the character of Elizabeth Street, while enhancing connectivity, workplace amenity and the quality of Brisbane’s public realm,” a development application lodged with the council said.



Artist impressions show the first 10 storeys will be clad in white concrete, with the remaining being a more conventional glass design. The ground level will comprise a large atrium-like space called a “City Room” with pedestrian access through to Edison Lane. Early demolition work on the Edison Exchange at 280 Elizabeth Street had begun on Thursday afternoon. William Davis Just six car parking spaces are planned, but there will be room for 192 bicycles. Cbus Property bought the existing building in 2026, and is developing the tower.



It said significant effort had gone into making the building’s design blend with its heritage-listed surroundings, which includes the post office. The building was designed by Hassell, and Richards and Spence. Hutchinson has been contracted to build it. An impression of how the new building at 280 Elizabeth Street will look from the front on the heritage-listed GPO building. This masthead has contacted Cbus Property for comment on when it expected work to begin. Early demolition work on the existing building had already started on Thursday afternoon.



The Edison Exchange building was developed in 1963 by the federal government for telecommunications, and used for years by Telstra. Cbus Property was also the developer behind the tower at 205 North Quay, completed in 2024. The building will replace Telstra’s existing 10-storey Edison Exchange at 280 Elizabeth Street. According to a JLL report in 2025, vacancy rates in Brisbane’s CBD office market were the least volatile in the country during the past decade. World.title: Captain, commentator, coach: The life Tiana never could have seen for herself during her HSC
World.content:
A rugby sevens career split her HSC across two years, but with support,Tiana Penitani Gray was able to do it all.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Tiana Penitani Gray sat her HSC more than a decade ago, never could she have foreseen where she would end up 13 years later. It’s not becoming a professional athlete that would have shocked her, she says – after all, she became the youngest player to represent a senior Australian rugby team when she was selected for the rugby sevens team for the 2013 World Cup aged 17 and still at Maroubra’s South Sydney High School – but everything else that has followed has been a surprise. “I started playing rugby sevens professionally at the age of 17, so that was my first year of year 12, and that obviously required me to travel around the world a handful of times a year and be in training camps down at the Australian Institute of Sport,” Penitani Gray says of her high school experience. “I sat down with my deputy principal and my year adviser and basically came to the decision to take up pathways, which split year 12 over two years, just so I wasn’t missing too much school, and that essentially halved the workload for me over a couple of years. So, I did the first year at school, and then they did the second year by distance.” Thirteen years on from her HSC, Tiana Penitani Gray is the Sharks NRLW captain and a NSW and Australian representative player. Steven Siewert Any alternative wasn’t an option, says Penitani Gray. She always knew she wanted to give football her all.



“I was quite determined. I just remember really not accepting anything other than being a professional athlete, that was always on my radar, and I never really kind of looked outside of that,” she says. Related Article NRL 2025 From playground to playmaker: The schools that make NRL stars It’s certainly paid off. The 30-year-old is the captain of the Cronulla Sharks NRLW team, she’s been part of four NSW teams that have lifted the Women’s State of Origin shield, played in two NRLW grand finals and was part of the Jillaroos squad to play in Las Vegas last year. However, she loved school, and her favourite subjects during her HSC were PDHPE and legal studies. If football hadn’t worked out, a career in sports science or criminology and law is something she would have explored. A 17-year-old Tiana Penitani at South Sydney High School in Maroubra when she was first photographed by the Herald in 2013 ahead of the 2013 World Cup. Kate Geraghty Tiana Penitani-Gray in action for NSW last year. Getty Images



But life is full of surprises, and even with the NRLW still part-time, Penitani Gray has managed to make rugby league a full-time career – as a coach at Endeavour Sports High School and a sideline commentator for Fox Sports. “I didn’t gravitate towards journalism. I wasn’t interested in being on TV,” she says. Related Article HSC They topped the HSC decades ago. Where are they now? But it comes with the territory. Since starting her career as a teenager, she’s done hundreds of interviews for newspapers, television and radio, and that’s given her invaluable experience and exposure in the media. “I got a bit of practice in front of the camera, and I feel like I can string a sentence together, and that’s helped me along the way,” she says. “I’ve been so fortunate to have people see something in me and give me opportunity over the years, and it’s definitely like springboarded me into broadcast.” Tiana Penitani Gray interviews her brother Talanoa Penitani in her sideline commentary role for Fox. NRL Images

World.title: Respected public servant Dame Helene Quilter dies
World.content:
Dame Helene Quilter, who was honoured for her work in the public service over 45 years, has died.

The Public Service Commissioner, Sir Brian Roche, said Dame Helene died overnight.

Dame Helene served as Secretary of Defence, Deputy Commissioner of the State Services Commission and, most recently, as Deputy Public Service Commissioner at the Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho.

She retired as deputy Public Service commissioner in February 2023.

She was recognised as a Dame Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2023 for services to the public service and the arts.

Her citation noted her advocacy for diversity and inclusion in public sector appointments, her leadership in strengthening public service capability, and her commitment to serving New Zealand through some of its most important institutions.

Sir Brian said Dame Helene was one of New Zealand's most respected and influential public servants.

"Over a career spanning 45 years, she dedicated herself to strengthening the institutions that serve New Zealanders and to upholding the values of integrity, professionalism and public service," Sir Brian said.

He said she played a central role in the appointment and development of Public Service chief executives, championed greater diversity in leadership, supported the public service through the Covid-19 response, and brought extraordinary wisdom and judgement to some of the most important issues facing government.

"She combined intellectual rigour with humanity, integrity with courage, and a deep understanding of what it means to serve the public good," Sir Brian said.

"Throughout her career, she helped shape the modern public service and was a trusted adviser, mentor and leader to countless public servants. She believed strongly in developing people, building diverse leadership, and leaving our institutions stronger than she found them.

"Those who worked with Helene knew her as someone of immense capability, wisdom and generosity. She challenged us to be better, supported others to succeed, and never lost sight of the purpose of public service - improving the lives of New Zealanders."

World.title: Battle lines drawn over proposed LNG facility
World.content:
Proposed LNG import terminal unlikely to cause disruption Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Port Taranaki has reassured nearby residents that initial assessments of a proposed LNG import terminal indicate it is unlikely "risk management zones" will impact on the community or popular recreational areas like Ngāmotu Beach and Breakwater Bay.

In a letter sent to hundreds of local properties, port chief executive Simon Craddock confirmed both shortlisted proposals involved a ship being moored alongside the Main Breakwater.

Opponents of the project argue Port Taranaki is the wrong place for a liquid natural gas (LNG) import facility.

Former oil and gas industry project manager Rob Green's home on Port View Crescent overlooks Port Taranaki.

"I can look straight down on the port, all the ships at anchor here, and I can see all the logs and so on. So, I'm looking straight down on the port at the Main Breakwater and all those berthing possibilities for ships," he said.

"It's very close, all the noises from the port operations I can hear. I'm looking straight at it."

Green was not convinced the port, about 1km from his apartment, was the right place for an LNG import facility.

"I keep hearing that safety is the top priority, but quite frankly I won't believe it until I can see the risk assessment analysis for myself.

"Here we are bulldozing on to a contract the government seems totally committed to regardless to the concerns of the neighbourhood."

Port Taranaki's letter and an article on the Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment's LNG webpage explain that the vessel to be moored at the Main Breakwater would store LNG and be capable of regasifying it and distributing it into existing transmission pipelines.

Other vessels from suppliers overseas would deliver LNG - which was frozen - to the moored vessel.

The Main Breakwater was about 200m away from popular recreational areas at Ngāmotu Beach, Breakwater Bay and the Lee Breakwater, where recreational fishers both surfcasted and launched boats.

Port Taranaki referred questions about the safety assessment to MBIE, which was managing the procurement process.

In a statement, MBIE said safety was the bottom-line and the plant would not get built if it could not meet safety standards.

"An initial safety evaluation has been undertaken as part of both of the providers' feasibility work, and detailed health and safety assessments will be carried out through the Safety Case process under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 once the preferred provider is contracted," it said in a statement.

"This includes a quantitative risk assessment which is location-specific and will cover the facility and all phases of its operation, as well as generating risk contour lines (or 'buffer zones') to keep the community safe."

MBIE said it was inappropriate to make the initial safety assessment public as it was commercially sensitive.

In statement, WorkSafe said it had no role in the choice of location, but it would work with the preferred provider on the more detailed Safety Case.

"Before the facility can be built and operated, the preferred provider must submit both a design notice and a Safety Case to WorkSafe.

WorkSafe would assess these to determine whether the facility could comply with major hazard facility requirements and that risks had been identified and appropriately managed.

"WorkSafe will either accept or decline the Safety Case. If it is declined, the facility will not go ahead."

The regulator said it didn't publish safety cases in full.

However, if the LNG project was designated a major hazard facility, prescribed information must be published on the WorkSafe website.

This would include an explanation of activities undertaken at the facility, hazard classifications of substances that could cause or contribute to a major incident, and the characteristics of those substances that made them dangerous.

General information about how the public would be warned in the event of a major incident would also be published, and information on how the public should act and what precautionary steps they should take if a major incident occurred.

Taranaki Energy Watch's Sarah Roberts RNZ / Robin Martin

Taranaki Energy Watch spokesperson Sarah Roberts said that would be a case of too little too late.

"What we're saying is this location is not the right place for an LNG import terminal. We know that there's a known potential worst case fatality distance to approximately 2km from these types of facilities. There are thousands of people and a number of schools in this area."

Roberts said right from the outset former Minister of Energy Simon Watts talked about working alongside the Port Kembla Energy Terminal in New South Wales.

"Over there, they have built a new terminal and they have the 2km separation distance between the terminal itself and the nearest residence."

Roberts worried people in the area surrounding Port Taranaki would be hurt if something went wrong.

"We feel like they're purposely avoiding the RMA and Fast Track legislation to get something through that should have been looked at primarily at the beginning. Looking at the location, seeing if there's any alternatives, and making it publicly available, making the safety assessments publicly available."

MBIE said the exact size and details of the safety buffer zones around the LNG import facility at Port Taranaki would be determined independently to the procurement process, once it had been completed.

"It is inappropriate to estimate the exact size of the buffer zones ahead of this detailed Safety Case process. Until the Safety Case is accepted, the import facility will not be built."

People walking along Ngāmotu Beach and at Breakwater Bay had mixed views on the LNG proposal.

Kevin said he accepted it was necessary: "I suppose we have to have the gas to run the country. There's no great place to put it. Everyone wants it somewhere else, but Taranaki has had all the gas and gas production over the years."

His mate, Denis, wasn't so keen: "I'm not really in favour of the whole thing. It's all imported fossil fuels and a bit close to a residential area."

Don had an alternative idea and reckoned the infrastructure was mostly already in place: "Pipe it in, which would eliminate any need for changes around the harbour area."

Robyn was willing to put her trust in the process: "They've got very stringent safety things, that's the big thing with oil and gas."

Grant worried about access to recreational areas: "Not very happy at all.

"There's a lot of people who use this area here. So, is there going to be an exclusion zone for people walking around here? And what about the cafes here, are they going to remove those?"

Graham said he could see both sides of the dilemma: "It's probably no more dangerous than anything else, but it is an unnecessary addition to danger, and the actual plant itself is unnecessary."

Bernard's home was within 2km of the proposed site: "I think it is a bit risky. It is a highly volatile thing and that. I would prefer them going back to Marsden Point and doing it there."

World.title: No bridge too far for man behind new Aoraki Mt Cook bridge
World.content:
No bridge too far for man behind new Hooker Valley bridge Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

There is virtually no bridge too far for the man behind the new Hooker Valley suspension bridge at Aoraki Mount Cook.

The marvel of design and modern engineering is due to open next week and replaces the old one that closed due to erosion caused by storms in April last year.

It spans 189 metres across the Hooker River, making it the longest suspension bridge in the country.

The new 189m long Hooker Valley suspension bridge at Aoraki Mount Cook. Supplied

Construction started in August last year, and since then workers have faced the challenge of gales and snowfall during construction.

The man behind the design, bridge architect and engineer, Dan Crocker told Checkpoint that he feels amazed seeing the bridge in its finished form.

"It's been a lot of work getting to this point, but you know, one of the things is when you arrive on site and everything fits and you've got that beautiful scenery, it just looks right."

Bridge engineer Dan Crocker (right) Supplied

As the longest footbridge in Aotearoa, Crocker said it had been no easy feat getting to this point, with the remote site adding an extra layer of challenges.

"Conventionally with a bridge, you might roll up with a crane and concrete trucks. You can't do that in this environment, everything comes in via helicopter."

"You have to work backwards from what you can get to site and working in these challenging environments. It's a very different type of bridge construction in these remote areas"

The bridge will open to the public on 28 July. Supplied / Department of Conservation

Wild weather at the remote site had also presented issues.

"The contractor brings excavators and containers to site, the winds picked up and brought all the gravel with it and it ended up stripping the paint off the excavators and the containers."

"You can only imagine how much of a severe environment that is to work in... it's not much fun, but on the other days when it's beautiful sunshine and you can see the mountains it makes it worth it."

Unlike a traditional suspension bridge, the new structure lacks what gave the 'swing bridge' its name, so those taking on the near 200m journey don't have to worry about losing their footing.

"Some people are comfortable with moving structures and heights, but a lot of people aren't. So what we try and do is make it as stable as possible while still maintaining that lightweight kind of appearance."

"There is a little bit of movement, but it's definitely suppressed compared to what you would normally have."

While the Hooker Valley bridge may be the longest, it is certainly not the first pedestrian bridge Crocker has designed.

"We wake up every morning, jump out of bed ready to design bridges, that's all we do here."

"Generally we focus on cycle bridges, pedestrian bridges, the kind of bridges people want to come and see and want to visit."

The Hooker Valley bridge is the country's longest suspension bridge. Supplied

Crocker said for him, bridges serve as more than a way to get from A to B.

"They connect communities, they connect different areas that people want to visit, but I like to think of them as also placemakers and wayfinders."

"We've got some little bridges here in Cambridge that I've designed - they're wayfinders in Cambridge itself with a little blue pedestrian bridge.. everybody uses it... 'go past the blue bridge and turn left.'"

Crocker said he also loves the way he's seen his bridges instil a sense of community pride, something he's seen in Westport with the Toki Poutangata bridge, inspired by the area's pounamu.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Who will win New Zealand's first medal at Glasgow?
World.content:
Glasgow Commonwealth Games

23 July-3 August (NZT)

Live blog updates on RNZ

Swimmers Lewis Clareburt and Erika Fairweather will take New Zealand's first shot at medals at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games overnight.

Clareburt, who captured three gold medals at Birmingham four years ago, will contest 200m individual medley heats tonight, with the final scheduled for Friday morning (NZT).

He won bronze in this event in 2022 and it will be an ideal tune-up for his favoured events later in the programme.
