World.title: Installation features 'forbidden' medicines denied to New Zealanders
World.content:
Locked up medicines on display to highlight unfunded treatments Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Patients waiting for life-changing medicines to be funded say people should not have to fundraise, go into debt, or travel overseas for treatments and therapies that could be administered here.

More than a dozen patient organisations are hosting the Forbidden Pharmacy, online, and this weekend at Auckland's Shed 10.

Supplied/ Forbidden Pharmacy

It's an installation that shows shelves of white medicine packets and bottles locked behind doors - representing what people may need but can't access, because they are not funded by Pharmac.

When Jemma Gerring was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in late 2023 she had no symptoms till the day she went to the doctor thinking she might have appendicitis.

"It was surreal. It was just like being hit by a freight train. It took a long time to process what that meant," she said.

"You start off really optimistic about, okay, that's great, we'll have treatment and be all better. Very quickly you start looking at the statistics and realise it's not going to be that easy."

Jemma Gerring RNZ/ Amy Williams

She has health insurance but that has a cap for the unfunded drug that is buying her more time with her family.

It has so far cost her hundreds of thousands of dollars for the drug and life-prolonging surgeries in Australia; something she said is unfair to anyone without such means.

"I think the thing for me is I feel guilty that I can afford to pay for this. It's inconvenient and it costs money, but I can pay for it and I really do credit this drug with making a difference in my life," she said.

"I'm still working full-time, I'm still being a mum full-time."

Supplied/ Forbidden Pharmacy

Gerring drives six hours from New Plymouth to Palmerston North each fortnight to have the drug she pays for, Bevacizumab, administered.

It is funded in other countries, including Australia and the UK.

"It's that sort of continual guilt that you feel too, of 'Am I taking money away from my children's future, from my husband's ability to live when I'm not here?'," she said.

"But I'm literally in the situation of buying time, and I like to think it's worth it.

"It's certainly worth it for me."

Locked up medicines on display to highlight unfunded treatments Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Tim Edmonds RNZ/ Amy Williams

The Forbidden Pharmacy has the medication on a shelf, and spokesperson for the installation, Tim Edmonds, said for patients waiting for medicine to be funded, the cost of living is a burden.

"This is having to make decisions no New Zealander should ever have to make, remortgaging homes, setting up Givealittle pages, moving to another country," he said.

"There is a financial cost, an emotional cost, but actually for many people those aren't options and the cost is going without, worsening health and less time with family and loved ones."

Edmonds is chief executive of Blood Cancer NZ and said a recent international report found patients in New Zealand have the poorest publicly-funded access to modern medicines out of comparable OECD countries and that the majority, 95 percent, of modern medicines don't make it to the shelves here.

"We want the future government to solve this for New Zealand," Edmonds said.

"We want the medicines that Pharmac have recommended to the government to be funded over three years and clear the backlog, and we want to plan for sustained investment so that we stop getting further behind the countries that we like to compare ourselves to."

Bart Schroder RNZ/ Amy Williams

For Bart Schroder, having access to an unfunded cancer medication means he is still alive after being diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer five years ago.

His health insurance has covered the cost since diagnosis, otherwise he would have had a long wait.

"In my case, I'm still here four years later, which is pretty good, and I'm still feeling really good," he said.

"That wouldn't have been the case, because my cancer is very aggressive... it would have taken me out so the standard treatment wouldn't have been very effective."

Schroder would like to see the medicine funded so everyone with his diagnosis can access it early on.

An engineer, he is still working for the company he founded and recently sold, it sells specialised equipment around the world.

"Five good years of working, contributing, selling stuff all over the place is way better than six months in a hospital. Hospital is much more expensive than just looking after me for five good years," he said.

"So why don't they fund it? It makes a lot of sense."

Looking ahead, Gerring wants more life-changing medicines funded so everyone can have the same chance as she has to enjoy more of their life.

"I was sort of told average life expectancy from diagnosis is two and a half years. I'm beyond that now, so... I definitely feel like I'm living on borrowed time, but every extra month I get with my children at this very formative age for them is worth it."

Politicians from National, Labour, ACT and New Zealand First visited the Forbidden Pharmacy today.

World.title: Police execute search warrants in relation to Wellington homicide investigation
World.content:
Police investigating a homicide in the Wellington region want information about sightings of two cars.

Nathaniel Sturmey, 29, was found dead at a property on Malone Road in Lower Hutt on 9 April.

Police say they have executed a number of search warrants across the Wellington region as enquiries into his death continue.

Detective Inspector Jamie Woods said the investigation team was making significant progress.

Police want to hear from anyone who saw a grey 2007 Audi A4 in and around the Waterloo area on the night of Wednesday 8 April and the early hours of Thursday 9 April. Supplied / NZ Police

Police were focusing on a number of people, including some who were known to Nathaniel Sturmey, he said.

"Thanks to those who have spoken with us - anyone else who has information and has not yet talked with us please get in touch."

Police are seeking sightings of a black 2010 Nissan Qashqai in and around the Waterloo area of Lower Hutt on the night of Wednesday 8 April and the early hours of Thursday 9 April, as well as in the Naenae area on Sunday 12 April.

Police also want to hear from anyone who saw a grey 2007 Audi A4 in and around the Waterloo area on the night of Wednesday 8 April and the early hours of Thursday 9 April.

Anyone with information that may assist the investigation is can call 105, quoting reference number 260409/9927 or provide information anonymously through Crime Stoppers on 0800 555 111.

World.title: Police rescue team phones in local farmer, who saves elderly man and dog
World.content:
Rescuers had grave concerns for an elderly fisherman stranded at night in the cold near a South Island river, until they called in a farmer with local knowledge who was able to locate the man in the dark.

The lost 87-year-old man rang emergency services for help about 8:15pm on Thursday, after becoming disoriented following a fishing trip near Lake Tekapo, at the Cass River mouth, police said.

Search and Rescue teams were swung into action, and police "remained on the phone with the 87-year-old, encouraging him to keep himself moving to stay warm, and provided reassurance while efforts were under way to locate him," they said.

But, they were worried the response would not reach the lost man and his dog in time: "While [he] was dressed warmly, Police were concerned he was not equipped to spend the night outdoors in the cold conditions".

So, looking for a faster way to get help to him, police made a call to a nearby farm manager, Grant Murray, who knows the area well.

Murray agreed to help. And "after 35 minutes on the phone, the lost man was successfully located by Mr Murray".

The elderly man and his dog were taken home to warm up and rest.

The rescue showed the value of local knowledge, and strong community relationships, police said.

World.title: Universities feel out of favour over 'shambolic' teacher training funding
World.content:
* An earlier version of this story stated students received a bursary of $20,660, but the correct 2026 bursary was $19,930.

Universities are feeling hard-done-by following the release of figures that show government funding for in-school teacher training heavily favoured a newcomer to teacher education that was headed at the time by the chair of the Teaching Council.

The Teachers' Institute was allowed to triple its intake of school-based teacher trainees this year while universities were denied similar growth in what they say was a shambolic and odd process.

Students on one-year School Onsite Training Programme (SOTP) courses were paid $19,930 and were placed in their host schools for three days a week, excluding classroom practicum, while completing a teaching diploma or masters degree.

Figures published by the Education Ministry (MOE) show the government gave more than half the 533 places for this year to non-university providers and most of those to the Teachers' Institute, a charity set up by Auckland schools and led at the time by the then-chair of the Teaching Council David Ferguson.

Information provided by the ministry show some of the organisations did not have Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) funding for those students prompting a late appeal to the commission to approve the money.

Universities say the process for allocating student places for 2026 was overly complex and delayed, which resulted in many failing to fill all of the student places they were allocated.

Overall, 286 of the 533 SOTP places allocated for 2026 went to non-universities and 152 of those to the Teachers' Institute.

The institute was much more successful than most other organisations at filling the student places it was allocated.

The then-chair of the Teaching Council, David Ferguson. RNZ/ Luka Forman

RNZ requested the figures under the Official Information Act (OIA) on 25 February, but was denied in a letter dated 25 May on the basis they would soon be published - which happened this week.

The OIA response said the ministry assessed applications for funding and allocated places for 2026 based on its Teacher Demand and Supply report which showed where teachers were most needed.

Text messages released as part of the OIA response showed Ferguson asked the ministry for tips ahead of a meeting with Tertiary Education Commission chief executive Tim Fowler on 20 November 2025.

The meeting apparently concerned a late request for an increase in the number of tertiary students the commission would subsidise in 2026.

A ministry staff member told Ferguson: "With tim it's really unusual to grow their tec allocation so much, so I think focus on the fact that the business model is aligned with what govt and moe and tec all think is the future.

"He needs you to make a case so he can make a case to his board. He's doing us a big favour and will blame the ministry for not telling them about the sotp allocations. Feel free to let him."

The ministry said the texts referred to a situation where the ministry allocated school-based teacher training places to organisations that did not have Tertiary Education Commission funding for their students.

"The TEC subsequently approved funding for the additional places across the providers who had not received that funding," it said.

The sector had previously alleged favouritism of the Teaching Institute.

The Council of Deans of Education and teacher union the Educational Institute asked earlier this year if the Education Minister Erica Stanford had helped the institute get funding, suggestions the minister and institute denied.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Nick Monro

The ministry told RNZ a potential conflict of interest was identified.

"David Ferguson's appointment to the Teaching Council was included on the SOTP project risk register in August 2025. The conflict was deemed to be a perceived conflict only, as Mr Ferguson's roles on these boards held no bearing or influence on the way that allocation of places to providers were determined. Procurement was not involved in this process," it said.

Asked why the institute's allocation was tripled, but other providers' was not, the ministry did not provide a direct answer.

"As more ITE providers participate in the SOTP programme, the distribution of places may result in some providers receiving fewer places and others receiving more depending on their capacity, host school availability and levels of school and student interest," it said.

A shambolic process

Auckland University's head of School of Education and Social Practice Aaron Wilson said the university started offering an in-school programme for trainee secondary teachers in 2023 - before the Education Ministry began backing the scheme and expanding it.

He said the university developed good relationships with schools and filled all or nearly all of the places it was allocated each year.

But late in 2025 it was told that some of the schools it worked with had been allocated to the Teachers' Institute for 2026, he said.

Wilson said it had never worked before with many of the schools it was partnered with for 2026 contributing to it filling only 40 of its 69 allocated places.

Auckland University's head of School of Education and Social Practice Aaron Wilson. Supplied / University of Auckland

"Last year the ministry initially allocated schools to different providers and we weren't allocated schools that we had long-standing partnerships with and who had actually been with us right from the beginning," he said.

"There was a real change in the process that the Ministry of Education used... a lot of our partner schools were very unhappy and basically it ended up being a scramble at the end of the year trying to establish new relationships that were sort of foisted on us by the ministry."

Wilson said some of the schools the university had worked with in the past were allocated to other providers.

"We did request a review of that decision and there was a bit of a release of some extra places later in the year but it had already caused difficulty for us and the partner schools we had."

Wilson said he did not believe the university was treated fairly.

"I don't think we were treated respectfully, or our partner schools," he said.

"We felt messed around and the schools that we worked with felt messed around by that process."

"It would certainly feel in that process that the Teachers' Institute were in favour and we were out of favour."

The ministry did not confirm whether schools that were formerly assigned to the University of Auckland were assigned to the institute.

"Joint applications from both the ITE providers and schools were required for the 2026 allocations. Schools determined which ITE provider or providers they wanted to work with. Some schools chose to apply with more than one ITE provider," it said.

University of Waikato Pro Vice-Chancellor Education Claire McLachlan told RNZ the process for allocating 2026 places was shambolic and odd.

She said schools had to go through a complicated application process including stating support for government's favoured approach to teaching.

University of Waikato Pro Vice-Chancellor Education, Claire McLachlan. Supplied / University of Waikato

"Last year was shambolic," she said.

"What they did last year was very odd. They went through a process where schools had to explain a whole bunch of complicated things about how they were delivering the science of learning."

McLachlan said Auckland schools that were previously involved with the scheme were furious that some were dropped from it.

"It did feel unusual," she said.

She said she had been told the Teachers' Institute programme was more practically-focused than Waikato's and involved less assessment.

She said some people criticised universities' teacher-training as overly theoretical but that was not true.

"If you only go with practice you wind up with some very, very poor teachers over time because they've got a recipe, they've got a script and that's not going to help them when they're dealing with a diverse group of students," she said.

"I don't accept the criticism that we're overly-theoretical but I would accept the criticism that we probably over-assess."

The Teachers' Insitute said in a statement it received more applications from students this year because it added primary and "foundation programmes" to the courses it offered and increased the number of partner schools it worked with.

It said it had also "developed a strong reputation for training quality teachers in the real-world environment of schools".

Asked why its funded places increased much more than other organisations, it said: "Our funded places increased because we had an increase in the number of confirmed applicants to our teacher training programmes."

Meanwhile, David Ferguson said he had no comment.

A cohort of new teacher trainees are welcomed to The Teachers’ Institute in January 2026. Supplied / The Teachers' Institute

How the SOTP places were allocated

Overall, the 10 organsiations funded to provide SOTP this year filled only 413 or 77 percent of the places they were allocated.

The Teachers' Institute had 48 students in 2025, requested funding for 181 students in 2026, received 152 and filled 143 places.

The University of Waikato filled 52 places in 2025, requested funding for 162 in 2026, received 76 places but only filled 49. It expected to add a further 20 through a mid-year intake.

The University of Auckland also had 52 students in 2025, requested funding for 178 in 2026, received 69 places and managed to fill 40 of them.

Te Rito Maioha Early Childhood New Zealand had 42 students in 2025, asked for 171 for this year, received 90 places and filled 62.

The Open Polytechnic was the only other non-university provider approved for funding this year. It sought 121 places, was granted 44 and succeeded in filling 25.

Massey University sought 109 places, received 40 but filled 54 places after a boost to its initial allocation.

World.title: Have the AFL's rule changes worked? Not exactly
World.content:
There is nothing more constant than change.

People have argued about the future of football for as long as the game has existed.

Every year players, fans and football staffers await the new direction or interpretations handed down from high.

Some changes are winners and stand the test of time — such as the 50 metre arc and the centre square.

Others are destined for the dustbin of history, such as the flick pass and around the ground bounces.

Regardless, change is never far from sporting administrators of different codes and sports. The AFL is not immune from this want to improve the sport.

Rule changes among what's new in the AFL for 2026 The new AFL season is only days away, and there are plenty of new things to get your head around. Get up to speed before Thursday night's opener.

Ahead of the 2026 season seven rule changes and interpretation shifts were heralded as being common sense solutions to perceived long-standing problems surrounding the sport.

Changes to the centre bounce, kick-ins, shrugs, the "stand" rule and last disposal out of bounds were implemented. Some elements of the footy fan base were excited by the changes, others horrified.

"We have consulted clubs and other industry stakeholders over the past six months and taken on board their feedback and ideas, and we believe these changes will make a positive impact on the game," AFL executive general manager Football Performance Greg Swann said before the commencement of the season.

The aims of each change were varied but aligned to increase scoring, reduce game time and improve the look and feel of the game.

So far scoring has increased about 3.5 points per game compared to last year.

Scoreboard operators haven't been this busy since the 2017 season, with early season scoring rates threatening to push the clock back even further.

But that number alone may not tell the whole story.

With the season winding towards finals, research undertaken by the ABC and Andrew Whelan of Wheelo Ratings looks at whether the changes have had their intended impact.

Centring the truth

Rule changes around centre ball-ups have increased the numbers of ruckmen leaping for the ball. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

To the casual fan there were few more iconic parts of the Australian game than the centre bounce. The biggest optical change to the game in 2026 was the removal of the centre bounce and changes to how rucks engaged at the restart.

The bounce had been the start of each game since its formal introduction in 1887.

For many the bounce was integral to the look and feel of the sport — a unique element that set the native code away from the other global codes of football.

AFL rule change injury fears Geelong's Shannon Neale might have escaped a serious injury, but coaches and players are beginning to voice concerns the AFL's rule changes could lead to more rucks getting hurt.

But it had become untenable in the face of umpire injuries and skill barriers, seen to reduce the ranks of vital recruits.

"Currently, umpire pathways are being narrowed by the requirement of the bounce. By removing the skill aspect of bouncing the ball, umpires can focus their energy on adjudicating the game and consistency of decision-making," Swann stated.

At the same time that they removed the bounce, the league also instituted a change to encourage more rucks to leap at centre ball-ups.

According to the AFL, just 21 per cent of centre bounce ruck contests had at least one ruck leaping last year. That's down from about two-thirds just two years prior.

After the preseason Swann was keen to sell the success of both changes.

"The unintended consequences from a good perspective is scores out of the centre bounces have gone up. It's a very small sample size, but the things that we wanted — the game length has gone back, the scoring has gone up, scoring from centre bounces has gone up, so we're hopeful that goes into the season proper as well."

At face value the rule changes — in combination — have delivered in spades. Scoring from centre bounces are at their highest level for at least 20 years.

Digging a little deeper presents more questions as to its impact.

While scoring is up from centre bounces, the major reason why they are up is a little more unconventional.

Instead of fast flowing play from the restart the biggest contributor to the jump are scores from free kicks.

Free kicks at the restart have surged in 2026, perhaps sparked by confusion around the new rules.

More points are being put on the scoreboard from these free kicks than in recent years.

Instead of the dynamic future promised from the new ruck set up, the reality is more of the same buttressed by a surge in indiscretions.

With more centre ball-ups overall, teams are scoring 0.96 points per live ball centre clearance, up just 0.02 points per clearance on last year.

There's also been a subtle tactical evolution as the season has progressed.

As teams have become accustomed to the new rules, scoring from centre bounce has also dropped.

The predictable new ball-up has become easier to defend as winter has gone deeper and teams have become better equipped at limiting damage from the middle.

In the last five weeks teams have averaged just 10.6 points per game from the middle — a big drop on the fast start to the year and the past three full seasons.

While centre bounce scoring is up about 12 per cent on last season, it still only makes up around 14.5 per cent of all scoring. That's only 1 per cent more than the contribution last year.

Teams are better at getting the ball inside 50 from centre bounces this year than years past however, contributing to the territory game so important to many teams.

While rule changes often take a season or two to fully bed down, it appears the early optimism for increased centre restart scoring may be diminishing.

The new centre bounce revolution may be more a minor change in the grand scheme of football things.

Where do I stand?

Far more contentious has been the introduction of the "stand" rule six years ago.

For a sizeable cohort of fans across the league it is the single most hated rule in the AFL rule book.

Some of the rule changes have allowed teams to move the ball easier with limits on defenders' encroachment. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Designed to anchor the mark to a single spot, and prevent the creep of defenders, it aimed to open up aggressive ball use into the middle of the ground.

This year the rule has been slightly tightened to prevent a nearby player retreating "outside 5", instead requiring them to remain in place or to head to the actual spot of the mark or free kick.

Since 2021, many have attributed improved transition success from defence to the new rule. The accepted wisdom is that there has been at least a small improvement in the ability to move the ball due to 'stand'.

This trend has continued through 2026 so far, with a bump in both categories so far. But much like the centre bounce successes, there's more than meets the eye initially.

The increase in transition from defence to attack is largely down to stoppage and kick-in transitions. This matters because these areas are less impacted — or not impacted at all — by the 'stand' rule.

Teams usually escape the contest via broken (not set) play from stoppages.

The 'stand' rule has the biggest impact in set play in the back half of the ground. With the ball already entering in pressurised general play, the 'stand' rule has a far smaller impact on play than in the intercept game — if it has any real impact at all.

The rise in kick-in transition is even more fascinating to consider.

The introduction of a reduced time limit for restarting play has seemingly led teams to becoming more aggressive when bringing the ball back in after a behind.

With teams taking more direct kick-ins, there is more risk of defence's being caught if the ball is turned over. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt Roberts)

The average length of kick-ins is about 3 metres longer in 2026 than three years ago. Kick in targets have also gone more central, with about 40 per cent this year heading up the corridor versus about 25 per cent in 2023.

This has led to a rise in full field transition, and an increased risk of the ball going back the other way.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

By contrast, the ability to move the ball after intercepting has actually declined from last year.

Despite a rash of teams focusing on overlap handball, the overall trend has seen a decline in success of this type of movement.

There's also been a slight decline overall in the ability to move the ball from defensive 50 to the front half of the ground.

This is usually seen as the break-even success measure for teams to achieve in transition.

While the changes to 'stand' may look dramatic, the ability for defenders to trail overlap runners has not changed, nor has the ability for sides to zone off defensively up the ground.

Many of the scintillating highlights that are attributed to stand are more down to poor defending than the "intrusive" new rule.

What hasn't changed dramatically is the number of 50m penalties called due to stand infractions, or general unhappiness with the rule from some quarters of football fandom.

For these people, the only solution is complete overhaul.

In the balance the reality probably sits somewhere in the middle — not truly transformative, nor game destroying.

Stopping the stoppages

This season also brings about a radical change to the game's out of bounds laws. Following the lead of the SANFL and AFLW, the league introduced a "last disposal" rule to encourage play through the corridor and away from the boundaries.

The rule provides a free kick to the opposition where a side clearly disposes the ball via kick or handball before it passes over the boundary line — regardless of intent or whether it is on the full.

The impact of this rule change has been clear — but again with an interesting caveat.

Throw-ins are unsurprisingly down, with approximately five fewer boundary umpire overheads per game. Far more surprising is the drop in ball-ups per game.

The number of around the ground ball-ups has fallen by almost the same amount as throw ins.

The effect for both is quite dramatic through the middle of the ground. For the first time since the start of COVID there have been more stoppages in each arc than outside them.

This has led to individual stoppages being more threatening than ever before.

But as a result of the reduced volume, the stoppage game has also contributed less to the overall scoreboard than ever.

The intercept game remains the bedrock of football, despite the focus of media and fans on the dead-ball contest.

This reduction in stoppages has likely had the biggest impact on the reduction of game time.

Around two and a half minutes on average, or about two minutes on median, has been reduced from game lengths in 2026.

While better than nothing, for most fans this difference would barely be noticeable.

Next changes up?

While length of games is the hot topic of conversation, there is still more to do in trying to prevent head knocks and concussions. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Already focus has begun to turn to the next wave of rule changes.

Chief amongst them is the length of the game.

"We've knocked off 3 minutes per game but is it enough? Probably not," Swann told Channel 7 this week.

More radical options have been tabled to further reduce game time. The most radical of these appears to be a reduction in the length of games to 16 or 18 minutes plus time on — similar to the COVID-impacted 2020 season.

This would likely occur when the league expands its home and away schedule to 24 games per team once Tasmania enters the competition in 2028.

Such a change is popular amongst many football people, but is a harder sell to a cynical and change-fatigued public.

"The COVID quarter (length) felt about right. Now maybe (that's) too short — I don't know. But it keeps the game close. You know I think we want close games," GWS coach Adam Kingsley told the ABC earlier this year.

Kingsley is far from alone in this desire, with premiership coaches Chris Fagan and Chris Scott — as well as former AFLPA president Patrick Dangerfield — calling for similar reforms in previous years.

The unspoken part of these continuous sets of rule changes and interpretation amendments are the bigger fish that are yet to be fried.

For too long the AFL have seemingly been unwilling to substantially address the elephant in the room — that of player safety and head trauma.

For example, when introducing the changes to the ruck engagement rule, Greg Swann was clear about the risks, specifically around PCL injuries to rucks.

"I think you'd be naive to say it's not going to happen — it'll happen," Swann acknowledged at the start of the year.

"If there was a pandemic of them you might change it back."

This approach appears to run contrary to much of the rhetoric around the importance of player safety in the modern game.

When limits to run up and changes of engagement at centre bounces were originally introduced they were backed by a robust base of evidence including academic research.

Instead of leaning on this, the league appears to be throwing caution to the wind for little real gain.

As a whole, injuries still are prevalent across the league, and still often affect the best of the best.

This carries through to the biggest challenge currently facing the sport.

There is still an uneasy tension between the potential for traumatic brain injuries to occur as a result of the sport that players and fans love and the enjoyment of the sport itself.

The AFL and clubs are facing class action suits over past responses to these risks.

As of next season clubs will have mandated limits around contact training following a recommendation from the Victoria State Coroner's inquest into the death of former AFL player Shane Tuck in 2023.

In that inquest the AFL provided a submission that they were considering a limitation at that time as to be guided by medical evidence.

That inquest recommended that the AFL should implement contact training rule restrictions by the commencement of the 2025 AFL/W preseason.

These rules are still yet to come into force.

While there has been a focus on training, there are also the on-field rule-based elements that seemingly have not been publicly considered by recent administrations.

Since the AFL changed the "prior opportunity" element of the holding the ball rule to better reward tacklers in 1996 the number of tackles per game has increased sharply.

In this time there has been a sharp rise in tackles per game and direct contact pressure. Tackle coaches have been introduced across the league, and an intense focus developed on locking the ball in during tackles.

In addition, the evolution of the game has meant that there is an increase of contested marking events — particularly with a third or fourth player present to spoil the ball.

Prior research funded by Monash University and the AFL suggests that these two situations account for the vast majority of head acceleration events in a game of football.

This research suggests that men's AFL players face 5.7 head acceleration events per game, and women's players 3 per game, on average. While this is less than other sports such as American football and rugby union, a reduction of these events should be a priority for the league.

Until these issues are substantively addressed the biggest need for reform will still be on the table, while much of the football landscape is inundated by relatively benign, minor changes.

One can hope that commonsense can be found soon.

World.title: Live: Storm shrug off sluggish start to punish Souths
World.content:
A Daly Cherry-Evans match-clinching field goal and a treble from James Tedesco have propelled the Sydney Roosters to a thrilling 23-22 win over an injury-smashed Newcastle.

In one of the games of the season, the host Knghts were brave throughout, while losing Origin backrower Dylan Lucas to a dislocated and suspected broken left ankle in the first period, and star half Dylan Brown to a worrying knee injury early in the second.

If the title favourites Penrith have wobbled over the weeks around State of Origin, the high-flying Roosters have been building, and Friday night's win was their fifth in a row — the competition's best record in that period.

Tedesco was brilliant for the victors in a wonderful return from the Origin series and concussion.

Newcastle, who were already without injured skipper Kalyn Ponga, have now lost their last three games and remain sixth on the ladder.

That streak aside, they were in this match right until the dying stages and will not be overawed come the big games in September.

The game started at breakneck speed worthy of a finals match, and it took 15 minutes for Tedesco to open the scoring with a brilliant stepping try through the heart of the Newcastle defence.

The Knights bounced back within 10 minutes when Francis Manuleleua, who was immense for his side, burst onto a peach of a Brown pass 30 metres out to power over for his first NRL try.

Undeterred by the injury to Lucas, Newcastle took the lead approaching the half hour mark when hulking middle forward Mat Croker pushed off Tedesco and Reece Robson to score.

The Knights then dominated possession in the next 10 minutes and led 10-6 at the break.

The second term began with more drama when Egan Butcher was placed on report for a shoulder to the head of Manuleleua, who was forced from the field for a head injury assessment.

Tedesco had a double shortly after but when Sam Walker missed the conversion things were all locked up.

Nat Butcher joined his brother on report when an errant swinging arm caught Tyson Frizell on the nose, sending the veteran for a HIA.

Newcastle responded again, Fletcher Hunt sending Dom Young over as the momentum see-sawed once more before Brown's injury, only for Tedesco to nab his third try, backing up a break from Nat Butcher.

Billy Smith put the Roosters in front in the 68th minute but the Knights would not go away and when Manuleleua again burst into the backfield before unleashing Bradman Best, the scores were level with six minutes remaining.

Enter the game's most clutch field goal kicker to seal the win as veteran Cherry-Evans kicked the 31st field goal of his career in the 77th minute.

The Roosters weren't without their injury woes either, losing Egan Butcher with a calf problem and Daniel Tupou with a shoulder complaint in the second half.

AAP

World.title: Sidelined for seven years by lack of funds, Aussie BMX rider now No. 1
World.content:
The road to the top has been anything but smooth for Clarence Valley BMX rider Tahlia Marsh.

But the six-time Australian champion finally got her chance to compete against the world's best and prove she was better than them all.

The 23-year-old left her rivals in her wake to claim top honours in the 17-25 women's cruiser class at this week's BMX Racing World Championships in Brisbane.

"I haven't been to a world title since 2019, purely because of the money and the high cost that goes into [the sport]," the freshly crowned world champion said.

Financial struggles hindered Tahlia Marsh's career but she is now a world champion. (Supplied: Bruce Morris)

Small town girl

Born in the Northern Rivers city of Grafton, Marsh started BMX riding with her two older brothers at the age of seven, and by nine she was riding competitively.

Tahlia Marsh started riding when she was seven years old, following in her brothers' footsteps. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

"Obviously being in a small country town you're not open to a lot of opportunities so I've just got to make it work," she said.

"I do a lot of training by myself, so it's hard to stay motivated, but I did have a goal to come back with a [podium] from the world titles."

At the age of nine, she started competitive BMX racing in the Clarence Valley. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

But national and even world titles do not necessarily bring big financial rewards.

"It's extremely tough, I think that's honestly the biggest issue, that's what drives people away from BMX because they can't make a living out of it," Marsh said.

"I work as a support worker back home, I've got a mortgage, I'm doing university and training full time too.

"So it definitely makes it tough for people with great ability."

Tahlia Marsh did not expect to win the final in Brisbane. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

For many riders without sponsorship, even finding the right bike can be a daunting prospect.

"They'd be around 10 grand, because they're all carbon fibre and high spec," Marsh said.

"They're expensive, but luckily I've got a good sponsor, a bike shop in Brisbane who helps me out a bit."

Just pure joy

Her partner, Jamal Laurie, has been along for the ride and said her determination had never wavered.

Growing up in a small town, Tahlia Marsh had to work hard to make it onto the world stage. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

"She's been working nearly every day for the last couple months leading up to worlds, and to come out with the world title is unreal," he said.

"Coming down that last stretch, every [Australian] in the grandstand stood up cheering for her.

" I looked to my right and her family were in one big huddle tearing up, just pure joy. "

A fairytale day

The result was no fluke.

The 23-year-old entered the final race of the day having won all six prior heats.

The Grafton local won every race throughout the day leading up to the final. (Supplied: Bruce Morris)

"When I made it to the finals and had won all my races, I thought, 'Righto, I think I can do this,' and I can't believe I did," she said.

"There's always a goal of the Olympics, but [right now] I want to get over to America.

"They call it 'the greatest race on earth,' so I'm hoping to go over there in November."

World.title: Brown slams Crows coach for his response to Quaynor booing
World.content:
Former AFL player and LGBTQIA+ advocate Mitch Brown says the culture of footy is ripe for change and more men need to call out bad behaviour after repeated booing of Collingwood's Isaac Quaynor.

A section of the Crows fans at Adelaide Oval for Thursday night's match against Collingwood could be heard booing every time Magpies defender Quaynor got the ball.

Last year, Quaynor had a homophobic slur used against him by Adelaide's Izak Rankine in a game in round 23.

Rankine received a four-match ban after an investigation by the AFL's Integrity Unit.

The ban effectively ended his season as the Crows lost their first two finals while he was suspended.

Matthew Nicks said it was "not ideal how it played out" after some Crows fans repeatedly booed Isaac Quaynor. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

In the aftermath of Thursday's game, Crows coach Matthew Nicks was asked about the incident and the booing.

"The game, it's about entertainment, enjoyment, passion," he replied.

"The game's a passionate game, and sometimes we lose our way in that a little.

"And with the backdrop, and the background leading into this game, it's not ideal the way it played out tonight."

Brown, who last year became the first current or former AFL player to come out as bisexual, told ABC Melbourne on Friday that men needed to "stand up … use our voices and not fear calling things out."

"I look at the best leaders in Australia, and the ones that I admire are the ones that are prepared to put their hand up and say, 'We are part of a problem,'" he said.

"I was really disappointed in the response by Adelaide's coach by not just saying this is completely out of order and [not] seeing the players and coach actually stand up and say we don't want to see this [booing] as part of our game and completely reject that any player should be targeted after they were the victim of abuse.

"When you don't call something out with conviction, silence is deafening.

"And I'm sure Matthew Nicks and coaches … consider themselves strong leaders.

"They say this phrase and we've all heard it: The standards we walk by are the standards we accept."

Crows say behaviour of some fans 'crossed the line'

The Crows released a statement on Friday from club CEO Tim Silvers.

"We … strongly believe there is a line between passionate support and behaviour that falls short of our values and those of the game," he said.

"We want our people to be vocal, engaged and passionate, but to do so respectfully.

"The overwhelming majority of our members and supporters represent the club exceptionally well.

"However, the behaviour of some crossed the line last night. Put simply, it was inappropriate and not good enough.

"Respect for all players, coaches, officials and fellow supporters is paramount, and it is a standard we must all uphold."

Loading Instagram content

The AFL Players Association condemned the actions of the section of fans, saying the game had to be safe for everyone.

"The incessant and targeted booing last night was unacceptable and should never happen," AFLPA CEO James Gallagher said.

"Targeted booing can cause significant harm to the person subjected to it. It also causes harm to others across our football community and signals that the game isn't safe for them.

"Our game must be inclusive and safe for all. Thank you to those who have shown leadership by calling it out."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The AFL also released a statement from CEO Andrew Dillon.

"AFL footy fans are some of the most passionate in world sport, and that passion is one of the things that makes our game so special," he said.

"But the targeted booing last night should not have happened and is not what we want to see in our game.

"We see the best of our fans every single week at matches across the country as they cheer, barrack and support their respective clubs, however, what we saw last night at Adelaide Oval fell well short of that."

World.title: Socceroos star allegedly tests positive for cocaine after speeding
World.content:
Socceroos star Cristian Volpato has allegedly tested positive for cocaine while driving in Sydney.

The 22-year-old was stopped in a BMW Coupe about 1am today, allegedly travelling 109 kilometres an hour on the Anzac Bridge, a 60km/h zone.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test, which allegedly returned a positive result for cocaine.

Mr Volpato was issued with a speeding fine and has had his international driver's licence suspended for six months, meaning he cannot drive in New South Wales.

A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis, with police confirming inquiries were continuing.

Police will allege they stopped Mr Volpato a few hours earlier, about 11pm yesterday, in the same area where he was also speeding.

He was subjected to a roadside alcohol breath test, which returned a negative result.

In a statement, Football Australia said the association "was aware of the allegations involving one of our players."

"We have been in contact with the player and continue to monitor the matter and support the player throughout this process," a Football Australia spokesperson said.

The 22-year-old professional soccer player made headlines when he switched allegiance from Italy to Australia in the World Cup this year.

Football Australia has a strict drug regulation policy managed through Sport Integrity Australia.

Players and officials who test positive to prohibited substances without a valid therapeutic use exemption can be suspended for up to four years.

That can be reduced to three months if the use was out of competition and not performance-related.

World.title: Swimmer praises Rinehart for bonuses amid warning to not thank billionaire
World.content:
Freestyle king Kyle Chalmers has welcomed potential windfalls for Australia's Commonwealth Games swimmers after Gina Rinehart offered up cash bonuses for medals and world records.

Amid a spate of high-profile athlete withdrawals from Glasgow 2026, Dolphins squad members have been given a significant incentive to take part.

Billionaire Rinehart said she would deliver the same bonuses that were on offer in the pool at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

Individual swimmers will pocket $20,000 for a gold medal, $15,000 for silver and $10,000 for bronze and $30,000 for a world record.

Gina Rinehart and swimming legend Dawn Fraser watch on at the 2024 Australian Swimming Trials. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Relay team members will also be rewarded with $7,500 per person for a world record, $5,000 for a gold medal, $3,750 for silver and $2,500 for bronze.

Australians are well placed to cash in, with Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh skipping the Glasgow Games as she and other rivals focus on the ensuing Pan Pacific championships.

The swimming bonanza comes as many athletes in other sports lament a lack of financial support, despite Commonwealth Games Australia (CGA) providing a $5,000 grant to every member of the Glasgow team.

Glasgow was asleep and the Games weren't open as Australia got its first win Australia's first victory of the Commonwealth Games comes in a surprise extra session as the bowlers start before the opening ceremony.

"I'm super grateful to have the support of CGA to get us here, but to be able to have some medal incentive, it gives us a lot more purpose and reason," sprint star Chalmers said ahead of the opening ceremony.

"Otherwise you get a medal and the uniform ... so [I'm] very grateful to have supporters.

"CGA's made this possible, and the Commonwealth Games internationally being able to put it on, but to have some incentive for all of our hard work is crucial, especially for us older athletes."

The 28-year-old said Australia's swimmers were "very lucky" with the level of support they received compared to some other sports.

But the seven-time Commonwealth Games gold medallist said it remained "very challenging" for many swimmers to juggle arduous training schedules with work and study.

"It's a choice you make and I guess you kind of understand the financial position of the sport," Chalmers said.

"But fingers crossed there can be change for the next generation to kind of motivate them to continue to make the sacrifices and choose our sport, just to keep those talented athletes in there."

Petria Thomas has distanced the Commonwealth Games team from Ms Rinehart's bonuses. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Rinehart's bonus scheme was announced by Swimming Queensland, of which the mining magnate is patron, while Australia's chef de mission Petria Thomas distanced CGA from it.

"That's a separate arrangement and it's not something that Commonwealth Games Australia is involved in whatsoever," former swimmer Thomas said.

"Good luck to the swimmers, I guess. They have someone backing that performance, but that's a separate matter for them."

A statement from Commonwealth Games Australia "commended" Rinehart for her support of the swimmers, while stressing existing sponsors had committed millions of dollars to get the whole 255-strong team across all sports to Glasgow.

"Mrs Rinehart and her companies are not Australian Team partners," a spokesperson said.

A report in the Sydney Morning Herald today said swimmers had been told not to thank Rinehart when talking to the media after swimming.

Shortly before flying to Scotland, a number of swimmers, including Shayna Jack and Sienna Toohey, posted messages on social media thanking the mining magnate for allowing them to "chase [their] dreams".

Loading Instagram content

The bonuses come on top of annual payments Rinehart makes to many of Australia's top-tier swimmers.

Athletes who win multiple medals will receive a payment for every medal they win.

Your guide to every day of the Comm Games in Australian time Here's the full schedule of every day of the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games with all times and days in AEST.

In a statement, Rinehart said the bonuses were a way of Australia showing appreciation.

"There is something very uplifting about seeing an Australian athlete stand on the podium while our flag is raised," Rinehart said.

Meanwhile, Katarina Johnson-Thompson heads a list of nine members of the England athletics squad that pulled out of the Games on the morning of the opening ceremony.

Four more Olympic medallists – Dina Asher-Smith, Daryll Neita, Matthew Hudson-Smith and Amber Anning – are also out.

Like Keely Hodgkinson, the Olympic 800 metres champion who did not pursue selection, the injured and "gutted" Johnson-Thompson indicated she would switch her focus to the European championships in Birmingham next month.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
